items.fullDescription: Call for Papers From its inception, cinema has transcended borders through the movement of people, capital, narratives, and visual technology. However, over the past two decades, the term transnational cinema has evolved into one of the most influential and contested frameworks in film studies. Scholars such as Elizabeth Ezra, Terry Rowden, Deborah Shaw, Will Higbee, and Song Hwee Lim have variously expanded, critiqued, and redefined the concept, emphasizing its aesthetic, political, and industrial dimensions and prompting new questions about its theoretical and pedagogical implications. While these approaches have illuminated the circulation of films, filmmakers, and spectators across borders, they have also raised questions about the continuing relevance of the national cinema framework and the analytical boundaries of the transnational itself. This symposium revisits the concept of transnational cinema at a moment when two distinct currents seem bound for collision. On the one hand, global migration, digital media, the global climate catastrophe, geopolitical conflicts, and transregional collaborations have blurred distinctions between the local and the global, as well as the national and the transnational. On the other hand, isolationism, authoritarianism, and protectionism have re-erected physical and ideological borders across the globe. Is the world more or less transnational as a result of these competing impulses? We invite proposals that address theoretical, historical, or pedagogical questions, such as: How can the familiar concept of transnational cinema elucidate emergent and unfamiliar problems in the contemporary landscape? How do we define and teach transnational cinema now? Is transnational cinema best understood as a framework, an approach, a mode of filmmaking, or a category of world cinema? How does transnational cinema intersect with, or diverge from, national, world, and global cinema theories? What are the political, aesthetic, or ethical stakes of emphasizing transnationality in film studies today? We welcome both theoretical interventions and case studies from diverse regions and traditions. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: • Theories and definitions of transnational cinema • Pedagogical approaches to transnational cinema • Feminist, queer, and trans approaches to transnational cinema • Transnational authorship and stardom • Memory, trauma, and postmemory in transnational film • Digital technologies and virtual transnational spaces • Streaming platforms and global distribution • Cinemas of diaspora, exile, and migration • Cross-border activism and solidarity through film • Environmental and ecological transnationalism • Film policy, censorship, and cultural diplomacy • Transnational labor, precarity, and creative economies • International film festivals and global circulation • Archival and historiographical approaches to transnational film • Politics of translation, dubbing, and subtitling • Regional and transregional filmmaking practices • Anti-colonial, postcolonial, and de-colonial aesthetics and narratives • Global Hollywood and transnational co-productions• Transnational spectatorship and global audiences • State, statelessness, and belonging in transnational cinema • Borders, border-crossings, and redefinitions of home • Transnational genres • De-Westernizing film studies Presenters will be invited to submit completed papers for consideration in an edited collection or special issue developed from the symposium. Proposals (250-300 words) and short bios (100 words) should be submitted by June 1st, 2026, using this Google Form: https://forms.gle/R7Jw98KpMEc7BAHo6 For questions, please contact the organizing committee at ahtfilmstudies@utdallas.edu.

items.fullDescription: Call for Proposals Transformative Synergies Harmonizing the Future: Interdisciplinary Pathways for a Resilient Society Transformative Synergies brings together faculty, scholars, graduate students and practitioners to explore how disciplines can intersect to address the complex challenges shaping our world. As technology, public health, social policy, education and the arts continue to evolve, meaningful solutions increasingly require collaboration across traditional academic boundaries. This conference invites researchers and creators to examine the connections among arts, business, STEM, health and education and consider how these fields can work together to build a more resilient society. Submit Your Work We welcome proposals that explore innovative ideas, research and creative approaches related to the conference theme, including: Pedagogy for a New Era: Interdisciplinary curriculum design, trauma-informed education and the future of the R2 research institution Creative Technologies: Digital preservation, emerging technologies and the ethics of the human-machine interface Social Equity & Policy: Research addressing systemic health and educational disparities Health-Arts Nexus: Narrative medicine, art therapy and the role of the humanities in public health Sustainability & STEM: Environmental science, Indigenous knowledge and resilient urban design These topics are not exhaustive. Proposals that explore meaningful connections across disciplines are encouraged. Graduate Student Symposium The conference will feature a Graduate Student Panel designed to give emerging scholars an opportunity to share research in progress, completed projects, theses and dissertations. The session will provide a supportive environment for scholarly feedback, interdisciplinary dialogue and networking with scholars from across institutions. Proposal Formats We welcome: Individual papers Panel discussions Poster presentations Creative and multimedia works Workshops and interactive sessions Who Should Submit? Graduate students, faculty, researchers and practitioners from all disciplines are encouraged to submit original work that engages with the conference theme. Proposal Guidelines Proposals should be 300-600 words, depending on disciplinary standards, and address: Title - A concise, descriptive title that engages an interdisciplinary audience. Purpose and Central Question/Problem - The primary aim of the work. Conceptual, Theoretical or Disciplinary Framework - The intellectual foundation of the work. Methods, Materials or Creative Approach - How the work was conducted or developed. Findings, Claims or Scholarly Contribution - The work's intellectual contribution. Interdisciplinary Significance and Broader Impact - The relevance of the work beyond a single discipline. For panels, submit an individual abstract for each paper. How Proposals Are Reviewed All proposals will undergo peer review and will be evaluated based on: Clarity and coherence Scholarly rigor Methodological or interpretive soundness Originality and contribution to knowledge Interdisciplinary engagement and accessibility Relevance to the conference theme Conference Information Nov. 8-10, 2026 The Hotel at the University of Maryland Discounted rates are available for conference attendees. Ready to Contribute? Share your research, scholarship or creative work with an interdisciplinary community exploring new approaches to the challenges of the 21st century. Submit your proposal: graduateschool@bowiestate.edu Transformative Synergies Arts, Business, STEM, Health & Education for a Changing World Bowie State University | The Graduate School

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS / COLLEGE ENGLISH ASSOCIATION ANNUAL CONFERENCE APRIL 1-3, 2027 / ST LOUIS, MO SUBMISSION SITE IS OPEN: https://www.conftool.pro/cea2027 DEADLINE: 11/01/2026 For its 2027 annual conference,the College English Association (CEA) invites proposals for papers and panels that explore the theme of "Gateways" and their significance in literature, criticism, and pedagogy. we also encourage proposals on GENERAL TOPICS, including AMERICAN, BRITISH, AND WORLD LITERATURES. DON'T KNOW CEA? YOU SHOULD! In December 1938, a group of young academics attending the MLA convention in New York took on the biggest name in their field-the MLA. They chose to forge a new path by organizing into the College English Association and offering a voice to "the college English teachers of America." Their aim was to upend the scholar-teacher dynamic by recognizing teaching as paramount. Today, more than eight decades later, the CEA continues in that same spirit. At our core, we strive to meet these goals through two venues: our Annual CEA Conference and our journal, The CEA Critic. With over 400 active members and a collection of regional affiliates, the CEA welcomes teacher-scholars at all levels-from graduate students to emeritus faculty-who share our belief that teaching is central to who we are and what we do. CEA WELCOMES GRADUATE STUDENTS As always, the CEA extends a special invite to students pursuing a graduate degree, not only to attend the conference but to submit their presentations to the CEA Outstanding Graduate Student Paper competition. The award carries a grand prize of $250 and publication of the winning essay in the CEA's flagship journal, THE CEA CRITIC. NEW FOR 2027:UNDERGRADUATE ROUNDTABLES CEA invites undergraduates to enjoy the conference experience by sharing their work in flash-essay roundtable sessions. A flash essay is a highly condensed, high-impact presentation (typically 300-1000 words, or 2-5 minutes) that delivers core research findings, a specific argument, or a compelling narrative. During roundtable sessions, the speakers and audience engage in discussion with each other in more of an open conversation than in traditional panels. Learn more about roundtables here: https://cea-web.org/about-roundtables. LEARN MORE: https://cea-web.org/cea-2027-%2F-st-louis

items.fullDescription: CFP: Let's Dance: Musicals, Dance, Bodies and Popular Culture PopCRN Online Conference 26-27 August 2027 Popular culture dances. Across stages and screens, ballrooms and nightclubs, streets and stadiums, dance has produced some of popular culture's most enduring images of bodies in motion. From musicals and music videos to television, theatre, popular music and sport, dance crosses cultural forms and national boundaries, continually reinventing how bodies move, perform and become visible. Dance is rarely only entertainment. Dancing bodies carry meanings about beauty, sexuality, gender, race, class, youth, age, disability, nation and cultural identity. They can communicate desire, resistance, freedom and belonging, while also being trained, disciplined, watched, judged and commodified. Popular culture determines which bodies appear graceful or awkward, desirable or excessive, disciplined or unruly, and which bodies are permitted to occupy the centre of the floor. The history of popular dance is therefore also a history of inclusion, exclusion and cultural ownership. Dance forms emerge from particular communities before travelling between cultures, nations and media. Movement can preserve cultural memory, assert identity and create community, but it can also be appropriated, commercialised and detached from the people who created it. These histories raise questions about who creates movement, who owns it, who profits from it and whose contributions remain visible. Dance also makes power visible through the body. Behind apparently effortless performance lie labour, repetition, discipline, endurance and sometimes pain. Ideas of technical perfection, beauty, athleticism and bodily control shape who is recognised as a dancer and how dancing bodies are valued. Dance can reinforce expectations surrounding gender, race, class, age, size and ability, while also providing a means of challenging them. The dance floor can be a political and social space. Dance creates communities, produces collective identities and allows bodies to occupy spaces from which they may otherwise be excluded. Social dance, club cultures, street dance and dance crazes transform audiences into participants and make movement part of everyday popular culture. Dance can be intimate and collective, regulated and rebellious, commercial and political. Who leads, who follows, who watches, who judges and who is allowed onto the floor all matter. Dance continually crosses boundaries between cultural forms. Choreography moves between theatre and cinema, popular music and music video, television and digital media, concert performance and sport. At its largest scale, it transforms individual bodies into mass spectacle, bringing together celebrity, commerce, national identity and collective participation. These crossings also unsettle distinctions between dance, athleticism, performance and entertainment. Let's Dance: Musicals, Dance, Bodies and Popular Culture invites papers exploring dance as representation, performance, narrative, labour, pleasure, identity and embodied politics. We welcome historical and contemporary approaches across film, television, theatre, literature, popular music, sport, celebrity culture, digital media and everyday life. We are particularly interested in intersectional approaches considering how race, gender, sexuality, class, age, disability, nation and cultural identity shape who dances, how bodies are represented and what movement is permitted to mean. The conference asks how popular culture teaches us to understand the dancing body. What happens when movement crosses racial, cultural and national boundaries? How are dancing bodies disciplined, sexualised, celebrated, ridiculed or excluded? When does dance create community, and when does it reinforce hierarchy? Who owns movement and choreography? Who gets to dance for the nation? What happens when bodies expected to remain at the margins claim the centre of the floor? At its centre, Let's Dance asks one overarching question: who gets to dance, and what can the dancing body tell us about power, identity and belonging in popular culture? Possible papers might include: Making the Dancing Body: training, rehearsal and discipline; virtuosity and amateurism; bodily labour, pain and endurance; beauty and perfection; the professional dancer; auditions and competition; the ageing dancing body; The Red Shoes (1948), A Chorus Line (1975 stage musical, 1985 film), Fame (1980), Black Swan (2010) and Dance Moms (2011 to 2019). Race, Culture and Ownership: Black dance traditions and popular culture; tap, jazz and segregation; Lindy Hop and the Savoy Ballroom; disco and ballroom culture; breaking and hip hop; Indigenous dance and cultural sovereignty; Bollywood and diaspora; appropriation, ownership and cultural memory; Stormy Weather (1943), West Side Story (1961, 2021), Paris Is Burning (1990), Pose (2018 to 2021) and Hamilton (2015). Gender, Sexuality and Desire: the dancing female body; dancing masculinity; queer dance cultures; drag, camp and performance; sexualisation and respectability; gender transgression; romance and bodily intimacy; Gentlemen Prefer Blondes (1953), Saturday Night Fever (1977), The Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975), Dirty Dancing (1987), Billy Elliot (2000), RuPaul's Drag Race (2009 to present) and Barbie (2023). Class, Work and Social Mobility: dance as labour; working class dancing bodies; dance and fantasies of escape and mobility; professional ambition; unemployment and masculinity; elite and popular dance cultures; unequal access to training and opportunity; Saturday Night Fever (1977), Flashdance (1983), The Full Monty (1997), Billy Elliot (2000), Step Up (2006) and Swing Time (2016). Who Gets to Dance?: age, disability, body size and bodily difference; exclusion and belonging; normative ideals of the dancer; humiliation and judgement; visibility and the right to perform; Hairspray (1988, 2007), The Full Monty (1997), Billy Elliot (2000), Finding Your Feet (2017), Dumplin' (2018) and Wicked (2024). Dance Floors and Dancing Together: ballrooms, nightclubs, streets, schools, weddings and stages; social dance and dance crazes; dancing alone and together; dance floors as spaces of freedom, desire and exclusion; and collective pleasure; The Twist (1960), Footloose (1984), Strictly Ballroom (1992), Pose (2018 to 2021) and Dancing Queen (1976). Dance, Politics and Protest: dancing as resistance; regulation and censorship; race and segregation; religion and morality; national identity; protest choreography; public space and collective movement; Dancing in the Street (1964), Footloose (1984), Hairspray (1988, 2007), Sarafina! (1992) and Hamilton (2015). From Stage to Screen: vaudeville and the Hollywood musical; Busby Berkeley and mass choreography; Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers; Gene Kelly and dancing masculinity; the decline and revival of the screen musical; choreography across theatre, cinema and television; Singin' in the Rain (1952), Moulin Rouge! (2001), Chicago (2002), Glee (2009 to 2015), La La Land (2016) and Wicked (2024). Dance on Television: dance and the construction of youth culture; Black dance and cultural visibility; television variety and the spectacular body; reality television, competition and judgement; amateur and professional dancers; drag and choreographed gender performance; musical television and belonging; American Bandstand (1952 to 1989), Soul Train (1971 to 2006), Solid Gold (1980 to 1988), Dancing with the Stars (2004 to present), So You Think You Can Dance (2005 to present), RuPaul's Drag Race (2009 to present). Dance, Celebrity and Mass Spectacle: music video and the choreographed pop star; concert performance and celebrity bodies; cheerleading and athletic spectacle; stadium choreography; bodily endurance and audience participation; Michael Jackson's Thriller (1983), Madonna's Vogue (1990), the Super Bowl halftime show (1993 to present as a major pop spectacle), Bring It On (2000), Beyoncé's Homecoming (2019), Taylor Swift's The Eras Tour (2023 to 2024) and breaking at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games. Dance Across Popular Culture: dance in film, television, theatre, literature, popular music and music video; dance memoir and fiction; reality television and competition; songs about dancing; advertising and celebrity culture; digital choreography, viral dances and social media; the circulation of movement between media, communities, bodies and audiences; and the changing boundaries between dance, sport, spectacle and everyday cultural practice. Registration is free. The conference is welcoming of early career researchers, postgraduates, Indigenous scholars, people with diverse identities, and industry experts or food practitioners. Please send any queries to popcrn@une.edu.au · Submit here - https://unesurveys.au1.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_8jjzaWnS732QsFE · Register here - https://unesurveys.au1.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_7TGWUYZidtlxVLU

items.fullDescription: Abstract: This panel reexamines life writing in the age of Generative AI, asking who controls the conditions under which individuals narrate their own lives. Submissions reflecting on how AI corporations and Generative AI models are reshaping life writing practices across textual, digital, and visual formats, or on the consequences of such practices for authorship, equity, and cultural power, are especially welcome. Full CFP: Generative AI has fundamentally changed how we think, articulate, and write. However, access to AI is not equitable, and its outputs frequently fail to account for diverse lived experiences and reflect biases. The corporations developing AI models are agents actively reshaping how we perceive, think, interpret, and articulate our identities and experiences. This panel examines what that means for Life Writing - defined broadly to include textual, digital, and visual formats - where individuals reflect, narrativize, and present their lived experiences in public-facing contexts. Submissions engaging the conference theme, "Our Ruling Classes: Culture, Power and Conflict," are especially welcome. The panel welcomes submissions that explore (but are not limited to): a) Questions of authorship for AI-assisted/AI-mediated life writings b) The aesthetics and formal transformations in the practice of Life Writing in the age of Generative AI c) Life Writings produced by or attributed to Generative AI models d) The 'Author' Persona in AI-generated/AI-mediated Life Writing e) Autoethnographic explorations of writing life with AI f) Reader/Audience response to AI-mediated/AI-generated life writings g) Questions of ethics, trust, and safety, when narrating life with AI h) Impacts of AI-mediated life writing on individuals from vulnerable and marginalized communities, diverse gender identities, racial, and cultural communities i) "Permanent Memory" of AI models and archival of individual identities j) Translation, multilingualism, and cultural limitations of Generative AI in supporting Life Writing activities Note: > Please submit your proposals only via the link: https://pamla.ballastacademic. com/Home/S/20174 > Extended Deadline to submit proposals is June 30, 2026 ; early submissions are encouraged. > The 2026 PAMLA Conference is entirely in person , in Seattle, WA, with no provision for virtual or hybrid presentations . > Please check the PAMLA website for dates and additional information

items.fullDescription: Italian Teaching Symposium 2026 - II edition "Creative Pathways in Italian Language and Culture Teaching" September 25-26, 2026 St. Jerome's University (University of Waterloo) & online Inspired by the theme chosen for the XXVI Week of the Italian Language in the World, "Lingua geniale: ideare, progettare, creare con l'italiano", we are pleased to announce the second edition of the Italian Teaching Symposium, once again endorsed by the Canadian Association for Italian Studies (CAIS). Building on the success of its inaugural 2025 edition, which welcomed more than fifty participants - including presenters, chairs, and attendees from both academia and cultural institutions - this year's symposium will take place on September 25-26, 2026, at St. Jerome's University, federated with the University of Waterloo (Ontario, Canada). While primarily designed as an in-person event, limited opportunities for remote participation may be available. The second edition of the Italian Teaching Symposium, Creative Pathways in Italian Language and Culture Teaching, aims to bring together scholars, researchers, language educators, teacher trainers, graduate students, and practitioners interested in exploring three interconnected dimensions of Italian language education: imagine, design, and create. As Marcel Danesi (2025) observes, "the study of creativity crosses all disciplinary boundaries", making creativity a particularly productive lens through which to examine the teaching and learning of Italian language and culture. This resonates well with the theme of the XXVI Week of the Italian Language in the World, inspired by the newly established Directorate General for Growth and Export Promotion of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which highlights the creative potential of Italian as a language capable of fostering ideas, innovation, and intercultural dialogue. In this sense, teaching Italian extends beyond the transmission of grammar and pronunciation to encompass cultural mediation, collaboration, and engagement with diverse forms of expression. In this context, we invite proposals that reflect on how this perspective inspires - or challenges - instructors to adopt creative and unconventional approaches to course design, including content, activities, teaching methods, and assessment. In addition to traditional paper presentations, the 2026 edition of the Italian Teaching Symposium will introduce a new hands-on session format designed to foster practical exchange, experimentation, and collaborative learning. These interactive sessions will give participants the opportunity to showcase classroom activities, digital tools and apps, pedagogical resources, multimodal projects, creative assignments, community-engaged initiatives, assessment tools, or other innovative practices implemented in Italian language and culture courses. This format is intended to encourage active engagement and discussion, allowing attendees to learn directly from colleagues' experiences and to leave the symposium with practical ideas and materials that can be adapted to their own teaching contexts. Exploring how Italian language and culture can be reimagined as spaces for creativity, identity formation, intercultural dialogue, and social engagement -new perspectives on Italian language, culture, and identity? -intercultural competence and global citizenship through Italian studies? -new imaginaries of Italy,?Italianness, and Italian-speaking communities? -heritage learners, multilingualism, and transnational Italian identities -the future of Italian studies and language programs in changing educational landscapes -reimagining the role of Italian language education in contemporary society? ? Examining the pedagogical, technological, and curricular frameworks that shape innovative Italian language education -curriculum development and innovative pedagogical models? -project-based learning in Italian language education? -multilingual and intercultural learning environments? -educational technologies, AI, and digital course design? -assessment design and innovative evaluation practices -Italian for specific purposes (LSP) and professional communication? -international collaborations and virtual exchange projects? ? Create? Investigating creative practices, cultural production, and multimodal forms of expression in Italian language and culture teaching. -creative writing and storytelling in Italian language?pedagogy? -language learning through music, performance, theatre, cinema,?and?visual arts?? -literature in the Italian classroom?as a tool for language acquisition and cultural?awareness? -student-generated content and multimodal?literacy? -digital creativity and media production -community-engaged learning, public humanities projects, digital creativity, and collaborations beyond the classroom? ? Submission Guidelines? We invite proposals for individual papers (15 minutes), thematic panels (90 minutes), and hands-on workshops (approximately 30 minutes) designed to engage participants in innovative pedagogical practices, classroom activities, digital tools and apps, teaching resources, and creative approaches to Italian language and culture education.? Submissions should include the presentation title, author name(s) and affiliation(s), an abstract in English or Italian of no more than 300 words, and a contact e-mail address. Proposals should be submitted via this form by July 25 , 2026. Notification of acceptance will be sent by July 24, 2026. Questions may be addressed to the symposium organizers, Gianmarco Bocchi (gbocchi@uwaterloo.ca) and Alessia Ursella (aursella@uoguelph.ca).?

items.excerpt: Date: October 10-11, 2026 Location: SMU Main Campus, Dallas, TX Theme: Movement & Borderlands Abstract Submission Deadline: August 28, 2026 Keynotes: Dr. Tim Bowman & Dr. Elda María Román Graduate students of Southern Methodist University's Departments of English, History, and Anthropology, in collaboration with the Moody School of Advanced...
items.fullDescription: Date: October 10-11, 2026 Location: SMU Main Campus, Dallas, TX Theme: Movement & Borderlands Abstract Submission Deadline: August 28, 2026 Keynotes: Dr. Tim Bowman & Dr. Elda María Román Graduate students of Southern Methodist University's Departments of English, History, and Anthropology, in collaboration with the Moody School of Advanced Studies, Dedman College Interdisciplinary Institute, and the department of English, have collaborated to hold the third annual Engaging Research Across the Humanities (ERAH) Conference at SMU from October 10-October 11, 2026. ERAH 2026 will prioritize the development of interdisciplinary connections and aims to foster a supportive environment for both graduate students and advanced undergraduates engaged in strong research. There will be special emphasis placed on creating opportunities for participants with limited or no prior conference experience. The theme for ERAH 2026 is Movement & Borderlands. If you have any questions, please email arundhatig@smu.edu. Borders simultaneously construct and limit meaning. By demarcating entities, we hold the power to define space and identity. In the same manner, those entities are restricted to oppositional definitions. What does it mean to occupy borderlands, to move across them and through them? How is the deconstruction of borders, or reconceptualization of definitional demarcation, itself an act of meaning-making that exists without opposition? How do borderlands complicate cultural conceptions rooted in duality? How does movement across and through borderlands produce opportunity for new forms of meaning-making not rooted in hard lines and limitations? This year's theme asks us to think critically about the roles of both movement and borderlands in our respective disciplines by considering these questions and others. We invite you to consider the roles of both movement and borderlands within the works you study-be it literary works, historical archives, etc.-as well as how pervasive disciplinary paradigms shape the ways in which you approach your scholarship. Possible topics may include but are not limited to: Migration, mobility, and displacement Citizenship and belonging Racial, ethnic, national, religious identity Borders as constructs Frontiers Artistic and embodied movement Indigenous perspectives on imposed borders Nationalism and borderlands Environmental and ecological borders Linguistic borders Tourism and global circulation We invite abstracts of 200-250 words for both individual presentations and fully-constructed panels (3-4 speakers). Papers in STEM fields that clearly articulate relevance to the theme are welcome. Full-panel proposals will be given priority. Panel proposals must include a 200-250 word proposal for the panel in addition to abstracts for each individual participant. A select number of travel grants will be awarded on a competitive basis for those traveling more than 100 miles. To qualify for a travel grant, you must submit your application by August 14, 2026. Further details will be included in your registration sign-up. Please submit abstracts via the following google form link: https://tinyurl.com/2026ERAH

items.excerpt: India's civilizational ethos is deeply rooted in its multilingual and multicultural fabric, where translation has enabled the circulation of ideas, texts, and knowledge across regions and traditions. Etymologically understood as "carrying across," translation in the 21st century extends beyond linguistic transfer to become a critical and interpretive prac...
items.fullDescription: India's civilizational ethos is deeply rooted in its multilingual and multicultural fabric, where translation has enabled the circulation of ideas, texts, and knowledge across regions and traditions. Etymologically understood as "carrying across," translation in the 21st century extends beyond linguistic transfer to become a critical and interpretive practice. A. K. Ramanujan, in his writings, draws attention to translation's context-sensitive nature, while G. N. Devy highlights the complex linguistic and cultural histories within which translation operates in India. Seen in this light, translation involves negotiation, re-articulation, and the making of new meanings within specific cultural settings. Practices such as transcreation, adaptation, and interpretation highlight the creative potential of translation. At the same time, the increasing use of machine translation and AI-based tools has introduced another dimension, making translation faster and more accessible, while also raising questions about accuracy and interpretation. In view of these varied contexts, practices, and concerns, this seminar aims to provide a platform for students, teachers, and researchers to reflect on the evolving role of translation in contemporary India across literary, academic, and everyday contexts. It seeks to bring together diverse perspectives on both the challenges and possibilities of translating Indian languages in the present day. Submissions are invited on the following themes: Translation in the classroom: pedagogy and practice Translation and cultural contexts: negotiation and interpretation Translating literary and non-literary texts Translation and cultural pluralism Translation across media: cinema, OTT, and digital platforms AI in translation: possibilities and challenges Translation, representation, and questions of voice Adaptation, transcreation, and rewriting Ethics and responsibilities in translation Emerging trends and research in translation studies The seminar is being held in Hybrid Mode. Register here: https://forms.gle/zYjXGehoDCu85UNm7

items.fullDescription: Pendant la période de l'Indochine française, les premiers vietnamiens sont acheminés en Nouvelle-Calédonie en tant que travailleurs sous-contrat dans les mines de nickel. Cette période marque en parallèle la rébellion très présente des autochtones de l'île - les Kanak - face à la dépossession territoriale des colons français. Le refus de participer à l'industrie minière d'un groupe favorise l'expatriation de l'autre sur l'archipel en pleine ère de la colonisation française dans plusieurs colonies. Le roi tonkinois Ham Nghi, à l'âge de 18 ans, a été placé en exil en Algérie après des années de mouvements de résistance contre la puissance coloniale française. Son expulsion fait écho à celle de la Reine malgache Ranavalona III, qui a eu lieu après l'annexion de Madagascar par la France en 1896. L'ensemble de l'empire français, étendu de l'Indochine à l'Afrique insulaire, est sujet à la déportation dans la plus grande colonie de peuplement. Ce réseau de déportation des colonies liées met en avant la question des outils de domination employés par le système colonial. Malgré les différentes populations colonisées, la stratégie de domination s'applique d'une certaine façon. **** Dans le cadre académique au sein des études francophones et françaises, nous voyons souvent des pistes de spécialisation distinctes, telles que les études européennes, les études caribéennes, et les études postcoloniales francophones. Les cours d'histoire et de littérature offrent également des réflexions particulières selon une région spécifique ainsi qu'une époque donnée. L'objectif de former les futurs chercheurs dans des domaines précis, faute d'études approfondies sur les caractéristiques transcontinentales, risque de faire oublier qu'au coeur de l'histoire de l'un est tissée celle de l'autre. Cette imbrication transnationale et transcommunautaire, inévitable soit-elle, est due à la fois aux déplacements migratoires, à l'exil d'après-guerre, et à la mobilisation de la force de travail par le système capitaliste et colonial. Lorsque l'on met en évidence ce lien intrinsèque entre des événements, on fait émerger un réseau transcolonial qui lie l'Afrique, l'Asie, et/ou l'Europe. Ce réseau nous oblige à réfléchir à l'interconnexion de l'un à l'autre, d'une communauté spécifique à une autre soi-disant éloignée. Dans le contexte du monde d'aujourd'hui, une telle conscience de l'interconnexion des histoires coloniales peut susciter des réflexions : Peut-on vraiment ignorer le combat de l'autre ? Quels seront les enjeux ? Communications à envoyer soit en anglais, soit en français.

items.fullDescription: The sea and marine life are often considered as pillars of cultural heritage, identity, and collective memories in Portugal (Lourenço 2001; Lourenço 2014). From the historical milestones of the sixteenth century transoceanic navigation (Cortesão 1978) to literary production (Avelar 2024), the ocean has shaped the national imagination of Portugal (Tomás 2013). As Antonio Barreto writes: "Heritage is a human creation and the results from history and culture. But there are natural realities that are transformed, through history, culture, and technology into heritage. Such is the case of the sea for the Portuguese" (2019: 15). As a form of heritage, this connection extends to gastronomy and, in a particularly profound way, to the musical sphere (Simões 2013: 45-62; Sardo 2013: 44-64). From fado, with its narratives of longing and loss, to the songs that gave rhythm to the the fishermen's daily work, the Portuguese musical repertoire has functioned as a living archive of human interaction with the environment. However, there is nothing natural or essentialist about this Portuguese relationship with the sea, for it is an imaginary that has been constructed and continously negotiated across historical periods, which also bears the imprint of colonialism (João 2015: 119-147; El-Shawan Castelo-Branco et al 2003: 73-142). More dramatically, the transformations driven by climate change and unsustainable industrial fishing in the twenty-first century threaten not only biodiversity (Ramos-Pereira 2004: 26-43), but also the cultural practices linked to it - a topic that still requires greater attention in schoarly research. In any case, beyond its material and economic dimensions, the sea in Portugal remains a space of imagination and transformation. As evoked in the songs of José Afonso, the sea is not just a site of identity and homecoming, but also a place of alterity and utopia. By singing of the sea, we evoke the possibility of a new era, in which culture and nature meet once again in a shared project of humanity - a vision that also resonates with the notion of the Blue Humanities (Mentz 2023; Oppermann 2019: 443-461). This call seeks to explore the intersection between what we have inherited and what we must protect. Therefore, we invite researchers, artists, and cultural practitioners to reflect on how these environmental changes reshape the meaning of the arts and their role as vehicles of identity and resistance. Papers are welcome on the following topics, amongst others: The sea as a cultural construct in Portuguese music and the arts; Music, critique, and resistance to climate crises in Portugal; Intersections between literature, music, and environmental heritage; Representations of the sea and music in literature and written culture; Music, sound, identity, and the politics of ocean memory; Collective memory, local identities, and soundscapes; The sea in film, the media, and popular culture; Folklore, folk groups, and the preservation of intangible cultural heritage; Coloniality and decoloniality of contemporary maritime identity; Transcultural and postcolonial perspectives on the maritime imaginary; Blue Humanities and music as an environmental archive; Resistance, utopia, and sound activism in the face of climate change; Tourism and heritage preservation of coastal musical cultures; Technology, marine sciences, and music; Ocean ethics, music, and maritime imaginaries; Phenomenology, aesthetics, listening, and maritime experience. Submission Guidelines Proposals should be sent to the email: cecc.fch@ucp.pt, and include paper title, A 300-word abstract in Portuguese or in English should be submitted for a 20-minute presentation, including a provisional title, a brief biographical note (max. 150 words) and contact details. Contributions may be in Portuguese or English. Abstract submission deadline: July 31, 2026 Notification of acceptance: September 15, 2026 After acceptance of abstracts, participants must register for the conference. Registration Fees and Deadlines The registration fee includes coffee breaks and conference materials. Early bird registration (September 16-30): €75 (student) | €100 (non-student) Regular registration (October 1-20): €100 (student) | €150 (non-student) Keynote Speakers Diana Gonçalves, Catholic University of Portugal Susana Sardo, University of Aveiro Organizers Alyse Kaweng Fan e Thales Reis Alecrim Scientific Committee Ana Matoso, CECC Ana Margarida Abrantes, CECC Carla Ganito, CECC Joana Moura, CECC Mário Avelar, CECC Nuno Amado, CECC Patrícia Anzini, CECC Pedro A. items.fullDescription: Abstract : This roundtable explores contemporary directions in life writing, biography, and memoir, with a particular interest in how we narrate the self amidst evolving issues of identity, culture, and power. We welcome both traditional scholarly essays and creative nonfiction/memoir submissions accompanied by a brief meta-analysis. Potential topics include, but are not limited to, autoethnography, digital self-representation, intersectional approaches to life writing, and the emerging impacts of technological shifts-such as generative AI-on authorship and equity. Desctription : How do we articulate, preserve, and present our lived experiences in an era marked by rapid cultural and technological change? Aligning with the conference theme, "Our Ruling Classes: Culture, Power and Conflict," this roundtable invites participants to investigate the shifting landscape of life writing across textual, digital, and visual formats. To foster a vibrant, multi-voiced dialogue, we encourage submissions from a wide range of perspectives, including traditional literary criticism, biographical studies, and creative pieces that feature a reflective or meta-analytical component. Presenters will deliver brief, 10-to-12-minute talks to maximize time for collective discussion. Link for submissions: https://pamla.ballastacademic.com/Home/S/20174 Submission Deadline: June 30, 2026 Conference format: In Person, in Seattle. No provision for virtual presentations If you have any queries, please reach out to the undersigned: Dr. Meghna Gangadharan Presiding Officer, "Narrating the Self Today" Email: phd1901261010@alum.iiti.ac.in

items.fullDescription: Building Bridges: Preparing for Global Business (39th Annual IATEFL BESIG Conference) When : Friday, November 20, 2026 (13.00 CET / 12.00 UK time) - Sunday, November 22, 2026 (14.00 CET / 13.00 UK time) Venue : Hotel Flemings Wien Stadthalle in Vienna, Austria. Call for Proposals Business English education sits at the intersection of education, professional communication, and global social change. In a world shaped by geopolitical tensions, economic inequalities, technological disruption, and cultural polarization, communication across cultural contexts is both more necessary and more complex than ever. Business English therefore involves more than teaching linguistic skills for the workplace; it also prepares learners to deal with cultural diversity, power structures, and ethical decision-making in international professional contexts. Effective professional communication today requires not only exchanging information but also negotiating meaning, building trust, and collaborating across cultures and perspectives. Business English courses support university students, vocational learners, and professionals in developing communicative competence, intercultural awareness, and confidence in multilingual workplaces. In many contexts, this work involves collaboration with corporate partners and engagement with current workplace practices, while also encouraging critical reflection on whose voices are heard in professional communication. The role of the business English educator is therefore to help learners bridge multiple gaps: between education and professional practice, between various cultures, and between local experiences and global systems. In a fragmented and rapidly changing world, business English education can help create spaces for inclusive, responsible, and effective professional communication. This year's conference invites contributions that explore how business English education can respond to these challenges and build the bridges needed for meaningful intercultural understanding. We particularly welcome contributions that combine practical experience, innovative teaching approaches, and reflective insights from educational and professional contexts. ----------------- Thank you for your interest in submitting a speaker proposal for the 39th IATEFL BESIG Conference. Only members of IATEFL BESIG can present at the conference. You may submit a proposal if you are not a member; however, if your proposal is accepted, you will be required to join IATEFL BESIG in order to be included in the programme. The call for proposals is open until 30 June 2026 at 16:00 (UK time). Click here for more information: https://www.iateflbesig.org/events/annual-conference

items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters Rhetoric and Communication. Interdisciplinary Studies in the Humanities The intersection of Rhetoric and Communication continues to attract the interest of many scholars, particularly within the fields of the Humanities and Social Sciences. The scope of analysis is wide-ranging, encompassing literature and culture, language studies and advertising, communication studies and politics, among other domains. In this Volume, we aim to bring together a set of studies that focus directly on topics shared by Rhetoric and Communication, from Classical Antiquity to the present, from an interdisciplinary perspective. Scholarly contributions across the Humanities will enhance our understanding of the influence of rhetoric and communication on society, taking into account, on the one hand, there is a vast legacy that merits further study and, on the other, new forms of communication require us to reassess the impact of the rhetorical art. This Volume welcomes contributions of a theoretical or empirical nature, including case studies, from within the field of the Humanities. Possible topics include: · Rhetorical and communication theory applied to discourse; · Treatises on rhetoric and communication; · The presence of rhetorical genres in contemporary forms of communication; · Argumentation techniques and persuasion in literary texts, the media, advertising, or other narrative forms; · The contemporary relevance of teaching rhetoric and communication; · The contemporary application of classical rhetoric in the media; · Rhetoric in political discourse and in literary composition; · Philosophical perspectives on rhetoric and communication; · The role of the audience and the addressee in rhetorical theory and in the communicative process; · Representations of rhetoric and communication in the Arts. Editors: Cristina Santos Pinheiro, Joaquim Pinheiro, Rui Carlos Fonseca, Samuel Mateus, Telmo Reis e Vanessa Cesário Proposals, in Word format, should be submitted by 10 September 2026 to the following email address: retorica.comunicacao@mail.uma.pt The Volume is scheduled for publication in March 2027 by a leading national publisher. All submissions will be subject to scientific evaluation (blind peer review). Authors will be notified of the review decision by 30 November 2026. 1. Accepted languages Submissions will be accepted in Portuguese, French, English, and Spanish. 2. Formatting guidelines 2.1. Length and formatting: main text: maximum of 20 A4 pages and minimum of 12 A4 pages; font: 11 pt, Aptos, 1.5 line spacing; footnotes: 10 pt, Aptos, single spacing. 2.2. Title centred, 12 pt, bold, Aptos. 2.3. Author name(s), affiliation (University, Institute, Research Unit or equivalent), email address, and ORCID should be provided in 11 pt, Aptos. 2.4. Two abstracts (maximum 250 words each) must be included: one in the language of the article and one in English, followed by up to five keywords. 3. General guidelines 3.1. Citations and references should follow APA style (7th ed.); all citations must be properly identified. 3.2. Quotations longer than three lines must be indented 1 cm from the left margin. 3.3. a) Italics should be used for the titles of works, modern monographs, and journals. b) Quotation marks (" ") should be used for quotations from modern texts. c) Italics should not be used for Latin abbreviations (op. cit., loc. cit., cf., ibid., in…). 4. Footnotes Footnotes should be brief. 5. Images/Graphs/Tables 5.1. Any graphical elements must be clearly identified and numbered. 5.2. Images must be submitted in .jpeg format, with a minimum resolution of 300 dpi, be free of copyright fees, and accompanied by official proof of permission or purchase of rights for academic publication. Each submission may include no more than four images (printing will not be in color). 6. Final bibliography The bibliography should be limited to essential works or cited references and must conform to APA style (7th ed.). 7. Publication The Volume will be published by a Portuguese publisher with extensive experience in scientific publishing. It will also be made available as an e-book in institutional repositories. 8. Copyright statement Submissions must be original, and authors grant publication rights upon acceptance.

items.fullDescription: The Centre for Research on Language and Culture Contact invites you to submit an abstract for Resisting Abandonment: Language, Culture, and Ecology, an interdisciplinary conference that will explore the ways in which ecology intersects with language contact, cultural transformation, and pedagogical practice. Conference Dates: October 15-16, 2026 Location: Glendon College -York University (Toronto, Canada) Keynote Speaker: Daniel Frost, Professor of Spanish and of Latin American, Latinx, and Caribbean Studies, College of the Holy Cross Abstracts Due: June 15, 2026 - - - - - - - - - - - - - Le Centre de recherche sur le contact des langues et des cultures vous invite à soumettre un résumé pour Résister à l'abandon : langue, culture et écologie, un colloque interdisciplinaire qui explorera les liens entre l'écologie, le contact linguistique, la transformation culturelle et les pratiques pédagogiques. Dates du colloque : 15-16 octobre 2026 Lieu : Collège universitaire Glendon - Université York (Toronto, Canada) Conférencier principal : Daniel Frost, professeur d'espagnol et d'études latino-américaines, latinx et caribéennes, College of the Holy Cross Date limite de soumission des résumés : 15 juin 2026 - - - - - - - - - - - - - International Conference Resisting Abandonment: Language, Culture, and Ecology Centre for Research on Language and Culture Contact Glendon College, York University (Toronto, Canada) October 15-16, 2026 The Centre for Research on Language and Culture Contact invites you to an interdisciplinary conference that will explore the ways in which ecology intersects with language contact, cultural transformation, and pedagogical practice. Resisting Abandonment is inspired by Sunaura Taylor's groundbreaking book Disabled Ecologies: Lessons from a Wounded Desert (2024), which challenges dominant environmental narratives by centring disability, care, and interdependence. The conference aims to build on Taylor's theorization of abandonment - material and ideological - which manifests in polluted landscapes, dispossessed communities, endangered languages, and marginalized bodies. Ecological degradation and linguistic erosion often unfold together, shaped by colonialism, extractivism, migration, and neoliberal restructuring. In Ecolinguistics: Language, Ecology, and the Stories We Live By (2020), Arran Stibbe articulates the ways in which ecolinguistic inquiry - including language-contact studies - reveals how knowledges of living sustainably in the local environment are embedded in endangered languages and are vulnerable to the global spread of dominant languages. Threats to linguistic diversity can be correlated to diminished biodiversity. Resisting Abandonment will foreground the idea that languages, like ecosystems, are sites of relationality and care. When communities are displaced by climate crises, economic dispossession, or other factors, their linguistic practices shift, hybridize, or face erasure. Yet contact zones also generate creative survivance: new vernaculars, embodied knowledges, and solidarities across difference. The conference convenes scholars, educators, translators, artists, and community advocates to examine how practices of naming, storytelling, teaching, and translating can resist ecological, linguistic, and cultural abandonment. How do metaphors of purity and contamination shape both environmental and linguistic policy? What can disability justice teach us about sustaining multilingual ecologies of access? How might translation function as a form of environmental care work? Participants will explore the ethical and political stakes of attending to fragile ecologies - human and more-than-human - without reproducing narratives of loss that justify further neglect. Resisting Abandonment invites collective reflection on care as method, contact as creativity, and interdependence as a framework for ecological and linguistic futures. Examples of subtopics by discipline: Cultural Studies : analyzing representations of ecological and linguistic wastelands - including their recuperation and adaptation - in media and literature of former and current power sites and/or in post/neocolonial texts. Linguistics : examining how ecological loss accelerates language endangerment or, conversely, how language erosion facilitates ecological loss; reflecting on whether documentation practices themselves risk reproducing extractive models Sociolinguistics : studies of language contact in climate-displaced communities; examining codeswitching as ecological adaptation Translation Studies : translating environmental knowledge across Indigenous and minoritized languages without epistemic extraction Pedagogy : designing care-centred, place-based curricula that link environmental justice with multilingual education Communication Studies : analyzing how environmental crises and linguistic marginalization are framed across media, policy discourse, and digital platforms; probing how choice of language used in the media influences how communities think about ecological issues and/or manufactures consent Second-Language Teaching : incorporating local ecological narratives into L2 classrooms to foster environmental and intercultural care Minority-Language Advocacy : examining how environmental policy, urban planning, and disaster response frequently neglect linguistic accessibility, thereby compounding abandonment or proposing strategies for integrating language justice into climate-resilience planning Those interested in contributing to the conference with a 20-minute paper should send a title, 200-word abstract, and short biography to crlcc@glendon.yorku.ca by June 15, 2026. Keynote speaker: Daniel Frost, Professor of Spanish and Latin American, Latinx, and Caribbean Studies, College of the Holy Cross Scientific Committee: Sibo Chen, Associate Professor & Associate Chair, School of Professional Communication, Toronto Metropolitan University Bruce Connell, Professor of Linguistics, Language, and Society, York University's Glendon College Maryanne L. Leone, Professor of Spanish, Assumption University Shanna Lino, Associate Professor of Spanish and Latin American Cultures & Societies; Director of the Centre for Research on Language and Culture Contact, York University's Glendon College Timeline: June 15: Abstracts Due July 1: Participants Notified of Acceptance July 1-31: Early-Bird Registration August 1-31: Regular Registration September 1: Registration Closes Registration Fees: Tenure & Tenure-Track Professors: $150 / early-bird $130 Tenure & Tenure-Track Professors (York University): $100 / early-bird $85 Sessional and Contract Faculty: $90 / early-bird $80 Sessional and Contract Faculty (York University): $60 / early-bird $50 Postdoctoral Fellows & Graduate Students: $75 / early-bird $65 Postdoctoral Fellows & Graduate Students (York University): $50 / early-bird $45 Include 3 coffee breaks + 2 lunches Options: Dinner Reception on Thursday Evening - Details and Fee TBD Eco-Cultural Excursion - Details and Fee TBD Languages of the Conference: French English Accommodations: York University's Glendon College is located in mid-town Toronto, about 30-40 minutes via public transit or car from the city's downtown, where many lodging options are available close to cultural attractions. Rooms in the College's residence will also be available at affordable rates for conference participants (single dorm rooms with shared bath, WiFi, linens). Colloque international Résister à l'abandon: langue, culture et écologie Centre de recherche sur le contact des langues et des cultures Collège universitaire Glendon, Université York (Toronto, Canada) 15 et 16 octobre 2026 Le Centre de recherche sur le contact des langues et des cultures vous invite à un colloque interdisciplinaire qui explorera les manières dont l'écologie interagit avec le contact entre les langues, avec les transformations culturelles et avec les pratiques pédagogiques. Résister à l'abandon s'inspire de l'ouvrage marquant de Sunaura Taylor, Disabled Ecologies: Lessons from a Wounded Desert (2024), qui remet en question les récits environnementaux dominants à la lumière du handicap, du respect et de l'interdépendance. Le colloque vise à approfondir la théorisation de l'abandon, à la fois matériel et idéologique, proposée par Taylor, qui se manifeste dans des paysages pollués, des communautés dépossédées, des langues en voie de disparition et des corps marginalisés. La dégradation écologique et l'érosion linguistique évoluent souvent conjointement, façonnées par le colonialisme, l'extractivisme, les migrations et les restructurations néolibérales. Dans Ecolinguistics: Language, Ecology, and the Stories We Live By (2020), Arran Stibbe met en lumière la manière dont les approches écolinguistiques, y compris les études sur le contact entre les langues, permettent de mieux comprendre les liens entre langue et environnement. Les menaces qui pèsent sur la diversité linguistique peuvent ainsi être reliées à l'appauvrissement de la biodiversité. Résister à l'abandon mettra en avant l'idée que les langues, à l'instar des écosystèmes, constituent des espaces de relation et de respect. Lorsque des communautés sont déplacées par des crises climatiques, la dépossession économique ou d'autres facteurs, leurs pratiques linguistiques se transforment, s'hybrident ou risquent de disparaître. Pourtant, les zones de contact engendrent également des formes créatives de survie: de nouveaux vernaculaires, des savoirs incarnés et des solidarités au-delà des différences. Le colloque réunit des chercheur·e·s, enseignant·e·s, traducteurs/trices, artistes et militant·e·s communautaires afin d'examiner comment les pratiques de nomination, de narration, d'enseignement et de traduction peuvent résister à l'abandon écologique, linguistique et culturel. Comment les métaphores de pureté et de contamination influencent-elles les politiques environnementales et linguistiques? Que peut nous apprendre la justice du handicap sur le maintien d'écologies multilingues accessibles? De quelle manière la traduction peut-elle fonctionner comme une forme de soin environnemental? Les participant·e·s réfléchiront aux enjeux éthiques et politiques liés à l'attention portée aux écologies fragiles, humaines et plus qu'humaines, sans reproduire des récits de perte qui justifient davantage de négligence. Résister à l'abandon invite à une réflexion collective sur le respect en tant que méthode, sur le contact comme créativité et sur l'interdépendance comme cadre pour penser les futurs écologiques et linguistiques. Exemples de sous-thèmes par discipline : Études culturelles : analyser les représentations des déserts écologiques et linguistiques, y compris leur récupération et leur adaptation, dans les médias et la littérature issus de centres de pouvoir, anciens ou actuels, et/ou dans des textes post/néocoloniaux Linguistique : examiner comment la perte écologique accélère la disparition des langues ou, inversement, comment l'érosion linguistique facilite la perte écologique; réfléchir à la possibilité que les pratiques de documentation elles-mêmes reproduisent des modèles extractivistes Sociolinguistique : étudier le contact entre les langues dans des communautés déplacées par les changements climatiques; analyser l'alternance codique comme forme d'adaptation écologique Traductologie : traduire les connaissances environnementales dans les langues autochtones et minoritaires sans extraction épistémique Pédagogie et didactique : concevoir des programmes axés sur les soins et ancrés dans le territoire, qui associent la justice environnementale à l'éducation multilingue Études en communication : analyser la manière dont les crises environnementales et la marginalisation linguistique sont représentées dans les médias, les discours politiques et les plateformes numériques; items.fullDescription: SAMLA Conference November 5-7, 2026, Atlanta CFP: Teaching Migrations and Diaspora in Language and Content Classrooms (Roundtable) Teaching classes on migration and diaspora can be both very rewarding and challenging. Whether it's a literature, documentary, and/or cinema class that focuses on migration, or an activity designed to introduce these topics in language classes at all levels, instructors must be able to navigate difficult conversations, making sure that the discussion remains productive and inclusive even when it creates discomfort. In line with this year's theme of "Hospitality", this roundtable invites short (5- 10-minute) presentations that explore ideas and content related to migrations and diaspora in any language and content classes. What texts do we include in our syllabi to address both hospitality and, more often, inhospitality towards migrants and refugees? What in-class activities, homework, and assessments do we design to elicit students' reflections on such complicated themes? In terms of teaching strategies, which ones can we use to make sure all students feel included in class and in the conversation? What decolonial practices can we utilize to foster both a positive class environment and impactful discussions? Can AI help us with any of these tasks? Presentations may focus on cultural production and primary sources used in L2/LS and content classes related to any languages, migrant communities, or diasporic cultures (including, but not limited to, Afro-Italian, Afro-Brazilian, Italian-American, Asian-American, internal migrations) or on pedagogical aspects, activities, and practices. Please submit a 200- 250-word abstract and a short bio through the SAMLA website by September 1, 2026 (https://samla. ballastacademic.com/Home/S/ 19672). For questions, don't hesitate to contact the roundtable organizers: Giuseppina Gemboni (ggemboni@andrew.cmu.edu) and Francisco (Paco) Chen-López (paco@spelman.edu).

EJERE is an international, peer-reviewed journal promoted by INVALSI, dedicated to advancing research on educational evaluation, large-scale assessment, and evidence-informed policy and practice. The journal aims to foster high-quality scientific debate and to bridge research, data, and decision-making in education systems. Aims and Scope of the Inaugural Issue The first issue of EJERE seeks to establish the Journal as a reference point in the field of educational evaluation, with a strong focus on the role of data, measurement, and evidence in improving education systems. We welcome contributions addressing, but not limited to, the following areas: -large-scale assessments and international surveys; -evaluation of learning outcomes and school performance; -use of educational data for policy-making; -methodologies in educational measurement and assessment; -equity, inclusion, and disparities in learning outcomes; -effectiveness of educational policies and interventions; -data-informed school improvement and accountability systems; -digital assessment and innovation in evaluation; -Interdisciplinary and comparative perspectives are particularly encouraged. Timeline Submission deadline: 31 August 2026 Notification to authors: 30 September 2026 Publication: November 2026 Author Guidelines Submissions must: -present original and unpublished work that is not under consideration elsewhere; -be written in English; -comply with Submission Guidelines and Instructions for Authors available on the Journal website; -include an abstract (no more than 200 words) and 3-5 keywords; -follow the required referencing style (a template is available on the Journal website). items.title: In Case of Emergency: Catastrophe, Climate, and Capitalism
items.excerpt: When we trace the genealogy of crisis, it can seem as if we've always been surrounded by catastrophe. Different factions of the ruling class tell us that we need to be prepared, but also that preparation may be fruitless. Crises shift and expand, strengthening their hold on us through their very instability. The state of emergency, after all, "is not the...
items.fullDescription: When we trace the genealogy of crisis, it can seem as if we've always been surrounded by catastrophe. Different factions of the ruling class tell us that we need to be prepared, but also that preparation may be fruitless. Crises shift and expand, strengthening their hold on us through their very instability. The state of emergency, after all, "is not the exception but the rule," as Walter Benjamin theorized. It is not a single event but what Lauren Berlant called a norm "embedded" in the everyday. In the zones of crisis and in daily life, the emergency overwhelms the senses, requiring constant self-governance and limiting our political imagination. The urgent threat of climate change, though often disavowed, is at the center of today's general atmosphere of crisis. Walls hold back displaced populations and rising seas. Earth systems sustain lasting damage. Species are devastated. And with apocalyptic alacrity, capitalist-imperialist competition crosses terrains that were once uninviting and hostile, from deserts to the polar regions and outer space. So far, discourses of risk and emergency have mostly been a boon for the racist right and anti-democratic technocrats, rather than contributing to a genuine project of planetary stewardship. The quest for "energy sovereignty" has unleashed a wave of extractive interventions in the Global South amid the collapse of the postwar international order, creating new sacrifice zones and colonial resource frontiers. Amid widespread doubts about electoral institutions' ability to deliver systemic transformation, some environmentalists have even embraced climate doomerism or the technosolutionism of geoengineering. We see how climate crisis is increasingly governed through biopolitical management, securitized borders, and technocratic forms of environmental control-and how the emergency becomes yet another opportunity for further administration. Crisis discourse often privileges spectacular catastrophe while obscuring the slow, uneven, and racialized forms of ecological violence embedded in everyday life. Unlike the "fevered immediacy that governs the society of the catastrophe-as-spectacle," as Rob Nixon writes, unspectacular "slow violence" is dispersed over time. With the sirens blaring, it is easy to lose sight of the material impacts of the ideology of crisis across time and space. We can also miss the ways in which the permanent emergency warps our cultural production and social relations, concealing the most pressing contradictions of capitalism today. How might we map the cartography of crisis? In doing so, might we open space for alternative ways of thinking and living within and against crisis? How do we hold crisis at bay long enough to bring about a "real state of emergency," as Benjamin says is our task? Jason W. Moore (Binghamton) and Gökçe Günel (Rice) will deliver keynote addresses at the conference, which will also feature a curated program of poetry readings and film screenings. In Case of Emergency is organized by Aditi Kini, Tadhg Larabee, Ernest Lee, and Yolian Ogbu in collaboration with the Chicago Center for Contemporary Theory, and with support from the Committee on Environment, Geography, and Urbanization. To apply, submit an abstract (max. 300 words) and a CV via this Google form by June 30, 2026: https://forms.gle/Fj4r9oAk5r8b6Q5K6 We want to investigate how crisis is produced, circulated, and inhabited across domains, including climate, culture, political economy, media, and governance. Through this cartography of crisis, we hope to understand how we might countermap and counteract this state of ecological and social emergency. We invite proposals from graduate students in the humanities and social sciences, as well as artists, writers, and other practitioners. Our goal is to create space for imagination and speculation with people of varied backgrounds, interests, and praxes. We welcome interdisciplinary scholarship and cultural criticism attentive to the cultural, aesthetic, historical, and political dimensions of crisis. We imagine submissions might discuss: Technosolutionism and the dilemmas of growth Speculation, commodities, and disaster capitalism Fossil life as economy and desire Green neoliberalism as a political and cultural form Enclosure and destruction of the commons: water, forests, air and more Hydrocolonialism, oceanic crisis, and blue humanities Border ecologies, displacement, and the production of space State-making, world-making, and the remaking of political, social and ecological orders Toxic temporalities, slow violence, and "post"-colonial precarity Apocalypse and new worlds in literature and culture Climate pessimisms and the politics of fear and hope in crisis Resistance, strikes, and land back: movements and solidarity Community, care, and affective ecologies of crisis Participants without access to institutional funding will have the opportunity to request travel support, though we cannot guarantee it. Questions for the organizers can be sent to ccct@uchicago.edu.

items.fullDescription: Engaging with PAMLA's 2026 theme, "Our Ruling Classes: Culture, Power, Conflict," this panel asks: How do esoteric ecological imaginaries reinforce, negotiate, or resist ruling ideologies? How have spiritualized visions of nature shaped elite cultural production, countercultural movements, or alternative political communities? What conflicts emerge when esoteric environmental ethics confront institutional religion, scientific rationalism, or capitalist extraction? Topics of interest include, but are not limited to, literary representations of enchanted ecologies, spiritual ecologies in travel writing or poetic form, occult environmental metaphysics, and the role of esoteric belief in shaping ecological imaginaries. We welcome historically grounded and theoretically informed approaches to literature, art, travel writing, popular culture, and critical theory. Topics may include ecospirituality, occult environmentalism, esoteric dimensions of deep ecology, and aesthetic practices that envision enchanted or spiritually animated landscapes as sites of cultural struggle and renewal. To submit a paper and present, you must become a PAMLA member by paying the member fee and the conference fee. For graduate students, there are scholarships available to help with the conference fee in exchange for some volunteer hours.

items.title: Artificial/Ancestral: Black Theatre and the Question of AI
items.excerpt: As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes cultural, educational, and creative institutions, the field of Black theatre confronts a familiar set of questions in a newly technological register: Who creates knowledge, who benefits from it, who gets remembered, and whose labor remains obscured? Public conversations about AI often proceed as though these tec...
items.fullDescription: As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes cultural, educational, and creative institutions, the field of Black theatre confronts a familiar set of questions in a newly technological register: Who creates knowledge, who benefits from it, who gets remembered, and whose labor remains obscured? Public conversations about AI often proceed as though these technologies have arrived without history, entering an empty landscape awaiting innovation. Yet Black theatre has long grappled with questions of representation, embodiment, archives, intellectual inheritance, collective memory, labor, and futurity. Rather than asking simply what AI can do for Black theatre, this issue invites contributors to consider what Black theatre reveals about AI itself: its assumptions, limitations, aspirations, and consequences. Volume 4.2 of the Black Theatre Review seeks essays, interviews, case studies, pedagogical interventions, archival investigations, artist statements, and process reflections that place Black theatre and performance studies in critical conversation with artificial intelligence and related technologies. We are particularly interested in work that moves beyond questions of adoption, utility, or rejection toward deeper examinations of power, ethics, governance, memory, embodiment, and knowledge production. We welcome contributions from scholars, artists, archivists, educators, practitioners, dramaturgs, designers, and cultural workers whose engagement with these questions emerges from both theory and practice. The issue is organized around five interrelated areas of inquiry. These themes are offered not as rigid categories, but as points of departure for further investigation. Taken together, these areas encourage contributors to approach AI not simply as a technological development, but as a site through which questions of labor, memory, embodiment, governance, spirituality, and future-making can be reconsidered. AI, Labor and Extraction: The beneficiaries of AI systems, whose labor makes them possible and required forms of accountability when Black creative work becomes data. Possible points of investigation may include: The labor of artists whose knowledge underlies any AI-readable record and what ethical stewardship of that labor requires. Generative AI in dramaturgy, script analysis, and design workflows, and models of artist-led intentional integration. Archives, Memory, and Black Theatre Histories: How do AI systems shape, distort, recover, or fail to capture Black theatrical histories and modes of remembering? Possible points of investigation may include: Digitization and AI-training projects involving Black theatre collections and their assumptions about what counts as trainable data. AI-assisted archival misreadings, flattening, erasure, and historical distortion. Embodiment, Liveness, and Performance: What happens when embodied, communal, and improvisational performance practices encounter technologies built on prediction, simulation, and abstraction? Possible points of investigation may include: Case studies of AI in the classroom, rehearsal hall, or production process. The complementary offerings of embodied, ensemble-based theatre training to university-wide AI adoption. Relatedly, how do such offerings get recognized, funded, or institutionally protected? Ancestral Intelligence, Spiritual Knowledge, and Black Futures: Understanding AI as a knowledge system entering into conversation with much older Black diasporic traditions of intelligence, memory, and futurity Possible points of investigation may include: AI as ancestral intelligence, or Black diasporic traditions of pattern recognition, forecasting, memory, and knowledge transmission. How do Black diasporic understandings of knowledge, memory, inheritance, ritual, and collective survival shape the technological futures we imagine? Refusal, Governance, and Alternative Technological Practices: Forms of resistance, opacity, governance, and the possibilities of misuse Possible points of investigation may include: How Black artists are bending, breaking, or refusing AI against its intended use. Teaching against technological inevitability. Photograph, Visual Media, and Digital Project Documentation tBTR welcomes photographic, visual media, and digital project documentation that illuminates the intersections of Black theatre, performance, and artificial intelligence. We encourage submissions featuring productions, rehearsals, classroom projects, design processes, digital or hybrid performances, archival initiatives, community-based projects, and artistic experiments that engage the themes of this issue. Submissions may include production photography, design renderings, screenshots, interface documentation, archival images, process documentation, and other visual materials that help narrate how artists, scholars, educators, and institutions are critically engaging AI and related technologies. All submissions must include the project or production title, names and roles of key collaborators, location, creator and/or photographer credit, date, and a 2-3 sentence description explaining the work's relationship to the issue's focus on labor, archives, embodiment, pedagogy, artificial intelligence, ancestral knowledge, refusal, governance, or Black futures. Contributors are responsible for securing all necessary permissions and reproduction rights prior to submission. Please contact the managing editor for additional information. Book Reviews, Performance Reviews, and Notes from the Field, and Multimedia Works In addition to scholarly articles, tBTR seeks book reviews, performance reviews, multimedia works, illustrative case studies, and notes from the field that engage the intersections of Black theatre, performance, and artificial intelligence. We are particularly interested in contributions that document pedagogical experimentation, archival initiatives, institution-building efforts, production processes, dramaturgical and design practices, community engagement, and artist-led technological interventions. We also welcome reflections on the ethical, political, and aesthetic questions surrounding AI, including issues of labor, extraction, memory, embodiment, governance, ancestral intelligence, resistance, and alternative technological futures. Submission Guidelines The last date for submissions is September 14, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. EDT. Please refer to the tBTR website for specific article section guidelines. Manuscripts must be submitted in Microsoft Word using standard formatting (1-inch margins, double-spaced, single-column layout, and 12-point Times New Roman font). Please include an abstract and a 150-word author biography with your submission. All submissions must include footnotes and a bibliography and must fully comply with The Chicago Manual of Style (18th ed.), using the notes and bibliography system. Please do not use the author-date citation system or another style guide. Please upload your complete manuscript through the journal's online submission portal via the website. Early submissions will receive preference in the review and publication process.

items.excerpt: About the Symposium The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) Symposium 2026 is an international academic symposium in film and media studies, with a primary focus on Vietnamese and Southeast Asian screen cultures and on how cinema documents, reimagines, and gives form to the region's landscapes, urban transformations, and contested histories.
