items.fullDescription: About the Symposium The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) Symposium 2026 is an international academic symposium in film and media studies, with a primary focus on Vietnamese and Southeast Asian screen cultures and on how cinema documents, reimagines, and gives form to the region's landscapes, urban transformations, and contested histories. Co-hosted by RMIT University Vietnam and Fulbright University Vietnam, the symposium brings together scholars from film studies and audiovisual studies, cultural studies, environmental humanities, postcolonial studies, and related fields to examine cinema's engagement with place, memory, and environment in an era of rapid urbanization and ecological change. The symposium underscores the significance of authorial and experimental film practices and of speculative fiction emerging in our region. The symposium is organised in conjunction with the fourth iteration of The Weight of Mountains, a periodic international film residency and research platform whose 2026/2027 program places international filmmakers in residence in Ho Chi Minh City for three months. This urban turn - situating the residency in a city shaped by colonial histories, wartime trauma, ??i M?i transformations, and accelerating development - provides the occasion for a focused scholarly conversation about cinema's relationship to place, history, and environment in Vietnam and the wider Southeast Asian region. The symposium will feature keynote addresses by leading Vietnamese and international scholars, artist presentations by TWOM resident filmmakers, and presentations of selected papers. Partners include: The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) team, RMIT Vietnam (DFV and SCD), Fulbright University Vietnam (Arts & Media Studies), Trigger Film Academy Call for Abstracts: Ho Chi Minh City is a city of layered temporalities - part and contemporary - and Vietnamese cinema has long been one of the most searching instruments for reading those layers. The city itself operates as a cinematic text: its streets and interiors producing divergent spatial imaginaries shaped by who holds the camera and from where they look. Like in Tran Anh Hung's Cyclo, urban space can be a site of the uncanny and memories, the promised land, or the space of autoreflective questions. Drawing on Guy Debord's psychogeography and Timothy Cresswell's understanding of place as practiced and performed, we ask how filmmakers navigate, intervene in, and reimagine the urban and ecological spaces of the region through experimental narratives, tools and future-oriented imaginaries. Contemporary film studies has been decisively shaped by the turn toward critical transnationalism, insisting on interrogating the uneven power relations, industrial infrastructures, and cultural politics that condition the movement of films, filmmakers, and capital across borders. For Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinemas, this means attending simultaneously to inter-Asian circuits of production and distribution, to festival economies and co-production networks, and to the diasporic communities whose experiences and investments shape what gets made and how it travels. The Weight of Mountains residency operates as what Foucault called a heterotopia - a space of productive dislocation and otherness, deliberately positioned at the margins of dominant film cultures. This symposium extends that heterotopic logic into the academic register, asking what forms of knowledge become possible when international filmmakers and researchers engage seriously with the specific textures of Vietnamese urban life: its soundscapes, its landscapes and ecologies as sites of historical sedimentation and environmental change, and its postcolonial politics of the gaze. The symposium is equally attentive to what cinema can do when it turns toward the nonhuman world - the Mekong Delta, the urban waterways, the forest edges and street ecologies that constitute the lived environment of Vietnam and the wider region, bringing further questions about how film documents landscape, registers environmental change, and attends to the nonhuman dimensions of place. Thematic Strands We invite submissions that engage with one or more of the following strands. Papers should present a clear research question, theoretical framework, and original contribution to the field. STRAND 1. Colonial and Postcolonial Cinemas of Southeast Asia Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinemas carry the unresolved weight of French colonialism, Cold War intervention, and the ongoing politics of decolonial representation. Papers in this strand might address: • The postcolonial gaze and ethics of representation in Vietnamese documentary and fiction film • French colonial cinema in Indochina and its afterlives in contemporary Vietnamese film culture • Decolonial aesthetics and counter-narratives in Vietnamese, Cambodian, Lao, and Thai cinema • The postcolonial condition of Indochinese cinemas across Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos, and the shared legacies of French colonialism • Colonial urban space and its cinematic re-inscription in Ho Chi Minh City, Phnom Penh, and Vientiane • The ethics of the outsider filmmaker in Vietnam and Southeast Asia - questions of access, positionality, and the politics of cross-cultural representation STRAND 2. Memory and the Afterlives of 1975 Post-1975 Vietnamese cinema remains one of the most contested sites of historical memory in world cinema. Papers in this strand might address: • Historical voices in post-1975 Vietnamese film • Wartime affect in Vietnamese cinema • Heterogeneous temporalities, colonial haunting, and the fantastic in Southeast Asian cinema • Uncanny urban spaces • Generational shifts in the remembrance of war and revolution across Vietnamese film STRAND 3. Transnational Return Papers in this strand might address: • Transnational desire, mobility, and national belonging • The aesthetics of displacement, longing, and return in film • Insider and outsider representations of Vietnam and the returning gaze • Transnational co-productions and festival circulation • Digital platforms, streaming, and new circuits of Vietnamese film distribution STRAND 4. Urbanism and the Cinematic City Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi are among the most cinematically rich urban environments in contemporary Southeast Asia, shaped by ??i M?i reforms, rapid development, and the layering of colonial and socialist pasts. Papers in this strand might address: • Ho Chi Minh City as cinematic city-text • Psychogeography, the dérive, and spatial practice in Vietnamese urban cinema • Postcolonial urbanism and the layering of colonial and contemporary temporalities in Vietnamese cityscapes • Rural-urban boundaries and migration narratives in contemporary Vietnamese cinema • Bangkok, Manila, Phnom Penh, and other Southeast Asian cities as sites of cinematic spatial inquiry • Infrastructural development, displacement, and the politics of urban transformation on screen STRAND 5. Independent Cinema and Alternative Exhibition in Southeast Asia Beyond mainstream production, a vital ecosystem of independent and experimental cinema has emerged across the region, creating alternative circuits of production, distribution, and spectatorship. Papers in this strand might address: • Critical transnationalism and the conditions of production, funding, and circulation of Southeast Asian independent film • Alternative film exhibitions • Independent film festivals and independent production circuits across Southeast Asia • The role of digital platforms and transnational funding in enabling independent Southeast Asian filmmaking • Distinct regional independent cinema identities • The sonic and haptic dimensions of place in experimental Southeast Asian films STRAND 6. Landscape, Ecology, and Environmental Cinema This strand invites scholarship on how cinema represents, interprets, and attends to the landscapes, ecologies, and natural environments of Vietnam and Southeast Asia. It encompasses documentary, essay film, and fiction practices that attend to environmental change, rural and riverine life, and the nonhuman world as subjects of serious cinematic inquiry. Papers in this strand might address: • Landscape cinema and ecocinema studies in the Vietnamese and Southeast Asian context - how films document, aestheticise, and bear witness to environments under pressure • The Mekong Delta as cinematic space - rivers, deltas, and rural waterways as subjects of documentary, fiction, and experimental filmmaking • Climate cinema and the Anthropocene in Southeast Asian documentary and fiction film • Sensory and immersive cinema - the use of duration, texture, and ambient sound to render nonhuman environments perceptible • Process cinema and the nonhuman agencies - water, weather, infrastructure, animals - that constitute urban and rural life in Vietnam and the region STRAND 7. Festival Aesthetics, Slow Cinema, and Global Circulation The growing international visibility of Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinema raises important questions about the institutional and aesthetic conditions of that visibility. Papers in this strand might address: • Transcendental style, slow cinema, and contemplative aesthetics in contemporary Vietnamese film • The construction of "Vietnamese cinema" as a category within global film culture • Co-production networks, international funding, and the shaping of film form for global audiences • The tension between local spectatorship and international festival circuits in Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinema • Transnational frames for Asian cinema and the risks of Orientalist programming logics • The role of film criticism, academic writing, and scholarly publishing in shaping the international reception of Southeast Asian cinema SUBMISSION GUIDELINES Abstract requirements: - Word count: 300-500 words, excluding references - Language: English Abstracts should include: - Paper title - 3 to 5 keywords - Indication of which thematic strand(s) the paper engages - Author name(s), institutional affiliation(s), bio note and email address(es) should be provided only in the submission form - Please indicate your presentation format: online/face to face in the form Author biography: A short biography of 100-150 words per author should be submitted alongside the abstract Presentation format: A 20-minute academic paper presentation, followed by 10 minutes for questions and discussion Review process: All submissions will undergo blind peer review by an international panel of scholars. Selection criteria include intellectual rigour, theoretical sophistication, methodological clarity, engagement with Vietnamese and Southeast Asian contexts, and relevance to symposium themes. Authors should remove identifying information from the abstract document prior to submission Submission portal: https://cmt3.research.microsoft.com/TWOM2026/Submission/Index Symposium format: The symposium will have a hybrid format. An additional online session will be held for online participants. KEY DATES: Abstract submission deadline: September 15, 2026 Notification of acceptance: October 2026 Full text submission: November 20, 2026 Symposium: December 10, 11, and 12, 2026 Symposium Venues: -December 10, Online -December 11, RMIT Unviersity, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam -December 12, Fulbright University, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Abstract submissions: https://cmt3.research.microsoft.com/TWOM2026/Submission/Index Please submit the abstracts through the submission system. *Some users encountered problems while using Safari browser. If you have problems with registering, please use a different browser. Registration details to be announced. Please contact the organising committee for queries regarding accessibility requirements. The organizers plan to publish an edited monograph containing expanded, selected articles submitted to the symposium. Details to be announced. Enquiries : dfvhub.staff@rmit.edu.vn Organising Committee Khoa Trong Nguyen, Digital Film and Video Program Manager, RMIT Vietnam Dr. Piotr Wajda, Lecturer, Professional Communications, RMIT Vietnam Dr. Agnieszka Kiejziewicz, Design (Games), RMIT Vietnam Tim Marshall, TWOM, Associate Lecturer, RMIT Melbourne Melody Woodnutt, TWOM, Associate Lecturer, RMIT Melbourne Dr. Linda Chen Zhang, Assistant Professor, Fulbright University Vietnam Trinh Dinh Le Minh, Lecturer/Filmmaker, Fulbright University Vietnam Director Lan Nguyen, Trigger Film Academy Le Binh Giang, Trigger Film Academy

items.fullDescription: Social Inclusion, peer-reviewed journal indexed in the Social Sciences Citation Index and Scopus, welcomes new and exciting research papers for its upcoming issue "Reimagining Inclusion: Legacy Media, Diversity, and the Representation of Differences in the Digital Age," edited by Axelle Asmar and Tim Raats. Submission of Abstracts: 1-15 September 2026 Submission of Full Papers: 15-30 January 2027 Publication of the Issue: June/December 2027 About the issue: The rapid expansion of global digital platforms and services (i.e., Netflix, Spotify, etc.) has profoundly altered the contemporary media landscape. While much scholarly attention has focused on the disruptive economic and technological impacts of these services and platforms, less has been said about how their (vocal) commitments to diversity, combined with the social demands for more inclusive representation, are shaping, challenging, and at times catalyzing change within legacy media institutions. Among these institutions, public service media (PSM) occupy a distinctive space as they hold a unique mandate to reflect and serve the full spectrum of society. However, their historical record on social and cultural inclusion is mixed, with critiques that they have often fallen short of providing meaningful visibility, voice, and participation for disadvantaged or underrepresented groups. In the digital age, these challenges have intensified. Not only are PSM responding to commercial pressures and new forms of audience segmentation, but they are also called upon to address intensified demands for representation, inclusion, and social cohesion. This thematic issue invites scholars and practitioners to critically examine the role of legacy media in promoting social and cultural inclusion in the digital age, and the ways in which legacy media negotiate and enact the representation and inclusion of differences across a wide spectrum of social and cultural dimensions. We welcome contributions that interrogate how PSM diversity discourses, policies, and practices are evolving in response to the pressure of the market and society, and how these strategies contribute-or fail to contribute-to social and cultural inclusion. How are PSM reimagining their public service mission and adapting their organizational models to foster more inclusive representation and participation? How do their strategies compare to those of global, local, and/or regional streaming services? What lessons can be drawn for building more socially inclusive media systems worldwide? Instructions for authors: Authors interested in submitting a paper for this issue are asked to consult the journal's instructions for authors and submit their abstracts (maximum of 250 words, with a tentative title) through the abstracts system: https://www.cogitatiopress.com/app/socialinclusion/abstracts When submitting their abstracts, authors are also asked to confirm that they are aware that Social Inclusion is an open access journal with a publishing fee if the article is accepted for publication after peer-review (corresponding authors affiliated with our institutional members do not incur this fee). Open access: Readers across the globe will be able to access, share, and download this issue entirely for free. Corresponding authors affiliated with any of our institutional members (over 100 institutions worldwide) publish free of charge. Otherwise, an article processing fee will be charged to the authors to cover editorial costs. We defend that authors should not have to personally pay this fee and encourage them to check with their institutions if funds are available to cover open access publication costs. Further information about the journal's open access charges can be found here: https://www.cogitatiopress.com/socialinclusion/about/editorialPolicies#publicationFees Abstracts welcome until 15 September 2026.

items.fullDescription: The erotic is a point of infinite signification, a navel in humanity’s symbolic circuit. However, despite its resistance to formalization, it is always in the process of not being written. As Octavio Paz insists, the erotic is a metaphor indelible to the human. As such, it is unsurprising that the manifestations of the erotic in subjective embodied experience are variable and correspond to equally plural treatments of it across the academic panorama. This diverse archive is bound by certain distinguishable threads, in terms of the potentiality of the erotic, its singular relation to language, and to the sphere of sexuality.

items.fullDescription: The Société Rencesvals, Pan-American Branch, invites proposals from scholars whose research examines Romance-language epics as sites of social discourse. Far from being merely “songs of deeds,” these texts were critical commentaries on contemporary ideologies. They thus speak profoundly to processes of self-conceptualization in far-ranging topics including –but not limited to– regional/national identity, faith, gender, and race. We are interested in the examination of how Romance-language epics use discourse to construct value systems that contribute to conceptions of the self, situating this literature in the larger study of the production of ideologies in the Middle Ages.

items.fullDescription: Human machine interfacing can be as simple as pressing a button or as complex and entangled (also entangling) as inserting a brain chip into the skull. science fiction. Humans with implants, prosthetic and hybrid humans with electronic and mechanical extensions are yet another level are no longer science fiction. Yet, human-machine interfacing has started long before the invention of these technologies. Machines did communicate with us and tell us about themselves even before chatbots were invented. The clanking of a hammer on the anvil tells us that it is old and dull. The whistle of a microwave tells us that dinner is ready. The process of interfacing is not a one-way process. Through it, humans also communicate with the machine.

items.fullDescription: As some institutions restructure academic priorities in response to various pressures in higher education, the Humanities can face contraction, marginalization, or elimination. These challenges are intensified at specialized universities, meaning institutions oriented toward fields such as STEM, health sciences, business, etc., where Humanities courses are often kept to general education requirements and could be perceived as peripheral to students’ professional training. Within such environments, Humanities faculty must navigate not only broader disciplinary challenges but also institutional cultures that may misunderstand or underappreciate the field’s contributions.

items.fullDescription: If American mass media is an ecosystem, we cast the press as predators, and the celebrity as their prey. We envision the reporters grouped in a posse, arranged for an ambush. Camera flashes crack as they capture their quarry. By now, these perceptions have become truisms that obscure our own role as consumers in a matrix of violence, spectatorship, and stardom. If we condemn the paparazzi for their alleged violence, we also continue to revise and revisit their heyday in the age of print media. This seminar seeks papers that explore how violent desire—of the spectator, the press, the star – shaped the profusion of tabloid and true crime print culture across the Americas.

items.fullDescription: About the Book Indian Cultural Heritage: Perspectives is an edited volume that invites interdisciplinary scholarship on the diverse and dynamic dimensions of India's cultural heritage. The volume welcomes original contributions exploring tangible and intangible heritage, indigenous knowledge systems, languages, literature, folklore, performing arts, architecture, material culture, cultural memory, museums, heritage conservation, digital heritage, and contemporary issues of identity, sustainability, and cultural preservation. By bringing together diverse academic perspectives, the volume seeks to advance critical understanding of India's rich cultural traditions and their continuing significance in a rapidly changing world.

items.fullDescription: This virtual seminar takes its inspiration from Saidiya Hartman’s citation of the Greek etymology of the word chorus : “to dance within an enclosure.” For Hartman, the chorus also furnishes a paradigm for thinking—to play on Jean-Luc Nancy’s notion—Black (non)being singular plural. In Wayward Lives , Hartman suggests that any of the minor figures can stand in for the others, not as a claim of homogeneity, but rather as a contention that their singularity can be read as paradigmatic of waywardness—in its queer heterogeneity—in general. The chorus of black femme and queer youth is thus at once a singular plurality and a plural singularity as they make beautifully riotous lives within the enclosure of social death.

You can submit your abstracts here: https://www.acla.org/cfp/70fe7418-c14a-468d-be1d-809e878f2e00/submit-paper/46d872df-9512-49a7-89f7-8bc710370693 Abstract from the ACLA CFP: Since the rise of World Literatur...
items.fullDescription: Please consider submitting to the ACLA seminar titled "South-South Literary Relations and the Remaking of World Literature" by September 21, 2026 . You can submit your abstracts here: https://www.acla.org/cfp/70fe7418-c14a-468d-be1d-809e878f2e00/submit-paper/46d872df-9512-49a7-89f7-8bc710370693 Abstract from the ACLA CFP: Since the rise of World Literature as a major field of inquiry, discussions of literary circulation have often privileged routes that pass through metropolitan centers, emphasizing translation into dominant European languages, global publishing networks, and institutions located in the Global North. Yet literary works have long traveled through alternative circuits that connect regions of the Global South directly, producing histories of exchange that challenge center-periphery models of cultural transmission. This seminar invites papers that examine literary relationships among Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Caribbean, SWANA, Oceania, and other locations within the Global South. Such relationships may emerge through translation, political solidarity, migration, anti-colonial movements, publishing networks, educational institutions, shared aesthetic projects, or indirect forms of influence. They may also involve moments in which Northern institutions, languages, or markets facilitate, mediate, redirect, or constrain South-South encounters, raising questions about whether these exchanges can ever be understood as entirely autonomous. Rather than treating the Global South as a unified category, the seminar seeks to explore its internal heterogeneity, asymmetries of power, and competing visions of solidarity. How do texts travel between Southern contexts? What historical, linguistic, and political conditions make these encounters possible? What role do translators, publishers, periodicals, archives, and digital media play in creating or sustaining South-South literary networks? How might these circulations reshape concepts such as influence, comparison, translation, reception, or worldliness? We especially welcome papers that interrogate the implications of South-South literary exchange for the study of World Literature itself. If literary circulation is not exclusively organized through Northern centers, what alternative maps of World Literature become visible? Can South-South networks offer different ways of imagining literary value, canon formation, and global comparison? By foregrounding overlooked routes of circulation and exchange, this seminar aims to reconsider how World Literature is conceptualized and to illuminate the multiple worlds through which literature moves. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: South-South translation; comparative studies across the Global South; Cold War and Non-Aligned literary networks; postcolonial and decolonial approaches; migration and diaspora; publishing and periodical cultures; digital literary circulation; transregional modernisms; indigenous and vernacular exchanges; reception studies; archives of literary solidarity; and new theoretical approaches to World Literature.

items.title: From Authenticity to Commodity: Italian Food in Literature, Film, and Popular Culture
items.location: University of Houston · American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA)
items.excerpt: Abstract This seminar proposes to examine Italian and Italian American food studies through the comparative frameworks of transnational circulation, intermedial representation, and cultural translation. Rather than approaching food as a stable marker of heritage or authenticity, the seminar treats it as a mobile signifying practice through which texts, im...
items.fullDescription: Abstract This seminar proposes to examine Italian and Italian American food studies through the comparative frameworks of transnational circulation, intermedial representation, and cultural translation. Rather than approaching food as a stable marker of heritage or authenticity, the seminar treats it as a mobile signifying practice through which texts, images, commodities, and affects travel across linguistic, national, and medial boundaries. Food thus becomes a privileged comparative object: it links literature to film, advertising to visual culture, and national discourse to diasporic rearticulation. The seminar invites papers that explore how Italian and Italian American food cultures are narrated, aestheticized, commodified, and contested across literary, cinematic, televisual, and digital forms. Of particular interest are projects that place works, archives, or media formations in relation to one another in order to theorize how "Italian" food is translated across contexts and how those translations produce asymmetries of value, legitimacy, and cultural capital. Such an approach underscores a central concern of comparative literature: the movement of forms, meanings, and imaginaries across borders, alongside the transformations that occur in passage. Theoretically, the seminar welcomes contributions grounded in food studies, diaspora studies, affect theory, queer theory, translation studies, media theory, postcolonial critique, and the study of racial capitalism. Food may be read here not only as representation, but also as material practice and epistemic structure: a medium through which embodiment, labor, memory, desire, and power become legible. This framing allows participants to ask how culinary discourse organizes identity and difference, how commensality produces or unsettles forms of belonging, and how domestic, commercial, and national narratives intersect in the production of italianità. The seminar is especially interested in comparative work on themes such as authenticity and simulacra; migration and coloniality; domestic labor and social reproduction; gastronomy and class distinction; queer kinship and alternative temporalities; and the branding of "Made in Italy" in global consumer culture. Papers may address novels, memoirs, cinema, television, cookbooks, food writing, advertisements, social media, or other cultural texts. By bringing Italian and Italian American materials into sustained dialogue, the seminar seeks to show how food serves as a crucial analytic for comparative literary study: one that illuminates mediation, circulation, translation, and the uneven politics of cultural value in a globalized world.

items.fullDescription: Although internet culture may have brought about the hashtag #WeirdGirlLit,” women authors have long used writing to explore taboo and forbidden topics deemed beyond the purview of polite/patriarchal society. While Heather Colley of Writers Digest has noted that “Women in literary fiction are becoming murderers, cannibals, psychopaths, and stalkers,” we contend that female protagonists have long been unhinged both across time and space. Historically, freaky (anti)heroines have served as a release through which women readers could escape the restrictive confines of ideal femininity and instead probe hidden desires and other illicit aspects of their identities.

items.title: Worlding Classrooms: What Do We Teach When We Teach 'the World'?
items.excerpt: This ACLA seminar asks what it means to teach the "world" in fields such as world cinema, world literature, comparative literature, and global media studies. Courses organized around the world often promise breadth, diversity, and cross-cultural understanding, but they also face practical and conceptual problems. What counts as the world? How does the nat...
items.fullDescription: This ACLA seminar asks what it means to teach the "world" in fields such as world cinema, world literature, comparative literature, and global media studies. Courses organized around the world often promise breadth, diversity, and cross-cultural understanding, but they also face practical and conceptual problems. What counts as the world? How does the nation appear in "world" courses? How do syllabi balance coverage, depth, translation, historical context, aesthetics, and political urgency? How do institutional expectations and restrictions mold the student imagination of the "world"? How does the positionality of the instructor presuppose, structure, or influence the "world" classroom? The seminar invites papers on the pedagogy of world cinema, media, literature, and related fields. We welcome reflections on syllabus design, classroom practice, study abroad programs, canonicity, national, regional, and transnational frameworks, diaspora, migration, colonial and postcolonial histories, language, accessibility, and the politics of curation. Participants might address how a single course constructs the world, how students respond to unfamiliar forms and contexts, how films or texts travel across classrooms, or how teaching the world changes across institutional locations. Through the discussions generated by this seminar, we hope to gather strategies for reimagining "world" courses in film, literature, and new media classrooms. Therefore, this seminar is especially interested in approaches that treat pedagogy as a site of theory. How do teaching practices revise our understanding of the world itself? What models of the world do our classrooms reproduce, and what alternative worlds might they make possible? We welcome both theoretical reflections and concrete case studies, including discussions of specific courses, syllabi, assignments, classroom practices, films, texts, or teaching contexts. Submit your proposal through this link: https://www.acla.org/seminar/6f456f04-ac0e-4024-9daf-ec6a4ca3e277

items.fullDescription: Environmental racism predates its own name. The term entered public discourse in 1982, but the conditions behind it, namely exposure to hazard and unequal claim to safety, go back to slavery itself. Historian Carl Zimring traces this to a basic split in American thought: white meant clean, Black meant dirty. That split decided who did the dirtiest, most dangerous work, and who lived closest to pollution, for generations. In 1968, Memphis sanitation workers went on strike over exactly that: unsafe, degrading labour shaped by the same racial split. Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated in Memphis while there in support of the very strike. That split still operates today.

items.fullDescription: “We are now in the middle of a deep and decisive moment towards a more disciplinary, authoritarian kind of society,” says Stuart Hall in his speech for Human Rights Day in 1979 (78). He proceeds to explain the components and manifestations of this “crisis,” which eventually morphs into a drive for more “Law and Order” (79). If that was the middle, are we at the end of the crisis? Our daily experiences prove otherwise, as the drive for more Law and Order keeps us in a chokehold. We seem to be in a perpetual global crisis in which we watch global systems of justice like international law and the International Criminal Court deteriorate in front of our eyes, while capitalist and genocidal systems globally continue to thrive and strengthen their hold.

items.excerpt: Emotions continue to attract critical attention across disciplines. Scholars have noted the growing prominence of emotion in media, politics, and internet culture, which some describe as an "emotionalization" of social life (Yanacek 2026). Over the past three decades, emotion theory has provided a multidisciplinary lens for understanding literary and cult...
items.fullDescription: Emotions continue to attract critical attention across disciplines. Scholars have noted the growing prominence of emotion in media, politics, and internet culture, which some describe as an "emotionalization" of social life (Yanacek 2026). Over the past three decades, emotion theory has provided a multidisciplinary lens for understanding literary and cultural texts, phenomena, and movements. Brian Massumi's distinction holds that emotion is socially coded and contingent on language, whereas affect is a pre-linguistic, asignifying intensity that exceeds discourse's capacity to fully capture it (1995). Sara Ahmed reframes emotion as social and relational rather than private, arguing that emotions "stick" to bodies and objects through repeated circulation, accumulating or losing affective value in the process (2004). Historians such as Barbara Rosenwein instead approach emotion diachronically, investigating the sanctioned "emotional communities" of different historical periods and how their norms of feeling and expression changed over time (2006). These frameworks are not fully reconcilable. For example, Massumi's model of pre-personal intensity has been challenged by critics such as Ruth Leys (2011), who question whether a truly pre-social affect is theoretically or empirically defensible. This tension among circulation, historicization, and the limit of pre-linguistic feeling remains a live and generative debate in the field. Game studies extend this inquiry into interactive media, asking scholars to account for procedure, system, and player agency alongside representation when studying emotion in play and design. Meanwhile, recent advances in facial recognition and artificial intelligence have pushed machines "from analytical processors to emotionally perceptive entities," if not to emotional entities themselves (Slimani 2026). These approaches resist treating emotion as ahistorical, private, or apolitical. Studying feeling as a legitimate, theorizable object reveals how power operates through affect, opens texts to modes of engagement beyond decoding, and invites us to reconsider the boundaries of the human, including where those boundaries fall in relation to nonhuman and machine forms of feeling. This panel invites papers that develop, test, or complicate existing theories of affect and emotion through close case studies, rather than merely applying them. We welcome submissions on any literary or cultural form, including but not limited to novels, poetry, drama, film, and video games, from any historical period and geographical region. This panel will be held online. Please go to https://www.acla.org/seminars, log into your ACLA account, find the panel, and submit your paper proposal by clicking the submit button.

items.location: University of Houston, Houston, Texas. · American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA)
items.excerpt: In the introduction to the Fourth Edition of The Norton Anthology of African American Literature, Henry Louis Gates Jr. and Valerie Smith emphasize the imitativeness of literature-Black literature, specifically. To them, literature begets newer literature. At the same time, readers have traced formal patterns of repetition and imitation in Black literatur...
items.fullDescription: In the introduction to the Fourth Edition of The Norton Anthology of African American Literature, Henry Louis Gates Jr. and Valerie Smith emphasize the imitativeness of literature-Black literature, specifically. To them, literature begets newer literature. At the same time, readers have traced formal patterns of repetition and imitation in Black literature across centuries, dating back to the antebellum. For instance, "Flight to Canada" by Ishmael Reed and "Kindred" by Octavia Butler; Harriet Tubman's "Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl" and Colson Whitehead's The Underground Railroad, published almost two centuries after Incidents; Mark Twain's Huckleberry Finn and Percival Everette's 2024 "James." These examples reinforce the notion that newer Black literature echoes, borrows, and imitates seminal literatures. This seminar thus seeks to investigate how Black literary and cultural productions have imitated other, earlier literary productions, even across genres and geographical boundaries-like what the editors of the anthology The Negro Caravan (1944) called "a sort of literary inbreeding which causes Negro writers to be influenced by other Negroes…" Even Kwame Anthony Appiah recently aver that "the history of art is the history of people borrowing and adapting techniques and tropes from earlier works." We seek papers that-using fictional and non-fictional Black writings and art-connect the past to the present-papers that explore "imitation," "influence," and "intertextuality" as central to Black literature and Black arts. Guiding questions to consider include, but are not limited to: What literary traditions have endured across generations, and how have they survived? What forms of continuity exist across Black literary history-Plantation to post-bellum literary and cultural productions, Africa to the Diaspora, across centuries, etc.? How do Black writers create new meanings from older texts? What role does memory play in Black literary traditions? How do contemporary writers preserve or challenge earlier literary traditions? How does Black literature reinvent its own past? What histories continue to shape Black literary expression? How do questions of race, identity, and freedom evolve across Black literary history? What earlier genres continue to influence Black literature today? How does Black literature balance tradition and innovation? What can earlier Black literature teach us about contemporary Black writing? Submit abstracts here: https://www.acla.org/seminar/defa99b9-6a8d-41ab-835d-2f1281fc3640 Session modality: Strictly in-person. Questions? Email: saadewumi@wisc.edu

items.title: Rethinking Authorship: Intercultural Genealogies of a Critical Concept in the Age of World Literature (ACLA 2027, online)
items.excerpt: Rethinking Authorship: Intercultural Genealogies of a Critical Concept in the Age of World Literature Virtual panel for the 2027 annual meeting of the American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA) This seminar aims to reconsider the critical concept of authorship from a strongly genealogical and transcultural perspective. While also focusing on world...
items.fullDescription: Rethinking Authorship: Intercultural Genealogies of a Critical Concept in the Age of World Literature Virtual panel for the 2027 annual meeting of the American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA) This seminar aims to reconsider the critical concept of authorship from a strongly genealogical and transcultural perspective. While also focusing on world literature theories, considered as an effective tool to rethink contemporary authorship issues, it encourages at the same time proposals that aim to identify and deepen conceptions of the author coming from understudied historical and geographical contexts, thereby broadening the cultural horizon of Western reflections on the subject. Indeed, we are mostly used to considering authorship as a romantic notion, strictly linked to the paradigm of genius and individuality, the authority of which was famously questioned by twentieth-century literary theory-relying primarily on such celebrated thinkers as Barthes and Foucault-before re-emerging in the post-structuralist era. However, other historical periods and cultures have not necessarily applied the same theoretical paradigms nor followed the same critical trajectory (think about collaborative or anonymous authorship in the Middle Ages, as well as the lack of the rhetoric of genius in most Far Eastern literary traditions, to give just a few non-exhaustive examples). In our opinion, it is therefore important to rethink the notion of authorship in the light of these divergent traditions, especially to ensure a more complex and multi-focal approach to it in an increasingly globalized literary context. Even though theories of world literature have profoundly transformed the ways in which the critical field of literary studies is currently understood, we argue that, in fact, the crucial category of authorship has received comparatively little sustained attention within this debate. While effectively highlighting how substantial changes in the literary system have simultaneously reconfigured the author as a global cultural agent whose visibility depends on complex networks of publishing, mediation, and institutional recognition, the world literature perspective has less frequently questioned the Western theoretical framework of authorship as a productive and individual stance. We therefore suggest that merging genealogical reflections on authorship with world literature studies could help to make the latter much more inclusive and global, rather than a mere framework of Western concepts superimposed on the literatures of the rest of the world. We welcome papers in English, French, Italian or Spanish. Possible topics include: - authorship in world literature theories; - the intersection of authorship, postcoloniality, and the global literary market; - twentieth-century theories of authorship and their global afterlives; - pre-modern, indigenous, and non-Western conceptualizations of the author; - multilingual, exilic, diasporic, and transnational authorship. Please submit your proposal through the ACLA's online paper portal by September 22, 2026 (an abstract of no more than 1,500 characters and a short bio-bibliography). Once your account has been created, simply click on the "propose a paper" button available at the following link: https://www.acla.org/ seminar/263adf13-fe6c-4fc3- 95f7-87083b14e3f9. Should you encounter any difficulty, please do not hesitate to contact the seminar organizers (giovanni.salvagninizanazzo@ parisnanterre.fr; federico. ristagno@phd.unict.it). Notification of acceptance will be sent by December 1, 2026.

items.title: William S. Burroughs as a Problem, Not a Subject
items.excerpt: This seminar proposes to approach William S. Burroughs not simply as a subject of study, but as a problem. We invite provocative papers grounded in comparative methodologies and attentive to less-travelled texts, episodes, affiliations, and cultural encounters. Rather than asking what Burroughs "was," we want to ask what his work does-and to pause over th...
items.fullDescription: This seminar proposes to approach William S. Burroughs not simply as a subject of study, but as a problem. We invite provocative papers grounded in comparative methodologies and attentive to less-travelled texts, episodes, affiliations, and cultural encounters. Rather than asking what Burroughs "was," we want to ask what his work does-and to pause over the categories through which we have learned to understand his oeuvre, asking what they illuminate and, perhaps more importantly, what they conceal. What notions of authorship, originality, literary value, sexuality, politics, nationality, identity, language, media, knowledge, or artistic production did Burroughs put under pressure? What happens when his writing is read alongside figures, traditions, media, or intellectual histories with which it is not usually associated? Can Burroughs's experiments still unsettle us? And what do we make of his political views today? We are interested in archival work, but not simply in the recovery of origins or the reconstruction of authorial intention. Archives can instead be approached as contested sites of selection, mediation, myth-making, and afterlife. We are equally interested in familiar Burroughsian techniques-cut-up, collage, montage, sampling, recording-when they are placed in unexpected comparative contexts. What do these techniques actually do? How have they travelled beyond Burroughs? How are they being used today, and by whom? We also welcome papers willing to be unfriendly to their subject. Is Burroughs overrated? Is he politically embarrassing, historically compromised, or aesthetically exhausted? Is he already "cancelled"-or has cancellation itself become another way of making cultural icons safe? Can Burroughs be restored, and if so, to what? Or is he damaged beyond repair? What might we gain by taking seriously the possibility that some of his work should be rejected rather than rescued? Possible approaches include, but are not limited to: Burroughs and writers, artists, or intellectual traditions with which he is rarely compared Burroughs and competing theories of authorship, originality, and literary value Archives, censorship, canonization, and the production of literary authority Burroughs and the politics of race, gender, sexuality, class, empire, and nationality Burroughs's relationship to religion, esotericism, anthropology, science, medicine, and alternative forms of knowledge Literary and non-literary media: sound, film, photography, visual art, performance, television, and digital culture Adaptation, appropriation, influence, imitation, and misreading The contemporary uses and abuses of Burroughs Critical reception, including hostile, skeptical, and revisionist readings We especially welcome proposals that are comparative in more than name: papers that put Burroughs into genuine friction with another author, tradition, medium, language, archive, or conceptual framework. We are less interested in proving that Burroughs anticipated everything than in discovering where he fails, contradicts himself, becomes strange, becomes ordinary, or becomes impossible to classify.

items.fullDescription: This seminar examines performance as a multilayered concept that is continually reshaped through travel and other mobilities. Performance, in this context, can be understood in its broadest sense as a dynamic practice through which identities, relationships, meanings, and experiences are negotiated and transformed. By bringing performance and mobilities into conversation as mutually illuminating frameworks, the seminar seeks to explore how their intersection creates new critical possibilities. Thinking about performance vis-à-vis mobilities draws attention to the varied forms through which these practices take shape and acquire meaning. For instance, Tim Edensor applies the "metaphor of performance" to tourism, examining how tourist practices may be "regulated, directed and choreographed" while also allowing for "improvisation and contestation" (59). The connection between performance and mobilities also foregrounds how performed identities mediate access to movement across different spaces. Jeanne Baret's participation in Louis Antoine de Bougainville's expedition in the eighteenth century while disguised as "Jean," for example, demonstrates how gender performance became a condition of mobility, as women "donned masculine garb when they wished to enter where women otherwise dared not tread" (Schiebinger 24). Travelling performances further demonstrate how mobility is not merely a context for these practices but can become part of the performative process itself. Little Amal, a giant puppet representing a young Syrian refugee girl and part of the art project The Walk, exemplifies this relationship by transforming her journey across cities and borders into an embodied encounter with displacement. This seminar invites further inquiry into the expansive relationship between performance and mobilities, exploring the many ways their intersection can be approached and rethought across historical periods, cultural contexts, literary genres, and modes of expression. Possible topics include (but are not limited to): Performances of identity (gender, race, nationality, class, caste, etc.). Tourism and the performance of authenticity. Migration, displacement, and belonging. Travelling theatre and other itinerant performances. Travel, empire, and performances of knowledge and authority. Religious performances, rituals, and sacred journeys. Social media and curated performances of travel. Writing, documenting, and archiving travel as performance. Travelling figures and cultural encounters. The travelling gaze: voyeurism, surveillance, and spectatorship. Museums, exhibitions, and the mobility of objects. Abstracts must be submitted through the ACLA portal by September 22, 2026. If you have any questions about this seminar, please feel free to contact us: tarafder.rini@gmail.com & achatt5@uwo.ca

items.title: Thinking in Images: Visualization, Imagination, and Empathy in Reading
items.excerpt: Visualization and imagination have long been recognized as vital to the act of reading. While Russian Formalist Viktor Shklovsky may have denounced the maxim "Art is thinking in images" in his seminal essay "Art as Device" (1917), in favor of strategies of defamiliarization, mental images and imagery are some of the most important ways we engage with a te...
items.fullDescription: Visualization and imagination have long been recognized as vital to the act of reading. While Russian Formalist Viktor Shklovsky may have denounced the maxim "Art is thinking in images" in his seminal essay "Art as Device" (1917), in favor of strategies of defamiliarization, mental images and imagery are some of the most important ways we engage with a text. In Dreaming by the Book , Elaine Scarry describes the function of poetry and novels as "instructions for mental composition" (244). That is, a text encourages readers to fill in the blanks; to reconstruct for themselves certain sensations, emotions, etc. These blanks, according to Wolfgang Iser in The Implied Reader , require readers to draw upon imagination, whereby meaning is created. Ultimately, literature encourages us to envision realities and modalities outside of our own. It is for this reason that reading fiction is considered to be an exercise in empathy--which Marco Caracciolo and Karin Kukkonen conceptualize to be a form of feeling with; of "imagining what we take him or her to be experiencing at a given moment" ( With Bodies: Narrative Theory and Embodied Cognition , 76). This seminar invites papers which attend to the function of visualization, imagination, and/or empathy in reading. In particular, participants are asked to consider how texts across a variety of genres, languages, time periods, cultural contexts, and subject positions, encourage similar or convergent ways of visualization, imagination, and empathy. Can we say reading is "thinking in images"? To what degree do texts encourage the generation of mental imagery and does this necessarily lead us to empathize? How does reading differ phenomenologically from engagement with other arts and mediums? What are the implications of cultivating an embodied and empathetic reading experience, particularly in an era of increasing polarization and automatization? How do certain texts reflect historical and cultural variations in bodily experience? We welcome interdisciplinary approaches drawing from affect theory, narratology, reader-response theory, phenomenology, psychoanalysis, cognitive literary studies, and other related fields. Possible topics may include, but are not limited to: Theories of mind (ToM) and cognitive approaches to reading; embodied models of reading. The impact of genre and form(at): fiction vs. non-fiction, literary vs. genre fiction, nonstandard/"non-literary" texts. Differences across bodies: gender, race, ethnicity, nationality, religion, and/or ability of readers, authors, narrators, and/or characters. Reading in translation or in different languages and effects on the ways we visualize, imagine, and empathize. Theories of imagination, literary imagination, and limits to imagination in reading. Narratological inquiries; impact of perspective and focalization impact on how we visualize and empathize. Reading in the age of Artificial Intelligence. How do AI/LLMs read and how do we read works produced by them?

items.title: Poetry and Pop (ACLA 2027)
items.excerpt: This seminar will convene a chorus of new approaches to the study of poetry and global pop music, sister arts dynamized by dizzying asymmetries. Where and when they are practiced as distinct or differently mediated forms of cultural expression, poetry and popular song are linked by histories both long and recent, by subject matter, by patterns of figural...
items.fullDescription: This seminar will convene a chorus of new approaches to the study of poetry and global pop music, sister arts dynamized by dizzying asymmetries. Where and when they are practiced as distinct or differently mediated forms of cultural expression, poetry and popular song are linked by histories both long and recent, by subject matter, by patterns of figural and prosodic design, and by their shared claims to those effects some call "lyric." At the same time, the trajectories of literary modernism and commercial music refract this common ground beyond recognition. In 1939, Clement Greenberg could decry a self-evident chasm of cultural difference between "a poem by T. S. Eliot and a Tin Pan Alley song." But of course that difference looks entirely different from the perspective of poets and rock singers in 1970s Poland (Jezinski 2022), the BreakBeat poets of the hip-hop generation (Coval, Lansana, Marshall 2015), reggaeton (Negrón-Muntaner 2009), Sinhala poetry and song (Field 2017), Nigerian hip-hop (Gbogi, 2025), and the music of Taylor Swift (Burt 2025) and Bob Dylan (Chasar 2025)-to invoke a random sample of objects whose conjunctions of verse and pop musical practice demand the conjunction of literary and musicological methods. Literary studies is home to a well-established tradition of formalist approaches to poetry and song: pop songs have often solicited the attention of literary critics because comparison with song holds out the pedagogical promise of a broader, more receptive audience for poetry on the page, or else because pop songs furnish an attractive archive to which scholars and students can apply the critical tools developed for that poetry (Booth 1981, Pence 2012, Culler 2015, Bradley 2019, von Hallberg 2023). Other approaches, inspired by developments in sound studies and by the particularizing study of traditions and archives like those listed above, have resulted in an expanding repertoire of methodological categories: "soundworks" (Reed 2021); "stereomodernism" (Jaji 2014), rock and pop's "literary capital" (Hibbett 2021); "poetic song verse" (Mattison and Suarez, 2021), etc. This seminar seeks to extend this critical ferment. We are particularly excited by papers that frame the pop mainstream "as something beyond a scorned other," to quote the new Oxford Handbook of Pop Music, and that regard "Top 40 music as an increasingly global and self-aware enterprise" (Weisbard 2026). But we are eager to collect a diverse array of objects, histories, and critical and aesthetic traditions, and we warmly invite papers informed by any approach to the intersection of popular music and poetry, poetics, or literary studies. Please direct any questions to mkilban3@nd.edu or nsurendr@nd.edu. Please submit abstracts via the ACLA proposal portal: https://www.acla.org/seminar/92de4ad0-1a89-4e44-a099-cbc29a13e461

items.title: The Poverty of Literature
items.excerpt: American Comparative Literature Association 2027 Annual Meeting University of Houston May 20-23 The Poverty of Literature Organizer: Gabriel Quigley, University of Victoria (gabrielquigley@uvic.ca) How does literature represent poverty? Is poverty available for representation? The title of this seminar is taken from Marx's The Poverty of Philosophy, which...
items.fullDescription: American Comparative Literature Association 2027 Annual Meeting University of Houston May 20-23 The Poverty of Literature Organizer: Gabriel Quigley, University of Victoria (gabrielquigley@uvic.ca) How does literature represent poverty? Is poverty available for representation? The title of this seminar is taken from Marx's The Poverty of Philosophy, which, in turn, subverts Proudhon's The Philosophy of Poverty. In it, Marx critiques the approach taken by Proudhon and other anarchist, communist, or socialist "theoreticians" who assume that economic categories exist independently of history. According to Marx, "so long as they look for science and merely make systems, so long as they are at the beginning of the struggle, they see in poverty nothing but poverty, without seeing in it the revolutionary, subversive side, which will overthrow the old society." A similar critique might be leveled at today's writers and critics: when literature and literary criticism engage with poverty at all, do they merely reduce it to an ahistorical economic category? What forms of reification, alienation, and exploitation does the literary assumption that poverty is available for representation produce? This seminar asks what literature owes to people experiencing poverty. At a time when 847 million people live in extreme poverty-95% of whom are in the Global South-it seeks to bring together research on the representation, history, and ontological status of poverty. Unlike Marx's "theoreticians," who "see in poverty nothing but poverty," scholars analyzing poverty through other frameworks-such as ethical demand, affective complexity, geopolitical disparities, aesthetic fetishization, and state failure-are strongly encouraged to submit abstracts. Papers may respond to such questions as: how should poverty be represented, if at all? Beyond an economic category, can poverty be conceived as an aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category? How is the concept of poverty entangled with conceptions of lack, deprivation, or destitution? How does the global distribution of poverty reflect the ongoing injuries of imperialism, colonialism, neocolonialism, globalization, and ecological catastrophe? Possible topics: - Poverty and realism; poverty and genre - The ethics of speaking for the poor - Testimony, life writing, and first-person accounts of poverty - Poverty and racial capitalism - Postcolonial and decolonial frameworks for poverty - Poverty and ecological catastrophe; climate precarity - Poverty and intersectionality (race, gender, sexuality, disability) - "Poverty porn," sentimentality, and voyeurism - Working-class literature and labor - Poverty in the Global South; imperialism and uneven development - Urban and rural poverty as literary landscapes - Homelessness and houselessness - Poverty and the archive - Poverty and affect: shame, solidarity, rage - The literary canon and class; institutional gatekeeping - Austerity, welfare, and the state in literature - Migration, displacement, and border crossing - Literature and human rights - Poverty as aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category - Poverty and ontology; being, lack, and deprivation - Bare life and destitution ACLA Seminar Description can be accessed here: https://www.acla.org/seminar/63e1eb87-fe99-49c9-aac0-517ccf904102. ACLA Paper Submission link: https://www.acla.org/cfp/2b603883-5d9b-44ae-a485-c732ba80d4bf/submit-paper. Papers can be submitted until September 22, 2026 .

items.excerpt: This call is for panelists to present on an approved in-person NeMLA 2027 panel on "The Gothic Servant." While the Gothic has long been associated with monsters, haunted houses, unstable hierarchies, and hidden knowledge, the servant's specific connections to the genre's core dynamics of space, affect, and plot have been critically undertheorized. items.fullDescription: This call is for panelists to present on an approved in-person NeMLA 2027 panel on "The Gothic Servant." While the Gothic has long been associated with monsters, haunted houses, unstable hierarchies, and hidden knowledge, the servant's specific connections to the genre's core dynamics of space, affect, and plot have been critically undertheorized. Yet Gothic narratives fundamentally depend upon servant figures to produce narrative tension, mediate hidden knowledge, and expose the instability of domestic, social, and political order. This panel therefore positions the Gothic servant not as a supplementary character but as a central Gothic mechanism and epistemological problem worthy of scholarly attention and analysis. We invite panelists to consider the following types of questions: In what ways does the servant function as a Gothic mechanism, producing narrative tension, circulating forbidden knowledge, and exposing the instability of domestic and class order? How do the servant's social and/or affective roles (as caregiver, confidante, observer, jailer, etc.) shape Gothic plots and complicate power hierarchies within Gothic narratives? How does the servant's structural invisibility produce, rather than merely reflect, Gothic preoccupations with spectrality, repression, identity and/or power? Topics may include but are not limited to: servants as uncanny, spectral, or monstrous figures; servants as central to Gothic plot and narrative structure; servants, secrecy, and forbidden knowledge; race, coloniality, and servitude in imperial and postcolonial Gothic; invisibility and the Gothic politics of service; servant figures in contemporary Gothic; and the afterlives of Gothic servant characters in adaptation and other media. We welcome papers on servant characters in Gothic texts from the mid-nineteenth century to the present, from any geographical area. All abstract submissions must be submitted through the NeMLA portal. When doing so, please submit to panel 22348, "The Gothic Servant" (https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22348).

Whereas digital accessibility is a technical standard that ensures that digital tools, documents, and platforms are usable by everyone, regardless of ability.

items.fullDescription: What strategies can paper ephemera teach us in the digital age? This panel invites conversations by writing instructors, educators, poets, and artists exploring the work that happens at/within the margins of writing. Both literally and figuratively, we take an expansive scope to the term “margins,” imagining not only the writing that appears on the space of the printed page, but writing that would normally be scrapped, discarded, remixed, or ephemeralized. This can include digital ephemera, such as “disappearing” messages in Instagram or other communication services. At another angle: margins can also mean the liminality of writing, the furthermost edges of what’s often standard and visible.

items.fullDescription: This panel session seeks to explore the cultural fascination surrounding "The Backrooms," an internet 'creepypasta' about an abandoned office building with endless corridors that became a popular YouTube series and most recently, a blockbuster horror film. What are the Backrooms? Do they represent an artificial or alien intelligence attempting to simulate reality? Are they a glitch in the imperfect fabric of an unstable universe? Are they a metaphor for the subconscious, techno-paranoia, wasteland necrocapitalism, corporate control, or the internet itself? Or is this all just a retelling of the Greek myth of the Labyrinth for a Gen Z audience?

This Knowledge systems place a strong emphasis on interconnection, moral behaviour, and harmony with the natural world - principles embodied in ideas such as Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam (the world is one family).

items.fullDescription: As Sidonie Smith and Julia Watson argue, “autobiographical storytelling is a performative act through which narrators construct rather than simply describe selves.” In recent times, “life writing” has become a familiar term in literary and cultural studies, encompassing a range of written texts, including autobiographies, biographies, letters, memoirs, slave narratives, prison narratives, captivity narratives, travel narratives, confessionals, conversion narratives and even in recent times, personal diaries. However, rather than remain transparent records of lived experience, life writings actively shape identities, produce historical knowledge, preserve cultural memory, and intervene in social and political worlds.

items.fullDescription: Panel Proposal for the NeMLA Convention, Newport, RI, March 6–9, 2027 Planetary crises—climate change, toxic pollution, biodiversity loss, and energy transition—are profoundly uneven in their distribution. Their material consequences are shaped by infrastructures of class, race, colonial histories, state power, and global capitalism. Increasingly, literary, artistic, and cultural texts across the world foreground these asymmetries, framing ecological crisis not only as environmental catastrophe but as a question of justice: Who breathes polluted air? Who profits from green transformation? Who consumes melting ice? Who bears the social and environmental costs of planetary change?

items.fullDescription: How do writing and general education programs create conditions for communities that empower themselves-sustaining, growing, and often exceeding their original design? This panel invites papers that examine collaborative relationships among students, near-peers, tutors, and faculty that form in and around writing instruction and beyond, with particular interest in work that attends to the unexpected: encounters, connections, and forms of growth that arise when pedagogy exceeds the transactional to become genuinely communal. Papers might address-for example-embedded tutoring or near-peer mentoring in composition; teaching-and-learning communities (communities of practice) among faculty, tutors, and students; writing or Gen Ed programs at HSIs, HBCUs, or open-access institutions; the relationship between first-year instruction and identity transformation; intergenerational writing communities and alumni engagement; or the challenges that AI poses to authentic intellectual and creative development. Empirical, theoretical, and reflective approaches are welcome, as is work that bridges composition pedagogy, approaches to general education, and literary (or other forms of) community-building.

items.fullDescription: In the definition given by Podnieks, matrifocal literatures are written and narrated by mothers in the first-person or limited third-person voice, rendering maternal identity and experience from subjective perspectives. Such narratives (re)value the significance and meaning of maternal figures in cultural, social, and national arenas, and often contest or negotiate traditional ideologies of the “good” mother as self-sacrificing, nurturing, and sexless with her antithesis, the “bad” mother. In the last few years, we have seen the rise of matrifocal writings published to break taboos about previously silenced reproductive experiences, create a sense of community, support, and care, and, overall, empower people.

items.fullDescription: Haryanvi Dalit theatre occupies a highly marginalised position within the broader landscape of Indian theatre. It may aptly be described as “the marginalised among the marginalised,” as it has remained largely excluded from both mainstream theatre studies and Dalit cultural historiography. Haryanvi Dalit Swang theatre was active long before the Dalit Panther Movement, but it received little attention due to its lack of publication and translation into English. This book seeks to recover, document, and critically examine the neglected legacy of Haryanvi Swang, with particular emphasis on its Dalit traditions and practitioners, thereby contributing to a more inclusive understanding of Indian theatrical heritage.

items.fullDescription: Philip Kan Gotanda’s play Yankee Dawg You Die centers a conflict between two Asian American actors. The aging Vincent Chang built his career playing bumbling Japanese soldiers and one-dimensional Asian stereotypes in classic Hollywood. He’s confronted by the up-and-coming Bradley Yamashita, who insists that Asian (American) characters should be played with dignity and accuracy. The heart of the play is an ambivalence about Asian (American) representation and whether viewers should sympathize with Chang for taking the only acting jobs available or with Yamashita in his condemnation of the racist roles—or with both.

items.excerpt: TITLE: Language Learning Beyond the Classroom: Virtual Exchanges, Platforms, and AI MODALITY: Hybrid: The session will be held in-person but a few remote presentations may be included. CHAIRS: Liana Ewald (Massachusetts Institute of Technology), Dagmar Jaeger (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) ABSTRACT: This session explores the growing role of virtu...
items.fullDescription: TITLE: Language Learning Beyond the Classroom: Virtual Exchanges, Platforms, and AI MODALITY: Hybrid: The session will be held in-person but a few remote presentations may be included. CHAIRS: Liana Ewald (Massachusetts Institute of Technology), Dagmar Jaeger (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) ABSTRACT: This session explores the growing role of virtual exchanges, commercial platforms, and AI-mediated interactions in language, literature, and culture courses. In recent years, many instructors have experimented with new ways of connecting students with speakers, authors, and communities beyond the classroom: Teletandem exchanges, Zoom conversations with writers and artists, commercial conversation platforms, and AI conversation partners. These exchanges can open up forms of communication and cultural contact that are difficult to create in a traditional classroom, especially for students who may not have access to study abroad or regular interaction with speakers from other linguistic and cultural contexts. At the same time, these tools raise important questions. What kinds of communities do these exchanges create? What changes when conversation becomes mediated through platforms or AI? How do students respond to the differences between speaking with another person and interacting with an AI system designed to simulate one? What happens when intercultural exchange becomes something organized and mediated by commercial companies, especially when those relationships may at times raise questions about inequality or exploitation? The session is especially interested in presentations grounded in classroom experience, as well as broader reflections on the pedagogical and theoretical questions raised by these forms of virtual and AI-mediated exchange. Possible topics include current and emerging forms of virtual exchange, AI-mediated interaction, commercial platforms, the changing relationship between human and technological forms of communication, and the pedagogical, cultural, and ethical questions these developments may raise in the years ahead. DESCRIPTION: This session explores the growing role of virtual exchanges, commercial platforms, and AI-mediated interaction in language, literature, and culture courses. It welcomes presentations on classroom experiences, emerging technologies, and the practical, cultural, and ethical questions these forms of exchange may raise.

items.title: Medical Humanities and Feminism in Literature and Film

items.fullDescription: In their special issue of Feminist Encounters on Medical Humanities, Foster and Funke observe the failure to acknowledge a debt to feminism, noting their work "offers the first targeted exploration of connections between both fields." This proposed panel seeks to extend their inquiry through papers that reflect feminist attention to gender and medicine/bioscience. Informed by twentieth century social movements (Women's Health, LGBTQ Rights, and Disability Rights), feminist theory and praxis understand healthcare encounters as more than bioscientific sites and as reflecting a range of social and cultural discourses, including regimes of gender, sexuality, race, class and debility that reflect and reproduce social relationships of power. Drawing on critical race theory, reproductive justice theory, and crip theory (among others), feminists have revealed the gendered facets of science and research, medicine/technology, medical institutions, medical authority, and provider/patient experiences, while navigating and intervening in biomedical discourses through advocacy. This proposed panel will take up the conference theme of "empowering communities" through papers foregrounding the connections between the fields of feminism and Medical Humanities. This panel encourages papers using an intersectional feminist lens to analyze literary and filmic representations of reproductive justice (including but not limited to gynecology, pregnancy, childbirth, abortion, surrogacy); disability (including but not limited to mobility, sensory, cognitive, psychological, invisible/chronic debility); and/or the body (including but not limited to gender affirming care, eating disorders, cancer, pain, and HIV). Abstracts should be no more than 500 words and include a works cited; the deadline for submission is 30 September. Submit abstracts here: https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22501

items.fullDescription: Romanticism, in its many cultural manifestations, oftentimes clearly draws the line between the subject and the object, or the speaker and the spoken for. Within the cultural cannon in Spain and Latin America, Romanticism has been used to project narrow-frequently problematic-visions of cultures and communities either within a nation, or to a broader, international public. But, could there be more below the surface than what initially meets the eye in these Romantic works? Through this panel, presenters are invited to reconsider cultural products that have been deemed Romantic (including Proto-Romanticism and Residual Romanticism) and the visions of community that they construct and/or deconstruct. Looking to NeMLA's theme of Empowering Communities, this panel seeks to rethink Romanticism-not through the perspective of the narrative voice, but instead, through the community that is voiced and the impacts that these works have had (or continue to have) within these spaces. Presentations that explore these questions and beyond through literature, film, music, visual art, and additional cultural products in Spanish or English are welcome. Abstracts can be submitted on the NeMLA portal through the link below. The submission deadline is September 30th. https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22654

items.fullDescription: Call for Proposals NeMLA's 58th Annual Convention - "Empowering Communities" March 6-9, 2027 | Salve Regina University, Newport, Rhode Island Roundtable Title: Writing and Wellbeing: A New Urgency for Human-Centered Composition Pedagogies Primary Area / Secondary Area: Rhetoric & Composition / Pedagogy & Professional Modality: In person only Chair: Miranda Lutyens, University of Massachusetts Amherst College is a time of excitement and novelty, but it can also bring about anxiety and uncertainty. Those unsettling emotions have been on an upward trend in recent years, with a host of factors - the fallout of the pandemic, social media's curation of idealized lives, and existential fears relating to climate change, generative AI, and political turmoil - raising concerns about the wellbeing of students. The college writing classroom has a long history of offering compassion through creative (and even countercultural) approaches to teaching and learning. This included affirming the rights of linguistically marginalized students to their own language, as well as efforts to keep struggling writers in school to keep them out of the Vietnam War. As we collectively face new urgencies, this roundtable session invites participants to share research projects and instructional practices that consider college writing classrooms as affective and embodied spaces. Recognizing concerns such as instructors' emotional labor and under-resourced writing programs, the session primarily focuses on putting forward innovative approaches to making writing instruction responsive to students' experiences in increasingly uncertain times. Insights gained from critical teacher research on human-centered pedagogies are particularly welcome, as are contributions from all levels of writing instruction, including first-year composition, writing in the disciplines, writing support for graduate students etc. The goal of this roundtable is for both participants and attendees to leave with expanded perspectives on how the college writing classroom might offer students more pleasure and new possibilities - to reimagine a more salutary relationship to writing, to engage with the written word in more personally meaningful ways, and to gain a greater awareness of themselves and others. The roundtable also aims to offer practical strategies for enacting - or at least experimenting with - new classroom practices. items.fullDescription: Early Twentieth Century Science Fiction serves as a lens into the functional and dysfunctional communities experienced in the Twenty-First Century. Focusing on the theme of this year's NeMLA convention, the issue of empowering communities can be assessed through the envisionment offered in works of early science fiction. The various processes of change, artfully told, offer warnings and solutions to combat authoritarianism as well as other types of oppressive regimes. Novels such as Zamyatin's We ; Huxley's Brave New World ; Orwell's 1984; and London's Iron Heel , as well as others, including early sci-fi short stories, offer glimpses into the realm of solving issues using knowledge, understanding, and initiative. One of many key points is learning and implementing resolutions, often through collaboration. NeMLA plans to have an online venue for those who wish to participant via Zoom. You do not need to be a NeMLA member to submit a proposal.
