items.title: Cripping Literary and Cultural Studies: Neurodivergent and Mad Methodologies
items.excerpt: Critical disability studies and the medical humanities have generated growing interest within cultural and literary studies in the past decade. Yet scholars in these fields tend to engage with disability and illness either thematically, examining their representations in literary and cultural productions, or rhetorically, tracing how they inflect the very...
items.fullDescription: Critical disability studies and the medical humanities have generated growing interest within cultural and literary studies in the past decade. Yet scholars in these fields tend to engage with disability and illness either thematically, examining their representations in literary and cultural productions, or rhetorically, tracing how they inflect the very form of these productions. Rarely do such approaches ask how disability and illness might transform criticism itself, that is, how neurodivergent or mad cognition might become a critical resource, transforming the ways we read, analyze, and inhabit literary and cultural studies. This panel invites papers that take up this question, exploring what new methodologies neurodivergence and mental illness-including, but not limited to, autism, ADHD, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, OCD, PTSD, and depression-can generate. How might neurodivergent and mad ways of thinking and being-in-the-world produce innovative, crip approaches to literary and cultural analysis that refuse sane- and neuronormative standards? Such a project finds grounding in Arseli Dokumaci's concept of disability-as-method, "a creative approach through which research methods are informed by, modeled after, and tailored to the situated knowledges of disabled people" (Activist Affordances, 11). It also resonates with Robert McRuer's call to challenge "straight composition, with its demand for composed and docile texts, skills, and bodies" (Crip Theory, 171), as well as with Jack Halberstam's notion of low theory, a voluntarily undisciplined mode of knowledge that defies the linearity and restraint of established academic discourse (The Queer Art of Failure). We welcome papers that generate or point toward new critical approaches grounded in neurodivergent and mad cognition and cripped methodologies. We particularly encourage submissions in which such cognition is presented as an embodied epistemological standpoint where neurodivergent or mad experience shapes the work from within, rather than serving as a structuring metaphor.

items.title: Human Rights, Violence and Dictatorship - 9th International Interdisciplinary Conference
items.excerpt: CALL FOR PAPERS: In the time when human rights are violated on a regular basis, violence triumphs, and feeble democracies ever more often back down before authoritarian rule, there obviously arises the need to reflect on the possible ways of counteracting such phenomena. Our interdisciplinary conference is intended as a fitting opportunity for this reflec...
items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS: In the time when human rights are violated on a regular basis, violence triumphs, and feeble democracies ever more often back down before authoritarian rule, there obviously arises the need to reflect on the possible ways of counteracting such phenomena. Our interdisciplinary conference is intended as a fitting opportunity for this reflection. We would like to look at various manifestations of dictatorship, violence and human rights violation, whether historical or current. We will describe them in political, social, psychological, cultural and many other terms. We also want to devote considerable attention to how the situation of human rights and dictatorship is represented in artistic practices: in literature, film, theatre or visual arts. ?During our previous conferences on human rights, violence and dictatorship we hosted over 300 scholars representing universities and research institutions from all over the world. We invite researchers representing various academic disciplines: history, politics, psychology, sociology, anthropology, philosophy, literary studies, theatre studies, film studies, fine arts, design, memory studies, migration studies, consciousness studies, dream studies, gender studies, postcolonial studies, medical sciences, psychiatry, psychoanalysis, cognitive sciences, economics, law and other. Different forms of presentations are encouraged, including case studies, theoretical investigations, problem-oriented arguments, and comparative analyses. We will be happy to hear from both experienced scholars and young academics at the start of their careers: doctoral students. We also invite all persons interested in participating in the conference as listeners, without giving a presentation. We hope that due to its interdisciplinary nature, the conference will bring many interesting observations on and discussions about the role of human rights and dictatorship in the past and in the present-day world. Our repertoire of suggested topics includes but is not restricted to: I. Societies? Genocides and ethnic cleansing Slavery and forced labor Nationalism, chauvinism, and xenophobia Religious dictatorships The Holocaust and totalitarian regimes Apartheid and systemic segregation (Neo)Nazism and political extremism Digital surveillance states and techno-authoritarianism Ecocide and climate injustice as human rights violations II. Individuals?? Domestic and gender-based violence Mobbing and workplace harassment Bullying in schools and the military Sexual abuse and exploitation Sadomasochism and power dynamics Symbolic violence and social exclusion Economic discrimination and ageism Cyberbullying, doxxing, and online hate speech Algorithmic bias and discrimination in AI systems III. Defense of Human Rights? Human rights organizations and humanitarian missions Resistance movements and civil disobedience The ethos of the freedom fighter Conspiracies, protests, and revolts Racial equality and the performativity of race Women's, LGBTQ+, and disability rights Intersections of human rights and animal rights Digital activism, hashtags, and cyber-resistance The role of whistleblowers in exposing state violence ? IV. Fallen Dictatorships Democracies in transition and post-communist states Amnesties, pardons, and transitional justice The revenge of the oppressed versus legal accountability Criminal courts and international tribunals The "escape from freedom" and regime nostalgia Psychological portraits of dictators The weaponization of nostalgia in populist politics De-radicalization programs and reintegration of former oppressors V. Violence and Subjectivity The politics of trauma and collective healing Fear, despair, and utopian visions Violence, discourse, and language Dictatorship as a social symptom Dictatorship, memory, and forgetting Intergenerational trauma and epigenetic memory of violence Gaslighting and psychological manipulation in totalitarian systems ? ? VI. Violence in the (Post)Modern World Cultural conditioning of violence Generational dynamics: "dictatorship" of the young or old Conformism and compliance under pressure The regime of political correctness and censorship Democracy and the tyranny of the majority Tensions between democracy, liberalism, and the free market Violence and propaganda in digital and mass media Deepfakes, disinformation, and the death of truth in the digital age Hybrid warfare, proxy conflicts, and invisible violence ? VII. Literature and the Arts Art and literature documenting human rights violations Aesthetics and narratives of violence Artistic practices engaged in the defense of human rights Art and literature as tools of censorship or rights violations AI-generated art: authorship, censorship, and ethical boundaries Cancel culture vs. freedom of artistic expression The architecture of oppression: monuments, ruins, and political space ? Please submit abstracts (no longer than 300 words) of your proposed 20-minute presentation, together with a short biographical note, by 30 September 2026 to: inconferenceoffice@gmail.com

items.fullDescription: The digital infrastructure in today's world mirrors the colonial administrative structure with its control over data, policing user's behavior, and pushing narratives for the majoritarian political power. The global tech giants have as much sway in geopolitics as the global leaders themselves. Previously the conditions of colonization created an unequal economic infrastructure that marginalizes the local communities, and even after independence from the colonial power, the trade relations remain that of a colonial appendage. Similarly, the upkeep of the digital sphere is not without its economic and environmental hazards. Anibal Quijano (1928-2018) a Peruvian sociologist, talks about the plight of this expansion for resources in his book, On the Coloniality of Power. He says: …the contemporary scientific community, insists on destroying the conditions for life on the planet. So, both the movement of the most subjugated people in this world, those who would not be able to exist if they sold their means of subsistence, and those who realize that if all this comes to an end no one will be able to survive, come together in a shared analysis. 359 He stresses on the role of the communities who've resisted the colonial and postcolonial measures to protect their land, water, and air over the years. It shows how the communities have more of a lateral structure which allows for debate and discussions as opposed to the hierarchy of the colonial administrative infrastructure. This panel seeks to garner discourse around the digital world's ambivalent nature of enhancing global communications and generating jobs at the cost of endangering local communities. Questions, challenges, and possible solutions for a community-oriented resistance will be among the many concerns discussed at this panel. Submit on NeMLA's website: Submit an Abstract

items.title: Utopias in Dystopias: Finding Hope and Inspiration in Dystopian Fiction
items.excerpt: People often draw inspiration from fiction. Such is particularly the case with utopian literature, which has inspired political thought and activism as early as Plato's Republic. Dystopian literature is equally instructive. But whereas utopian literature either inspires or provides the blueprints for the ideal society, dystopian literature either begins f...
items.fullDescription: People often draw inspiration from fiction. Such is particularly the case with utopian literature, which has inspired political thought and activism as early as Plato's Republic. Dystopian literature is equally instructive. But whereas utopian literature either inspires or provides the blueprints for the ideal society, dystopian literature either begins from the vantage point of a society in decline, or sets it up at the end, showing us what unjust and failed societies look like or how they come about. Dystopian fiction often mirrors aspects of our own world and is often written or interpreted as a warning. It might seem odd, therefore, to mine dystopian literature for details on how to develop an ideal and just society. And yet that is exactly what this panel hopes to do. Dystopian literature is replete with examples of both individuals who resist and communities of resilience and resistance which model values and activities that stand in contrast to and in spite of the dystopian setting of the story. Where better to turn for hope and inspiration than depictions of a broken world wherein people still find a way to survive and even thrive under less than ideal, even hostile socio-political and environmental conditions? Accordingly, this panel seeks to bring together critical investigations of dystopian literature which attempt to bring to the fore lessons that can be learned to help us (re)imagine just communities amidst a world of political, economic and ecological decline and regression. This is necessary as individuals become less certain of what to do, or have lost all faith that anything can be done, in a world increasingly hostile to justice. The session will be held in-person but a few remote presentations may be included.

items.title: The Classroom as Counter-Archive: Place-Based Pedagogies of Community Empowerment
items.location: Salve Regina University. Newport, Rhode Island · NEMLA
items.excerpt: Education is an ideal means of empowerment, for it enables students to take ownership of the historical and personal archives that stand for their communities. This panel regards the classroom as a privileged site of such empowerment-particularly for students from immigrant families-and seeks proposals on how to equip them to become active agents in produ...
items.fullDescription: Education is an ideal means of empowerment, for it enables students to take ownership of the historical and personal archives that stand for their communities. This panel regards the classroom as a privileged site of such empowerment-particularly for students from immigrant families-and seeks proposals on how to equip them to become active agents in producing their own interpretations of the cultural and spatial memory they share with their forebears. We draw inspiration from courses in which students articulate their personal, familial, and communal relationships with the tangible and intangible spaces of the city they inhabit: from their own homes to the streets they traverse daily, the buildings, neighborhoods, and monuments they encounter, and the individual and social practices that animate them. Setting their lived experience against the historical archives that purport to represent them, students produce analytical descriptions of urban space. Their work collectively assembles a shared repository of cultural memory - a "counter-archive" that weaves together place-based learning, immigration histories, and autobiographical narrative. In classrooms of diverse composition, this work empowers along more than one path. Immigrant students illuminate the place of their communities within the urban social fabric, while others discover-in their own projects and in those of their classmates-insights that transform how they perceive the city and their own identities in relation to it. We invite educators across languages, periods, and disciplines to share pedagogical projects and activities-assignments, archives, community-engaged work, digital repositories, creative and testimonial writing-that treat teaching as a practice of empowerment. We especially welcome contributions that reflect on the theory of change behind their work: when does a classroom project produce agency, and how do we know?

items.title: Resisting from the Edge: Marginal Characters and Collective Empowerment
items.location: Salve Regina University, Newport, RI · NeMLA
items.excerpt: This panel invites papers that examine the agency of marginalized characters in literary, visual, audiovisual, and artistic productions from the French?speaking world across any historical period. Artistic works offer numerous examples of figures who maintain an ambivalent relationship to their communities. Because of their social or ethnic origins, their...
items.fullDescription: This panel invites papers that examine the agency of marginalized characters in literary, visual, audiovisual, and artistic productions from the French?speaking world across any historical period. Artistic works offer numerous examples of figures who maintain an ambivalent relationship to their communities. Because of their social or ethnic origins, their divergent perspectives, or their transgression of established norms, certain characters find themselves pushed to the margins of social, familial, or professional groups. While such exclusion may appear to weaken those who experience it, this panel asks whether marginalization might also function as a source of strength. Can marginality become a generative position? Do marginalized individuals succeed in forming new communities that enable them to confront stigma and ultimately overcome it? This discussion seeks to shift our understanding of the place occupied by marginalized individuals and groups in fictional narratives. By considering the networks of solidarity that emerge among marginalized subjects, the panel explores what lies beneath their presumed inferiority, inviting critical attention to what is hidden, erased, or rendered invisible within dominant narratives. More importantly, we will examine how marginalized communities may become empowering spaces of resistance, mutual support, and hope. Drawing on approaches from cultural studies, postcolonial theory, sociolinguistics, and intersectionality, this session seeks to understand how literary, visual, audiovisual, and artistic narratives stage the tensions between marginality and belonging, strength and vulnerability. Proposals engaging with environmental humanities, posthumanism, Indigenous studies, as well as diaspora and migration studies are strongly encouraged. We also welcome submissions drawing on gender and queer studies, memory and trauma studies, digital humanities, or other interdisciplinary frameworks within the humanities. We welcome proposals of 250-300 words, in French or English, submitted by September 30.

items.fullDescription: Poetry is a perfect medium to explore all of the key issues planned for the 58th Annual NeMLA Convention. The focus of this year's convention is Empowering Communities," which is identified on the NeMLA website as evoking the "process of transformation from a state of passivity to being active agents of change. It represents a shift away from authoritarianism and toward a model that values (and solves problems through) local knowledge, collaboration, and collective action," terms which lend themselves well to the emotional expressions within poetry. For the past five years, the Closet Poets sessions have enjoyed many scholars who research and write papers for conferences as well as write poetry. Perhaps those poems are jotted on note pads, in the margins of your papers or in dedicated personal journals. This session is seeking those scholars whose poetry often remains unpublished due to the heavier responsibility of publishing scholarly journal articles, monographs and genre-specific books which demand much time in between teaching, and perhaps, administrating at the university. Even though those scholarly efforts may yield more rewards, such as job retention and hopefully, job promotions; personal poetry, intermittently created, yields a satisfying venue for emotional issues and satisfying creativity. The 2027 Revisiting Closet Poets Creative session is an opportunity to expand and share your poetry by perhaps featuring the key issues of this years' convention. I am pleased to report that MLS published several participants poetic work since 2023 in their online venue. Perhaps you will have an opportunity to have your work published in MLS in future publications of our Closet Poets work. Remember the words of Poet Laureate, Robert Pinsky, who shared his joy of telling poems during a previous NeMLA conference, "Poetry is the breath of humankind, and must be heard." NOTE: This session is hybrid. It will be seated and accessible on Zoom. Please indicate which you prefer when you submit your proposals. Thank you. You do not need to be a NeMLA member to submit a proposal.

items.fullDescription: What are the main avenues of innovation in language learning communities of 2027? How do we as language pedagogues lean in on culture and interculturality as a source of strength and empowerment in our programs, in order to collaborate with all stakeholders and foster innovation in our language programs? In the embattled environment that is the American university of 2026-2027, and particularly for the language and humanities programs fighting for enrollments and their own survival, how do we empower ourselves and our students in the language classroom, encouraging active engagement in extracurricular activities, and bringing cultural knowledge to bear in community-based outreach and programs? In what ways does interculturality take on new meaning in today's world, in the language classroom, and in academia? This roundtable will explore innovation and empowerment in the language classroom and in language learning communities, where culture is the key to empowerment and innovation. We will reflect on new ways for creating community, creating spaces of innovation, and connecting the classroom to the larger world outside the classroom and to the university through culture and collective action. We welcome presentations that showcase novel pedagogical ideas, lived experiences, and creative practices in language teaching and cultural engagement.

items.title: Beyond Hegemony: Masculinities in World and Comparative Literature
items.excerpt: This panel examines how literary and cultural texts from diverse global traditions imagine masculinity not merely as an individual identity but as a relational and communal practice. In an era marked by migration, political polarization, social fragmentation, environmental crisis, and renewed struggles for collective empowerment, narratives of masculinity...
items.fullDescription: This panel examines how literary and cultural texts from diverse global traditions imagine masculinity not merely as an individual identity but as a relational and communal practice. In an era marked by migration, political polarization, social fragmentation, environmental crisis, and renewed struggles for collective empowerment, narratives of masculinity have become central sites through which communities negotiate belonging, responsibility, vulnerability, and resistance. While dominant models of masculinity have often been associated with hierarchy, authority, nationalism, and exclusion, contemporary world literatures increasingly depict alternative masculinities grounded in care, ethical responsibility, emotional openness, solidarity, and collective survival. Such representations challenge inherited structures of power while opening new possibilities for community formation and social transformation. This panel invites comparative and transnational approaches that explore how literary texts, films, cultural narratives, and other expressive forms construct, critique, or reimagine masculinities within local and global communities. Particular attention may be given to how gender intersects with race, class, migration, coloniality, religion, ecology, technology, and cultural memory in shaping collective identities and practices of empowerment. Situated within the broader concerns of World Literature and Comparative Literature, this session seeks to foster dialogue across regions, languages, and traditions while investigating how masculinities participate in the creation-or disruption-of empowered communities. We welcome papers addressing, but not limited to: Comparative constructions of masculinity across world literatures Masculinity and migration, diaspora, or displacement Literary representations of fatherhood, mentorship, and communal responsibility Masculinities in Global South literatures Masculinity and environmental or ecological communities Masculinity, memory, and post-conflict reconstruction Queer and non-hegemonic masculinities in world literature Masculinity and cultural resistance under authoritarian regimes Masculinity, religion, and collective belonging Masculinity and affect in contemporary global fiction

items.fullDescription: This conference explores decay as a transformative, liminal state that bridges the physical, the political, and the conceptual. During the process of decomposition, systems and objects start to break down, existing in a precarious limbo that simultaneously signals contamination to the surrounding environment. As theorized by Julia Kristeva in Powers of Horror, the abject corpse and the decaying material remind us of the fragility of our own boundaries, confronting us with what must be cast off to constitute a stable self. This fear of bodily disintegration and abjection mirrors the anxieties we project onto broader cultural and institutional structures.

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS Christians and Muslims in Israel - Facts, Myths and Lived Reality International Online Academic Conference 25-28 January 2027 Online via Zoom Working language: English Call for papers for an international online conference on Christianity, Islam, religious minorities, interreligious relations, religious freedom, identity, society and politics in contemporary Israel. CONFERENCE OVERVIEW The conference will examine the historical, social, religious, demographic, legal, cultural and political realities of Christian and Muslim communities in the State of Israel. Its purpose is to distinguish empirical evidence and lived experience from simplified assumptions, stereotypes and politically driven narratives. Different scholarly interpretations are welcome, and participants are not required to adopt any predetermined political, theological or ideological position. In addition to Christian-Muslim relations, the conference welcomes research on Christians and Muslims as distinct communities and on their relationships with the Jewish majority, the State of Israel, public institutions and wider Israeli society. Relevant disciplinary perspectives include sociology of religion, religious studies, history, theology, anthropology, political science, law, demography, education, Middle Eastern Studies, Israel Studies, minority studies, media studies and related interdisciplinary fields. The session will be part of the XXI International Sociological Association (ISA) World Congress of Sociology, from July 4-10, 2027, at Chonnam National University in Jeonnam-Gwangju Special Metropolitan City, Korea. Karl Marx and Max Weber both thought about a time when machines would dominate labor. Marx wrote of a "perpetuum mobile" to describe the unceasing turnover of money by a machine of indestructible materiality, circulating a repeating and alternating flow of sale and purchase. Max Weber's "Sociology of Domination" theory warned that the power to coerce markets endlessly would cause endless conflicts. For Marx social change entailed communist revolution, while Weber, who was not a Marxist, worried that social change would be constricted to political coups to control the government's informational infrastructure. Social problems of alienation and rationalization, capitalist wealth and inequality, abuse of power and authority, coerced markets, money hording and social stratification are as alive today as when Marx and Weber set down theories about these social problems over a hundred years ago. What can we say about our AI dominated world using the concepts and writings of Marx and Weber today? Do their economic and historical comparative concepts help us understand our digital world? Why or why not? Submit presentation abstracts by October 14, 2026, through the ISA Congress Submission System link below. ISA XXI World Congress of Sociology Call for Abstracts: https://www.isa-sociology.org/isa-events/xxi-world-congress-of-sociology/call-for-abstracts Watch the 2025 ISA abstract submission tutorial here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p_dRzY4k_o4 Current Session Participants: Session Chair, Dr. Ece Kocabicak, The Open University Co-Chair, Dr. Pravat Ranjan Sethi, Central University of Himachal Pradesh, India Discussant, Proshant Chakraborty, University of Vienna, Austria Session Organizer, Dr. Noel Packard, Independent Scholar, USA Questions? Contact Dr. Noel Packard at npac825@aucklanduni.ac.nz. Further information available via Sociology Group interview with Dr. Noel Packard on Marx, Weber, and machines dominating labour: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/414162540_An_Interview_with_Dr_Noel_Packard_- Karl_Marx_and_Max_Weber_on_Machines_Dominating_Labour

items.fullDescription: Call For Paper Women And Art: Representation, Creativity, And Resistance Open Access | Maurer Press, Frankfurt am Main, Germany Edited by Habib Tekin & Ay?enur Özkan I??k Art has long served as a powerful space in which gender identities, social roles, cultural expectations, and forms of resistance are constructed, questioned, and reimagined. Across different historical periods and cultural contexts, women have participated in artistic production as creators, performers, patrons, critics, and subjects of representation. Yet their contributions have frequently been shaped by unequal access to artistic institutions, dominant aesthetic traditions, and gendered structures of visibility and recognition. The conference "Women and Art: Representation, Creativity, and Resistance" invites scholars, researchers, artists, and postgraduate students to explore the complex and changing relationship between women and artistic production. The conference seeks to bring together interdisciplinary perspectives on how women create, experience, interpret, and transform art, as well as how femininity and gender are represented within different artistic forms. We particularly welcome contributions that examine the ways in which art can function as a space of memory, identity formation, cultural negotiation, political intervention, and resistance. Papers may address historical or contemporary contexts and may focus on individual artists, artistic movements, particular works, comparative perspectives, or broader theoretical questions concerning women, gender, and aesthetics. The proposed book seeks to examine the representation, production, and experience of women in art from gendered, cultural, and interdisciplinary perspectives, including but not limited to the following areas: Women artists in historical and contemporary contexts Representations of women in art Women and literature Women in painting, sculpture, and visual arts Women in photography and film Women in theatre, performance, dance, and music Feminist art and feminist aesthetics Gender and artistic representation The female body in art Self-representation and female subjectivity Women, creativity, and authorship Women and artistic institutions Gender inequality and exclusion in the art world Women artists and cultural memory Art, trauma, testimony, and memory Women, war, migration, exile, and displacement Art and resistance Women and political art Women and censorship Queer and intersectional approaches to women and art Race, ethnicity, class, and gender in artistic production Postcolonial and decolonial approaches to women and art Women and indigenous artistic traditions Women and popular culture Digital art, social media, and new forms of female creativity Artificial intelligence, technology, and women in art Women as patrons, collectors, curators, and critics Gendered spaces and artistic production Comparative and interdisciplinary approaches to women and art The book particularly encourages contributions that offer close readings of literary works, films, visual artworks, photography, theatre, performance, music, digital media, or other artistic forms, as well as theoretically grounded analyses that advance current debates on women, gender, and art. We look forward to receiving proposals that critically engage with the intersections of women, creativity, representation, identity, memory, and resistance across artistic and cultural contexts and contribute to ongoing scholarly discussions within Gender Studies, Art Studies, Cultural Studies, Literary Studies, and related fields. Submission Guidelines Abstracts of 200-250 words with 5 keywords. A short biographical note (not more than 150 words), including institutional affiliation and key publications. Please include full contact details. The subject line of the email should state: Submission of Abstracts for the Edited Volume on "Women and Art: Representation, Creativity, and Resistance." Authors selected for inclusion will be invited to submit full chapters (approximately 6,000-7,000 words, including references) following acceptance of the proposal by the publisher. Abstract Submission Deadline: 15 October 2026 Full-Text Submission Deadline: 15 February 2027 Eligibility Contributors are required to hold a PhD. Alternatively, submissions may be co-authored, provided that at least one co-author holds a PhD. In addition, PhD candidates are welcome to submit contributions within their own field of research, particularly if the proposed chapter is directly related to their doctoral project and falls within the thematic and conceptual parameters of this book. Publisher The volume will be published by Maurer Press, Frankfurt am Main, an established publishing house with 35 years of publishing experience. Publication Fee The publication fee for accepted contributions is 115€. Abstracts and inquiries should be sent to: women.art.literature@gmail.com

items.fullDescription: Art and the Making of Belonging: Migration, Mobility & Communities in Formation March 19-20, 2027 State Historical Society of Missouri, Columbia, Missouri How do people create a sense of home and belonging in places shaped by migration and mobility? How do communities sustain traditions, negotiate change, and build connections across difference? In confronting these pressing issues of our time, art and culture often play a central role, serving as powerful tools in building relationships, negotiating difference, and making space for new forms of collective life. The Interdisciplinary Migration Studies Institute invites artists, activists, performers, faith leaders, educators, community organizers, cultural workers, students, migrants, and scholars to join us for a community event that explores this relationship between migration, mobility, creativity, and community. We welcome participants from all backgrounds and encourage contributions that draw on lived experience, creative practice, community engagement, research, or combinations of these approaches. We especially welcome participants who can share their knowledge and experience about the following questions: · How have artistic collaborations created spaces where people from different cultural, linguistic, or religious backgrounds can encounter one another in new ways? · How have communities used art to navigate difference, address tensions, and build connections across lines of migration, identity, and experience? · What role does participation in artistic and cultural life play in fostering belonging for both newcomers and established community members? · How have artists, organizers, educators, faith leaders, and community groups used creative practices to cultivate trust, solidarity, and a shared sense of belonging? · How have museums, cultural institutions, libraries, religious institutions, schools, public spaces, and community organizations used the arts to support meaningful encounters between immigrants and longer-standing community members? The event will feature short presentations, roundtable discussions, performances, workshops, and a gallery exhibition at the State Historical Society of Missouri showcasing projects and creative works. We encourage submissions from individuals and groups. Proposals may be submitted as individual presentations, performances, workshops, exhibits, panels, or other formats that support engagement and dialogue. If you have an idea that does not fit neatly into a traditional conference format, we would be delighted to hear from you. Participation Formats Presentations Presentations will typically be organized into thematic panels consisting of three 20-minute presentations followed by discussion. Presenters will have access to audiovisual support for slide presentations. Roundtable Discussions Roundtables bring together a small group of participants to engage in moderated conversation and audience discussion. Rather than formal presentations, roundtables emphasize dialogue, shared experiences, and collective reflection. We welcome proposals for complete roundtables as well as individual expressions of interest. Workshops Workshops are one-hour, hands-on sessions designed to teach attendees (up to 25 participants) a particular creative practice, collaborative method, or community-engagement approach. Audiovisual support will be available. Media and Performance We welcome both live and recorded performances that showcase or model artistic collaboration. Our venue can accommodate musical, dance, theatrical, spoken-word, and multimedia performances, as well as filmed versions of these forms. Gallery Exhibition The event will feature an accompanying exhibition showcasing artistic, cultural, educational, and community-based projects related to migration, belonging, and community formation. Projects may include visual art, photography, documentary work, storytelling initiatives, community-engaged arts projects, digital media, educational exhibits, oral history projects, and other creative or collaborative endeavors. Proposal Submission Guidelines All proposals must be submitted through the online application portal. The following information is required for all submission types: · Title of the proposed presentation, workshop, performance, or project · Name(s) of all participant(s) · Email address(es) of all participant(s) In addition, please submit the materials listed below for your selected participation format. Panel Presentations · A description of the proposed presentation (300 words or fewer) · A brief biographical statement, including institutional affiliation if applicable (50 words or fewer) Roundtable Discussions · A description of the experience, perspective, or expertise you would bring to the discussion (300 words or fewer) · A brief biographical statement, including institutional affiliation if applicable (50 words or fewer) Workshops · A description of the proposed workshop and its goals (300 words or fewer) · A brief biographical statement, including institutional affiliation if applicable, and relevant experience leading workshops (100 words or fewer) Media and Performance · A description of the proposed performance and its relationship to the event theme (300 words or fewer) · Length of the performance · A description of any on-site needs, including audiovisual equipment, changing rooms, or other accommodations Gallery Exhibition · A project description that includes a statement explaining the project's relevance to the event theme (300 words or fewer) · Up to five images, links, or other supporting materials · A description of display and technical requirements, including needs for wall space, table space, digital displays, audio equipment, or other resources Deadline for Submissions: October 15, 2026 Submit Proposals here: https://missouri.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_4Inv3NNBs7ov7P8

items.excerpt: European Comic Art Special Issue 'Francophone Graphic Narratives / Bande dessinée: Authority and Resistance' European Comic Art invites proposals for a special issue on 'Francophone Graphic Narratives/Bande dessinée: Authority and Resistance'. This issue will examine how francophone graphic narratives engage with, challenge, and reimagine authority in its...
items.fullDescription: European Comic Art Special Issue 'Francophone Graphic Narratives / Bande dessinée: Authority and Resistance' European Comic Art invites proposals for a special issue on 'Francophone Graphic Narratives/Bande dessinée: Authority and Resistance'. This issue will examine how francophone graphic narratives engage with, challenge, and reimagine authority in its many forms - political, cultural, institutional, and aesthetic - and how they forge practices of resistance and dissent. The bande dessinée is a medium that subverts hierarchies and blurs boundaries. Long regarded as the lowly offspring of literature and the visual arts, comics have since been legitimised by scholars and artists demonstrating their capacity to engage with complex sociohistorical, political, and cultural topics. This 'Ninth Art' now occupies an increasingly important place in university classrooms, academic publications, and public discourse alike. Its multimodal features - panel layout, gutters, framing, braiding, and complex interplay between text and image - allow comics to stage and challenge authority in formally distinctive ways. This aesthetic vantage point makes comics a powerful medium through which to bring displaced, excluded, and silenced narratives into view. From Chantal Montellier's impressive four-decade oeuvre of political cartoons and graphic novels contesting racism, misogyny and totalitarianism to Jessica Oublié's Peyi an nou , which provides a counternarrative to state discourse on the BUMIDOM, the bande dessinée has often served to undercut official rhetoric. This special issue of European Comic Art seeks articles that examine how Francophone bandes dessinées engage with dominant institutions and discourses from theoretical and pedagogical perspectives. How do comics represent power and powerlessness? How do they respond to hierarchies that exist in various settings and communities? How do they decentre and challenge 'standard' language practices? Finally, how might comics be used pedagogically to help foster students' critical thinking skills and question institutional, political, and social discourses? Possible topics include, but are not limited to: Migration Ecocriticism Social justice and political activism Gender and sexuality Comics and memory studies Class, labour, and economic inequality Pedagogy and second language acquisition Nationalism, cosmopolitanism, and globalization Colonial legacies, decolonial resistance/critique Monolingualism, multilingualism, and language politics Official histories, counter archives, and silenced narratives Humour, parody, satire, and subversion Submission Guidelines Please submit a 500-word abstract with a short biographical note to Liana Pshevorska at lpshevorska@wesleyan.edu and Valentina Denzel at vdenzel@msu.edu by October 15, 2026. Informal inquiries are welcome. Decisions will be communicated in November 2026. The deadline for submitting full manuscripts is February 28, 2027. Articles should be in English, approximately 8,000 words, including images, notes, and bibliography. Contributors may include up to four images, which will be factored into the overall length of the article. Each image will be counted as approximately three-quarters of a printed page, based on an estimate 400 words per page. Please note that authors are responsible for obtaining copyright permission for all included images. Documentation of permissions should be submitted alongside the manuscript.

items.title: Exploring the Boundary Waters of the Blue Humanities
items.excerpt: Call for Papers: NANO: New American Notes Online (ISSN: 2160-0104) Special Issue 18: Exploring the Boundary Waters of the Blue Humanities Special Issue Guest Editors: Eric Denbang Kunkuri and Dana Van Kooy Deadline: 16 October 2026 Publication: spring/summer 2027 Full CFP Details: https://nanocrit.com/index.php/home/cfp-plus-submissions-new The creative a...
items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: NANO: New American Notes Online (ISSN: 2160-0104) Special Issue 18: Exploring the Boundary Waters of the Blue Humanities Special Issue Guest Editors: Eric Denbang Kunkuri and Dana Van Kooy Deadline: 16 October 2026 Publication: spring/summer 2027 Full CFP Details: https://nanocrit.com/index.php/home/cfp-plus-submissions-new The creative and scholarly work being done in the blue humanities has deepened our turn towards exploring waterways and boundary waters. The currents circulating through the blue humanities flow into and from myriad disciplines, including anthropology, biology, decolonial studies, feminist/queer studies, geography, history, indigenous studies, literature, music, performance studies, philosophy, and the visual arts. The cultural and theoretical inlets being carved out by work in the blue humanities have proven generative in terms of developing a distinctive metaphor-laden language, analytic methods like Kamau Brathwaite's theory of "tidalectics," and new ways of submerging ourselves in both historical and unprecedented questions about the water that is in and, as Rachel Carson notes in her famous title, "around us." For this special issue, we invite submissions of traditional and multimodal essays of up to 5,000 words (excluding works cited) that explore the boundary waters of the blue humanities. We encourage essays focused on narratives as well as submissions that explore art installations and other medial forms that address the boundary waters circulating around and through the blue humanities. Topics may include but are not limited to the following: Boundary waters that divide and connect nations, classes, and/or ecological zones Mythic, cinematic, and visual narratives of how humans and/or nonhumans are "held," migrate, or are moved through watery littorals Critical explorations like those associated with "tidalectics," a term that comes from Kamau Brathwaite, who proposed an alternative framework for literary and political engagement that is grounded in the rhythm of waves and the cyclic ebb and flow of tides "Portraits" of littoral space(s) in literature, history, myth, the visual arts, and theatrical and musical performances Exploring the significance of physical, structural, and emotional vulnerabilities and instabilities within littorals, shoals, or port cities Hydrological infrastructure (colonial, postcolonial, urban, rural) associated with port cities, canal locks, and dams Relational undercurrents that speak to our ways of submerging ourselves into the watery worlds that surround us Traditional water ways: ways of being with or "holding" water The role of inland waterways in routing stories and/or facilitating/impeding human and nonhuman migrations items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters Proposals Submission Deadline: July 17, 2026 Full Chapters Due: October 30, 2026 Submission Date: October 30, 2026 Introduction This edited collection features scholarly voices with attention to horror in its transmedia representations, including film, literature, comics, art, branding, and more. Chapters give attention to the ways that fans take up the realities and ideas presented in horror, the affordances of the genre, and participation in this network of storytelling. The reactions of readers/viewers/fans, the decisions of creatives, the presentation of ideas within particular forms of media, and more form elements of the researched conversation in this volume. Objective This collection seeks to advance conversation about the theoretical functions of horror across media including notions of adaptation and literary/literacy-based choices in the work. This includes, but is not limited to, design structures, cultural influences, the role of lore, (re)considerations of the monstrous, embodiment in the genre, sub-genre considerations, and more. Target Audience This book is intended for academics in media, literacy, literature, communication, and interdisciplinary fields. Students enrolled in courses in these fields can benefit from this knowledge as they pursue courses of study and further academic work in these disciplines. Recommended Topics Emotional and Philosophical Reactions to Horror Media Themes and Interactions across Media Representations in the Genre Adaptation Processes/Decisions/Designs in Horror across Media Studies of Narrative and Response/Interpretation Recent Trends/Movements in Horror Theoretical Approaches to Horror Composition/Representation Analysis of Race, Gender, Class in Horror Considerations and Reconsiderations of the Monstrous Author/Creator Decisions and Purposes in the Genre/across Media Horror Character and Author/Director Studies Critical and Analytical Work on Embodiment in Horror Critical and Analytical Examinations of Cultural Stories in the Genre The Role of Lore/Mythology in Horror Studies of Writing/Creating Processes in the Genre Fandom Communities, Fan Fiction, Cosplay, and Other Responses Submission Procedure Researchers and practitioners are invited to submit on or before July 17, 2026, a chapter proposal of 1,000 to 2,000 words clearly explaining the mission and concerns of his or her proposed chapter. Authors will be notified by July 31, 2026 about the status of their proposals and sent chapter guidelines.Full chapters of a minimum of 10,000 words (word count includes references and related readings) are expected to be submitted by October 30, 2026, and all interested authors must consult the guidelines for manuscript submissions at https://www.igi-global.com/publish/contributor-resources/before-you-write/ prior to submission. All submitted chapters will be reviewed on a double-anonymized review basis. Contributors may also be requested to serve as reviewers for this project. Note: There are no submission or acceptance fees for manuscripts submitted to this book publication, Theory and Practice in Horror Transmedia Fandom and Creation. All manuscripts are accepted based on a double-anonymized peer review editorial process. All proposals should be submitted through the eEditorial Discovery® online submission manager. Publisher This book is scheduled to be published by IGI Global Scientific Publishing, an international academic publisher of the "Information Science Reference", "Medical Information Science Reference", "Business Science Reference", and "Engineering Science Reference" imprints. IGI Global Scientific Publishing specializes in publishing reference books, scholarly journals, and electronic databases featuring academic research on a variety of innovative topic areas including, but not limited to, education, social science, medicine and healthcare, business and management, information science and technology, engineering, public administration, library and information science, media and communication studies, and environmental science. For additional information regarding the publisher, please visit https://www.igi-global.com. This publication is anticipated to be released in 2027. IGI Global Scientific Publishing books are selectively indexed by the indexing organization after publication. Indexing cannot be guaranteed for any book prior to publication, and the indexing organization has complete control over the final selection and timeline. Is eco-centric thought a universally shared ideology, or does it develop in reaction to historical, philosophical, and socio-cultural contexts? Known for her sharp lyrics, her evolving cross-genre musical styles, and her dedicated, creative fanbase (the Swifties), Swift's influence has been noted within music, fashion, economics, politics, and other cultural spheres of power. As an interdisciplinary area, we invite papers from multiple perspectives and disciplines. Topics might include, but are not limited to: • Critical interpretations of Swift's lyrics, eras, and/or personas • Considerations of Taylor Swift and politics, feminisms, activism and social justice • Interrogations of Swift and gender, race, class, and other identities/identifications • Analyses of Swift's connections to business, law, psychology, philosophy or other academic disciplines • Arguments about fandom, belonging, relating, creating and other Swiftie concerns • Examples of Taylor Swift's pedagogical relevancy All proposals must be submitted through the conference's database at https://swpaca.org/app. For details on using the submission database and on the application process in general (including submitting proposals for roundtables and preformed panels), please see the FAQS & Resources tab on https://swpaca.org/. Esotericism, Occultism, and Magic invites proposals relating to magical worldviews, practices, and representations, as well as consciousness transformation, the preternatural, the paranormal, hidden meanings, the power of transmutation, and related phenomena. Characteristic methods, beliefs, perspectives, paradigms and techniques include: arcane symbolism, imagery, and aesthetics; unseen forces, spiritual intermediaries, invisible agencies, nonhuman intelligences; synchronous patterns, non-ordinary causation, and anomalous processes. Examples of ideas and systems include Hermeticism, Gnosticism, Sufism, Tantra, Rosicrucianism, Freemasonry, Satanism, witchcraft, sorcery, demonology, astrology, alchemy, yoga, shamanism, parapsychology, as well as psychic and paranormal phenomena, along with beliefs and practices relating to altered states of consciousness, overlapping with the study of mysticism and New Age spirituality, channeling, positive thinking, manifestation, reality shifting, the power of intention, numerology, guardian angels, and Ascended Masters. Esoteric, occult, and magical concepts, beliefs, and practices appear in every culture and civilization; contemporary media and popular culture have embraced them enthusiastically, yet at times have reacted against them. The impact of esotericism, occultism, and magic on genre formation/content and popular cultural perceptions has been profound. Their themes and tropes continue to become increasingly prevalent throughout all media of popular entertainment, including arts, music, literature, film, television, anime, comics and graphic novels, as well as being nearly ubiquitous throughout interactive gaming of all categories and genres. Examples include demonic intelligences in "AI" chatbots, anti-occult-conspiracism in QAnon; adrenochrome confabulations, Illuminati paranoia, bloodline of the Holy Grail beliefs, Satanic Ritual Abuse scandals. items.excerpt: CALL FOR CHAPTERS The Handbook of Boredom in Modern Literature Editors: Mariusz Finkielsztein (University of Gdan?sk) mariusz.finkielsztein@gmail.com Josefa Ros Velasco (Complutense University of Madrid) josros@ucm.es The Handbook of Boredom in Modern Literature is to be a comprehensive monographic study examining boredom as a central aesthetic, philosoph...
items.fullDescription: CALL FOR CHAPTERS The Handbook of Boredom in Modern Literature Editors: Mariusz Finkielsztein (University of Gdan?sk) mariusz.finkielsztein@gmail.com Josefa Ros Velasco (Complutense University of Madrid) josros@ucm.es The Handbook of Boredom in Modern Literature is to be a comprehensive monographic study examining boredom as a central aesthetic, philosophical, psychological, and socio-cultural category in the history of modern literature. Rather than relying purely on abstract theory, this volume approaches boredom through focused case studies devoted to individual authors and their works. Across these chapters, boredom-alongside adjacent states such as ennui, tedium, spleen, acedia, melancholy, existential malaise, and affective exhaustion-emerges variously as paralysis, protest, privilege, illness, and spiritual crisis. By situating close textual readings within the broader intellectual history of modernity, the volume, written by a multidisciplinary group of authors, is to demonstrate that literary boredom is a powerful diagnostic lens on social order, temporality, and the modern subject's experience of meaninglessness. Volume Structure & Epochal Scope The volume is planned as a Handbook or Companion and covers not only the most vital writers addressing the theme of boredom but also a broad selection of modern authors (around 60 chapters). The book is to trace the evolution of literary boredom across (tentatively) seven historical and thematic phases: Early Modernity & Enlightenment Foundations: Early reflections on existential void and social routine (e.g. Diderot, Laclos, Austen). Romantic Ennui (1770s-1840s): Melancholy, idealist frustration, and the world-weary anti-hero (e.g., Goethe, de Stae?l, Senancour, Byron, Chateaubriand, Constant, Stendhal, Sand, Balzac, Musset). The Superfluous Man: The Russian literary archetype of social paralysis, alienation, and unfulfilled potential (e.g. Pushkin, Lermontov, Goncharov, Turgenev). Bourgeois Boredom, Realism, & Decadent Spleen: Domestic stagnation, industrial monotony, social entrapment, and aesthetic decay (e.g., Dickens, Flaubert, Tolstoy, Fontane, Chopin, Ibsen, Gilman, Conrad, Chekhov, Baudelaire, Huysmans, Wilde). Modernist Stagnation (Early 20th C.): Temporal distortion, consciousness, alienation, and metaphysical paralysis (e.g., Proust, Joyce, Pessoa, Mann, Kafka, Woolf). Catastrophism & Existential Absurdity (Mid-20th C.): Totalitarian dread, the absurdity of existence, and postwar existential malaise (e.g., Broch, Platonov, Orwell, H. Miller, Gombrowicz, Sartre, Camus, Beckett, Buzzati, Gracq). Postwar Emptiness, Consumerism, & Digital Fatigue: Mass society, late-capitalist hyper-consumption, information overload, and contemporary affective exhaustion (e.g., Moravia, Perec, de Beauvoir, Ernaux, Bellow, Bernhard, Duras, DeLillo, Houellebecq, Ferrante, Rourke, Moshfegh). Chapter Guidelines & Scope Each chapter must offer an in-depth analysis of the theme of broadly understood boredom in the work of a single author (according to a formula: Boredom in...). The title should include the name and surname of a writer as a main part, and a freely formulated subtitle. Analytical Approach: Authors may focus on a single representative work but should analyse boredom across multiple texts of an author to demonstrate how boredom functions as a recurring motif in the author's oeuvre. Target Audience: Written primarily for readers seeking to deepen their understanding of boredom in a specific author's work (spoilers are permitted), while remaining accessible to a general literary audience. Comparative analysis with other writers should be kept to a minimum. Required Contextual Elements: o Biographical Context: Key details situating the writer within their epoch. Where applicable, personal engagement with boredom (e.g., excerpts from letters, diaries) may be included. o Socio-Cultural Context: Historical background necessary to understand the specific societal structures depicting boredom (e.g., aristocratic class dynamics, marital systems, late-capitalist work environments, author's country history and socio-cultural context). Submission guidelines: The abstract of the proposed chapter (between 250-500 words) along with a short bio (up to 150 words) and contact information should be sent to editors via e-mail before the end of October 2026. Contributors may propose up to two chapters. Each submission must include a brief statement detailing: (a) how the chosen author's work relates to boredom; and (b) what the contributor's expertise is on the writer. The minimum criteria for inclusion of a writer are: the author must address themes of boredom/ennui, possess at least some international recognition, and be available in English translation. Poetry is excluded. The comments and decisions on the proposed chapters will be provided before the end of December 2026. Then, the proposal for the book will be sent to prospective publishers (Routledge Handbook Series, The Oxford Handbooks, The Cambridge Companions or The Palgrave Handbooks). In case of a positive answer from a publisher, the authors will be asked to prepare the chapter, between 6,000 and 8,000 words including footnotes and references. Technical information will be provided after the publisher accepts the proposal and will depend on the publisher's style. In case of any doubts and/or questions, we encourage prospective authors to consult the editors directly. Prospective deadline for chapters: mid-2028

items.fullDescription: John Steinbeck once remarked that fellow-Californian Robinson Jeffers wrote some the "greatest poetry since Whitman." Steinbeck kept a significant collection of Jeffers work both in his personal library and Ed Ricketts' Lab, where Jeffers was an influential topic in their endlessly varied conversations. When asked about possibility of meeting the poet, Steinbeck declined with a telling degree of reverence: "His poetry is perfect to me, and I don't think one should get the man mixed up with his work." Although they did eventually meet-notably when Steinbeck lived in Monterey in 1944-their relationship was one of distant, though friendly, mutual respect. Although these two writers rarely crossed physical paths, their work maintains a wide concurrence of concern. They both deeply engaged with Californian geography and history; they both emphasized the influence of the natural world upon the individual and society; they both had social circles that revolved around the Monterey Peninsula; they both were interested in psychoanalytical theory; they both were students of classical literature and philosophy; they both experienced extraordinary recognition at the peak of their literary fame (at one point, Jeffers was on the cover of Time magazine); they both were deeply uncomfortable with such a cultural spotlight; they both admonished personal humility in the face of environmental forces. Intersections such as these (and many more) deserve to be explored with more depth and significance. The editorial staff at the Steinbeck Review invites submissions for a special edition, "John Steinbeck and Robinson Jeffers." We are particularly interested in perspectives which put these authors into conversation in productive and even unexpected ways. Although submissions are not required to examine both authors, we strongly suggest that they engage (even if briefly) both Steinbeck and Jeffers. We welcome all critical and theoretical perspectives. Please see the full guide for submissions here and submit your paper to the Steinbeck Review's online submission system, found at www.editorialmanager.com/Steinbeck, no later than October 31, 2026. Decisions will be made by December 1, 2026. Submissions should be accompanied by an abstract and key words.

items.title: Irony: Dramatic and Otherwise
items.location: University of Tübingen, Germany · Connotations: A Journal for Critical Debate
items.excerpt: Literary irony is a phenomenon that seems expressly invented for the approach Connotations: A Journal for Critical Debate (www.connotations.de) wishes to promote, namely combining the close reading of literary texts with wider theoretical perspectives. Clearly, irony is a textual feature, and it equally clearly reaches beyond individual texts in that it e...
items.fullDescription: Literary irony is a phenomenon that seems expressly invented for the approach Connotations: A Journal for Critical Debate (www.connotations.de) wishes to promote, namely combining the close reading of literary texts with wider theoretical perspectives. Clearly, irony is a textual feature, and it equally clearly reaches beyond individual texts in that it evokes and reflects basic constituents of human communication: in particular, the relationship between what is said and what is meant and the relationship between what is said and what is known. Irony comes into play when these relationships are marked by significant discrepancies. The discrepancy between what is said and what is meant is essential for verbal irony and the discrepancy between what is said and what is known is fundamental to dramatic (or narrative) irony. If and how these two kinds of irony belong together, however, is a moot point and one of the questions to be addressed by our symposium. Thus the unequal distribution of knowledge (between characters and/or between characters and the reader) which marks narrative and dramatic irony may be related to the divergence which characterizes verbal irony. When Viola in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, disguised as a boy, says to Orsino: "I am all the daughters of my father's house," Orsino, who believes Viola to be a young man, must regard this statement as verbal irony on Viola's part. What is said ("daughters") is very different from what appears to be meant ("sons"). To us, the audience, however, this is a case of dramatic irony since we know that Viola is a woman and we observe Orsino's ignorance. What makes this case particularly intriguing is that here dramatic irony is not based on a discrepancy between what is said and what we know since Viola literally speaks the truth. The discrepancy arises between what we know and what is supposed to be spoken ironically. The example shows that asking about the relationship between verbal and dramatic/narrative irony entails numerous other questions that the Connotations symposium is going to address. In particular, we will ask about effects of irony, both with regard to characters and the audience. What is the added value of an ironic remark? What does it tell us about the speaker? In what way does an ironic utterance signal that there is a common ground between the communication partners? Are the inclusion and exclusion of others, i.e. those who get the ironical meaning and those who don't, similar to cases of discrepant awareness? How do we know that an utterance is meant ironically and how are we to deal with ambiguity in this respect? Can non-verbal irony markers be encoded in literary texts? Are theories of verbal irony based on notions of echo and pretence relatable to drama and fiction? We invite papers focussing on these and related questions, based on literature in English from the Middle Ages to the present. Please send an abstract (300 words max.) to the editors of Connotations at symposium2027@connotations.de by 31 October 2026

items.fullDescription: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture, and Activism Call for Chapters Description: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture and Activism addresses the critical need for a comprehensive academic survey of Hip Hop's connection to sport as a preeminent sociological and political force among Millennials and Generation Z. This handbook maps the emerging critical terrain where Hip Hop intersects with the sports-industrial complex, digital activism, and the persistent structures of racial capitalism and white supremacy. As the culture enters its second half-century, it serves as an emergent space for self-expression and identity formation, both to hegemonic and counter-hegemonic ends. The leading objectives of this volume are to delineate how Hip Hop's relationship with sport provides narrative resources for youth to explore their social realities in the context of late-stage capitalism and its bedfellows: white supremacy and patriarchy. This handbook explores both the route and roots of Hip Hop expression through the lens of the African diaspora and the historical relationship between Black expressive history and social movements. This handbook is also interested in the ways in which Hip Hop's relationship with sport can be oriented both towards liberation and political conservatism, particularly in the context of Hip Hop's historical and presentist embrace of Donald Trump and his representative movements. This project aims to both engage Hip Hop's historical relationship with sports (professional and amateur) as well as its contemporary shifts,such as the institutionalization of breaking in the 2024 Olympics and the rise of representation activism in major sports leagues (NBA, NFL) that create new tensions between cultural authenticity and corporate appropriation. It is intended to define the current state of theory and establish a foundation for future scholarship across the interdisciplinary fields of hip-hop studies, sport management, and Africana studies. Since this project is a handbook and not an anthology, the chapter topics have already been pre-selected by the editors. However, we encourage submissions that engage the specific areas of expertise of each contributor, and the contributor is welcome to interpret the proposed topics according to their own research and experience. The targeted audience for this handbook are advanced high school students and undergraduates, so chapters should be written with this audience in mind. We invite abstract submissions from Hip Hop practitioners, sport sociologists, scholars, graduate students, postgraduate researchers, and early career researchers. Details for Submission: Abstracts of 250-300 words for the chapters listed below must be submitted by October 31st, 2026. Microsoft Word or PDF formats will be accepted. When submitting your abstract, please include your name, affiliation, email address, title of chapter, and short biography (100 words). Authors will be notified of their acceptance by November 30th, 2026. Full chapters of 4,000-6,000 words (including references) are due by April 30th, 2027. For further questions, contact Dr. Micah J. Dobson (mjdobson92@gmail.com ) and Dr. Tyler Bunzey (tylerbunzey@gmail.com). Table of Contents Section 1: Hip-Hop: A Cultural Politic Chapter 1: The Context of Hip-Hop's Roots and Routes in the Early 1970s Chapter 2: Political Movements that Impacted Hip-Hop's Foundation Chapter 3: Hip-Hop's Formal Political Movements like "Rock the Vote" Chapter 4: Hip-Hop and Moral Panic Section 2: Hip-Hop Generating Identity Chapter 5: Hip-Hop and Generational Identity in the "Post-Racial" Era Chapter 6: Obama, Neoliberalism, and Hip-Hop Mainstream Partisan Politics Chapter 7: From "FDT" to Kodak Black: Hip-Hop's Complicated Relationship with Trump Chapter 8: Hip-Hop and the Black Lives Matter Movement Chapter 9: "Alright" and Social Protests Against Police Brutality Section 3: Hip-Hop and the Sports-Industrial Complex Chapter 10: A History of the Relationship Between Hip-Hop and Sport Chapter 11: Subculture to Spectacle: The Evolution of Breaking and Olympic Institutionalization Chapter 12: Ice Cube, The Big Three, and Mogul "Activism" Chapter 13: Jay-Z and the Problematics of the Roc Nation-NFL Partnership Section 4: Representing: Hip-Hop and Sport Chapter 14: The Politics of Aesthetics: Street Fashion, the Tunnel Walk, and Racialized Pleasure Chapter 15: Generational Agency: From Michael Jordan's Brand to LeBron's "Representation Activism" Chapter 16: The WNBA and Queering Hip-Hop Aesthetics Chapter 17: Hip-Hop Dance as Art and Sport

items.fullDescription: Framing the Human in the Nineteenth Century 48th Annual Conference Nineteenth-Century Studies Association Philadelphia, PA March 11-13, 2027 Conference website: https://ncsaweb.net/2027-conference-information/ Call for Proposals Submission Deadline: October 31, 2026 Notification of Acceptance: January 2027 Please submit proposals via this Google Form Questions? Email the conference organizers at ncsa2027conference@gmail.com The Nineteenth-Century Studies Association (NCSA) invites proposals for 15-minute papers (300-word proposal) or complete panels of 3-4 papers (600-word proposal) that examine the shifting meanings and status of "the human" in the long nineteenth century-a period shaped by transformative scientific, social, and philosophical developments that continue to inform present-day thought. During this time, evolutionary theory and social Darwinism challenged the boundaries between humans and animals and raised new questions about human difference across race, class, and ethnicity. Theological and philosophical discourses reevaluated humanity's relationship to the divine, while pseudosciences such as phrenology, physiognomy, and anthropometry sought to codify human variation through tools of measurement often aligned with colonial and racial hierarchies. Advances in the natural sciences speculated on human origins and extraterrestrial life, situating "the human" within a larger cosmic framework. Industrialization redefined labor and bodily limits, generating anxieties about overpopulation, and paradoxically, race suicide and population extinction. Amid these pressures, labor and voting rights movements gained momentum, as marginalized groups fought for full inclusion. We welcome proposals from a variety of disciplines that engage with these and other transformations that redefined what it meant to be human-and to belong to humanity-across the long nineteenth century. Topics may include, but are not limited to: The influence of evolutionary theory on concepts of the human and the human/animal divide, including artistic and literary responses Scientific efforts to define human origins and difference through anthropology, racial theory, and other emerging disciplines Population anxieties related to degeneration, overpopulation, and demographic change Emancipated and enslaved bodies The effects of industrialization and technological advancement on understandings of the human body, labor, and automation The rise of the human sciences-psychology, physiology, and medicine-and new approaches to the mind and self Migration and the movement of people, and their impact on ideas of race, nation, and identity Secularization and shifting relationships between the human and the divine Changing human relationships to the environment and the nonhuman world Human rights, labor, and suffrage movements and the redefinition of personhood Transformations in education and access to knowledge The role of cultural institutions (museums, libraries, exhibitions) in shaping public and humanist discourse

Collecting now operates as a dynamic source for epistemic production, constantly redefining how popular culture is constructed, construed, mediated, valorized, historicized, and even contested. The 2027 PCA conference theme is "Revolutions & Revisions in Popular Culture." Presenters in Collecting and Collectibles Area are invited to consider how their work might engage with questions of transformation, reinterpretation, innovation, resistance, adaptation, or cultural change. Theme-related proposals are welcome but not required, and all submissions relevant to the area will receive full consideration. We welcome contributions that integrate practice-based, collaborative, comparative, transnational and cross-cultural approaches and involve innovative methods, community engagement, public and digital humanities to address topics including, but not limited to: --Emerging Technologies of Collecting: AI and collecting cultures, virtual archives, NFTs and blockchain collectibles, social media collecting communities, online marketplaces and economies, smart museums, mixed- reality collections, and AI-enabled smart twins of museums --Participatory Collecting Culture: Gaming memorabilia and sports collections, comic books, manga, anime, and graphic novels, fan archives, and exclusive/ limited editions --Popular Media collecting: Film and television memorabilia, music and vinyl records, cassettes, CDs, concert and artist-branded merchandise, celebrity memorabilia, fast-food promotional premiums, licensed toys, action figure and doll sets, LEGO, and theme park merchandise -- Heritage and Transcultural collecting: counter archives and collectibles, indigenous collections, digitality and heritage preservation, migration and portable collectibles, cultural diplomacy collections -- Crisis Collecting: Climate change and at-risk collections, pandemic collecting, trauma and collecting, sustainable and ethical colleting, resilient collections, commemorative coins and medals, satirical magazines, post-collapse souvenirs, war memorabilia -- Consumer Culture and Collecting: Auctions and collector markets and communities, investment collecting, branding and nostalgic collecting, resale platforms -- Materiality of Collecting: household collectibles, stamps, travel souvenirs, and their digital adaptations We welcome individual papers, complete panels, creative presentations, and interdisciplinary collaborations. items.title: Watching Cinema Theoretically: Psychoanalytic Perspectives on Film
items.excerpt: The relation between a theory and its so-called “object” always poses the danger of reducing an art form (in this case film) to a mere instance testifying to the validity of the theory. items.fullDescription: The relation between a theory and its so-called “object” always poses the danger of reducing an art form (in this case film) to a mere instance testifying to the validity of the theory. In this way, the theory provides the “genus” of which a given film will be a mere “species”. The application of psychoanalytic ideas or Marxist concepts to film would therefore run the risk of depriving the specificity and singularity of the object in favour of the hegemony of the theory. Here, theory would truly live up to its theological vocation (the “theo” in theory refers to God) standing transcendentally above its “object” upon which it would cast its daunting shadow.
