items.excerpt: Consuming US Popular Culture: Media Aesthetics, Ethics and Literacy Virtual Conference | 27-28 November 2026 The consumption of popular culture and media, particularly through platforms and social networks, has become one of the most common leisure time activities worldwide, and US productions are one of the most circulated. Television series, films, vide...
items.fullDescription: Consuming US Popular Culture: Media Aesthetics, Ethics and Literacy Virtual Conference | 27-28 November 2026 The consumption of popular culture and media, particularly through platforms and social networks, has become one of the most common leisure time activities worldwide, and US productions are one of the most circulated. Television series, films, videogames, TikTokers, podcasters, memes and other forms of digital culture reach global audiences and shape political identities and cultural imaginaries. Far from being mere entertainment, these texts have consequently become intertwined and virtually inseparable from the daily practices through which individuals get their news input and even their education. The purpose of this year's virtual conference is to open a space for the analysis of the ethical principles (or lack thereof) that seem to guide the construction, circulation and reception of public discourses within the popular culture ecosystem, including both more traditional mediums such as television and comics, but also the products that emerge from generative AI. Popular media content exists as a key source of information in public discourse and influences how we interpret contemporary political issues, how we teach and learn, and even how we exist and behave in society. Although media effects have long been proven to be negotiated rather than direct, the understanding of desirable aesthetics, mindless entertainment and the rhetoric used in political discussions have been hugely impacted by AI generated content. With this cultural media environment in mind, this virtual conference invites explorations of US popular culture through the perspective of media ethics, media literacy and aesthetics. We aim at establishing a space of discussion on the political, educational, ethical and social implications of contemporary media consumption through the analysis of US popular culture. The conference welcomes contributions that tackle the ethical dimensions and societal impact of US popular culture across a wide range of media forms and how they operate within the fragmented and algorithmically curated media ecosystem that we inhabit. We welcome analysis of both mainstream and independent productions, historical and contemporary texts, as well as emerging digital practices. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: × Media ethics and the social responsibilities of producers, platforms and audiences × Media literacy as a framework for analyzing contemporary popular culture × Popular culture as a case study for developing media literacy, ethical reasoning and critical thinking in education × The teaching potential behind popular media texts × Media effects and audience reception of US popular culture × Social media trends, influencers and memes × AI aesthetics in popular media × Polarization, misinformation, conspiracy narratives, and the circulation of disinformation through popular media × (Un)ethical representation of minorities × Political communication, civic engagement, and democratic participation through entertainment media × Representation of political and social problems in US popular culture Deadline for proposals: 1 November 2026 We accept abstract proposals for individual presentations (≈ 250 words), as well as full panels (3 presenters, ≈ 250-word description of the panel plus brief abstracts of all papers). Please, submit your abstract proposal via email at popmec.media@gmail.com as a single attachment (.doc, .docx, .odt) including name, affiliation (if any), and contact email.

items.fullDescription: The First International Conference "Genealogies of Healing: Nineteenth-Century Hispanic Culture and Dialogues with Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean in the Digital Age" will be held on March 29-31, 2027, at the University of Costa Rica, Western Campus (Sede de Occidente). This international academic event seeks to bring together researchers, academics, artists, educators, and professionals from different disciplines to explore the historical, cultural, social, artistic, scientific, and technological dimensions of healing and well-being. The Congress proposes a dialogue between nineteenth-century traditions and contemporary approaches to health and healing, examining continuities, transformations, exchanges, and tensions across the Hispanic world, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Particular attention will be given to the ways in which literature, art, spirituality, traditional medicine, bodily practices, digital technologies, and community experiences have shaped understandings and practices of healing. Suggested themes include: Genealogies of Healing in Nineteenth-Century Hispanic Culture Representations of Illness in Nineteenth-Century Literature and the Press Art and Healing: Music, Dance, Painting, and Theatre as Therapeutic Practices Dialogues between Allopathic Medicine and Traditional Healing Systems Spirituality, Religion, and Healing Practices Healing through Words: Narratives, Discourse, and Therapeutic Processes Convergences between Bodily Practices (Yoga, Pranayama, Sports) and Holistic Health Healing Traditions in Asia and the Caribbean: Exchanges with the Hispanic World Digital Health, Applications, Platforms, and Well-Being Monitoring Ethical and Clinical Risks of Chatbots and Mental Health Technologies Social Media, Virality, and Their Impact on Emotional Health Attention, Cognition, and Technology Digital Churches, the Spiritual Economy, and New Forms of Religiosity Education and Well-Being Public Health Policies in Digital and Multicultural Environments Interdisciplinarity in Health: Intersections between Art, Science, and Technology Imaginaries of Good and Evil in Processes of Illness and Healing Community Well-Being and Territorial Experiences Researchers interested in participating are invited to submit proposals in accordance with the Congress guidelines. items.excerpt: Call for Submissions MusicTheatreDance: The Journal of the Music Theatre Dance Association Issue 1 (2027) "Imagine it" Editors: Stephanie Lim, Kathryn Edney, Hye Won Kim, Vicki Hoskins, Shiraz Biggie, and Adrienne Oehlers Imagine it: Scholarship as performance. Performance as practice. Practice as inquiry. Inquiry as pedagogy. Join us in imagining what Mu...
items.fullDescription: Call for Submissions MusicTheatreDance: The Journal of the Music Theatre Dance Association Issue 1 (2027) "Imagine it" Editors: Stephanie Lim, Kathryn Edney, Hye Won Kim, Vicki Hoskins, Shiraz Biggie, and Adrienne Oehlers Imagine it: Scholarship as performance. Performance as practice. Practice as inquiry. Inquiry as pedagogy. Join us in imagining what MusicTheatreDance Journal can be. We call upon you, the scholars, educators, and practitioners in and across the performing arts, to help us envision how to break down the barriers in traditional scholarship and the communities in which we co-exist. We invite you to join us as we seek to open boundaries between fields of study in the arts, de-silo the material, and innovate the structure. We ask, how can this journal serve as a host to expand the edges of our fields and reach across the "in-betweens" to serve the varying needs of the wide range of the authorial voices in our communities? What form should scholarship take? What are the containers for scholarly rigor and thought and how can we expand and support all ideas? The Music Theatre Dance Association (MTDA) is pleased to announce a call for content for the first full issue of its flagship publication, MusicTheatreDance, intended for release in 2027. This free, open-access, peer-reviewed journal will be a multi-disciplinary space for investigations at the intersections of music, theatre, dance, and other disciplines. Seeking to disrupt traditional disciplinary boundaries, this multimodal journal will live online, playing host to both conventional scholarly essays and digital scholarship that takes other forms. We imagine a journal where a conventional 7,000-word article sits alongside choreographic analysis, a video essay, a conversation between practitioners, an interactive digital piece, an artist's notebook, or a speculative work-each reviewed according to criteria appropriate to its form rather than asking for everything to fit into the same mold. MusicTheatreDance seeks submissions across the full range of content and form, including traditional academic scholarship, artistic work, pedagogical scholarship, and other forms of research which may or may not address the theme of this first issue, "Imagine It." Our journal is poised to be a forum for timely, engaged, and innovative scholarship that fosters conversation across the field. We welcome both traditional and experimental forms of scholarly engagement that will ultimately guide the shape and scope of our three editorial sections. The editorial team offers these general categories for your submissions in the hope that the originality in form and content widens our own conceptual ideas of what our journal can be. As a starting place, your submissions can range from longer-form, more traditional, peer-reviewed article contributions (in the range of approximately 5,000-7,000 words) to non-text based submissions that engage with and build upon scholarship in the field. We are actively seeking less formal, shorter-form contributions, including and especially experiments in form and works-in-process. We are also soliciting a medley of traditional book and performance reviews, as well as less conventional and/or hybrid forms, such as interviews, dialogues, roundtables, letters to the field, commentaries, practice-as-research and pedagogical reflections, rehearsal or field documentation, annotated images, conference reports, and archive and media reviews. Submissions for the Summer 2027 issue will be accepted by November 18, 2026. Submissions will be accepted thereafter on a rolling basis for future issues, and authors/creators should submit directly via this link. The editorial team will determine the placement of work into respective sections internally. If your work takes a multimedia or nontraditional form that is not easily uploadable there, please send a query, including a complete project description and explanation of its form, in lieu of the completed work itself. Conventional texts should be prepared according to the Chicago Manual of Style. All submissions considered for the Peer-Reviewed section will be subject to anonymous evaluation. The editors of our inaugural issue (0.5) of MusicTheatreDance from Summer 2025 directed us to envision a publication that is global in its content and authorship. We continue to envision a publication that is open in every way and that does things differently. While the editorial team welcomes submissions on all applicable topics, special consideration will be given to submissions aligned with the objectives of MTDA: those which de-center white cis-heteropatriarchy. In particular, the editors encourage submissions that foreground equitable and anti-racist practices and methodologies, and/or that elevate the work of BIPOC, LGBTQIA+, disabled, women-identified, and global-majority artists and scholars. MusicTheatreDance will be published once annually online by MTDA. In addition to the sections described above, it will feature the emerging scholars' Bruce Kirle Memorial Debut Panel essays, honored each year at the annual conference of the Association for Theatre in Higher Education (ATHE), which will be edited for publication under the mentorship of a distinguished member of the field. The editorial team welcomes your questions, which you may send directly to Facilitating Editor Stephanie Lim at musictheatredancejournal@gmail.com.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers - Volume 37, Issue 1 & 2 (2027) Dear Colleagues, Litera: Journal of Language, Literature and Culture Studies - Dil, Edebiyat ve Kültür Ara?t?rmalar? Dergisi, the official publication of the Department of Western Languages and Literatures at Istanbul University, invites submissions for its 2026 issues (Volume 36, Issues 1 & 2). An open-access, peer-reviewed, and multilingual journal published twice a year (June & December), Litera is indexed in ELSEVIER SCOPUS, Web of Science ESCI, MLA International Bibliography, DOAJ (Directory of Open Access Journals), ERIH PLUS, EBSCO Communication Source, EBSCO Central & Eastern European Academic Source, Gale Cengage and Ulrichsweb. While our core focus remains on literary studies, linguistics, and cultural studies, we welcome interdisciplinary approaches that combine literary and linguistic analysis with insights from cultural theory and media studies-provided they maintain a clear relevance to our aim and scope We welcome original research articles that engage with current debates and critical issues in the study of Western (American, English, French, Belgian, German, Swiss, Austrian, Italian, Spanish, Latin American and Modern Greek) languages, literatures, and cultures. In particular, we encourage contributions that reflect cutting-edge scholarship in areas such as, but not limited to: · Contemporary literary theory · Disability Studies · Human-Animal Studies · Posthumanism and critical posthumanities · Ecofeminism and ecocriticism · Ecosemiotics and Ecolinguistics · Discourse Studies · Intersectional and decolonial approaches · Digital humanities and media theory · Film Studies · Medieval Studies · Posthuman Communication Studies · Gender studies · Narrative and identity in contemporary fiction · Transnationalism and migration literature · Crete studies Submission Windows: · Issue 1 (June 2027): November 1-30, 2026 · Issue 2 (December 2027): May 1-31, 2027 Submission Guidelines: Manuscripts must be original, unpublished, and not under review elsewhere. Re-use of thesis content, dissertations, or previously published conference material is not permitted. All submissions are subject to a double-blind peer reviewprocess. Languages of Publication: English, German, French, Italian, and Spanish No processing or publication fees. Eligibility: Submissions are accepted from authors who hold a PhD. For more information, visit our journal homepage. We look forward to receiving your innovative and thought-provoking research. Sincerely, Editorial Team Litera: Journal of Language, Literature and Culture Studies

items.fullDescription: 2027 marks the 50th anniversary of the film now generally known as Episode IV: A New Hope , the first instalment in the hugely successful Star Wars franchise created by George Lucas. As beloved as it is divisive, Star Wars now straddles multiple decades and generations while proliferating across narrative media (novels, comics, games, animation, TV). It provides a series of compelling case studies in the relationship between creativity and commerce, from the foundation of Lucasfilm during the New Hollywood period to the 21st century Disney-era, and it has developed via a complex interplay between cutting-edge technological innovation, nostalgia, and mythmaking.

items.fullDescription: In her book Bodyminds Reimagined , Sami Schalk asks us “What might it mean to imagine disability differently?” (2) Her work, situated in the exploration of black speculative fiction, engages with (dis)ability studies and black feminism to gesture toward a reimagining of what Margaret Price termed the ‘bodymind’, a concept predicated on “the enmeshment of the mind and body.” (5) How might this enmeshment be understood in the context of chronic conditions, themselves experienced as a direct result of climate change and biomedical violence? My own research has centered...
items.fullDescription: Call For Papers: Brecht in India - Translations, Adaptations, Performances, and Critical Perspectives Overview As a Researcher, with a focus on Kannada literature and performance, I am excited to invite submissions for an edited volume titled Brecht in India: Translations, Adaptations, Performances, and Critical Perspectives. My own research has centered on Bertolt Brecht's reception in Kannada theatre, where I uncovered an impressive 32 translations of his plays into Kannada, spanning from early post-independence efforts to contemporary reinterpretations. These findings highlight Brecht's significant influence on regional Indian theatre, blending his epic techniques with local forms like Yakshagana and modern Kannada drama. Building on this regional insight, I now seek to broaden the scope to a national perspective, gathering original research papers that examine Brecht's transcultural legacy across India's diverse linguistic, cultural, and sociopolitical landscapes. This volume will explore how Brecht's dramaturgy has been adapted to address pan-Indian issues such as caste dynamics, postcolonialism, and globalization, fostering a comprehensive dialogue on his enduring relevance. Rationale My journey into Brecht began with an in-depth study of his works in the Kannada context, revealing not only the 32 translations but also how directors and playwrights like B.V. Karanth and Prasanna have infused Brechtian alienation with indigenous elements to critique social hierarchies. This regional lens has inspired me to investigate Brecht's impact on a national scale, where his epic theatre resonates with India's multifaceted theatrical traditions-from Bengali Jatra to Tamasha . Brecht's emphasis on defamiliarization and sociopolitical engagement aligns closely with Indian folk forms that prioritize presentational styles and community involvement, making his theories particularly adaptable to addressing contemporary challenges like inequality and cultural hybridity. Nationally, Brecht's influence emerged prominently in the post-independence era, influencing Marxist theatre movements in Bengal and beyond, as seen in adaptations by figures like Utpal Dutt and Habib Tanvir. Translations of Brecht into languages such as Hindi, Bengali, and Tamil have democratized access to his works, while intercultural collaborations, including those with directors like Fritz Bennewitz, have enriched Indian performances. This volume aims to expand on such scholarship by compiling diverse perspectives, illuminating how Brecht's legacy contributes to a unified yet varied Indian theatrical identity amid global influences. Themes Contributions should address Brecht's works through a national Indian framework, drawing connections across regions. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: Relevance of Brecht in the Indian Context: Explorations of Brecht's pertinence to national sociopolitical discourses, including intersections with indigenous traditions and their role in shaping postcolonial and modern Indian identities. Translations of Brecht's Works: Analyses of translations across Indian languages (e.g., the 32 Brecht translations in Kannada, alongside those in Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, and others), focusing on linguistic nuances, cultural adaptations, and their impact on broader accessibility. Adaptations of Brechtian Drama: Studies of national adaptations, such as fusions with regional folk forms, reinterpretations by Indian playwrights like Girish Karnad or Badal Sircar, and hybrid productions that incorporate Brecht into pan-Indian narratives. Critical Views of Brechtian Performances in India: Evaluations of performances nationwide, including directorial innovations, audience responses, and critiques of how epic elements and alienation techniques appear in works by groups from various states (e.g., Kannada theatre, Bengali IPTA, or contemporary ensembles). Intercultural Exchanges and Collaborations: Examinations of cross-regional and transnational dialogues and collaborative projects that extend beyond singular linguistic or geographic boundaries. Brecht's Influence on Indian Theatre Movements: Assessments of Brecht's impact upon Indian theatre practices, including feminist, subaltern, and regionally specific perspectives. Comparative Analyses of Reception: Comparative studies of Brecht's reception across Indian languages and cultures that highlight both national commonalities and significant divergences. Submission Guidelines Abstracts: Submit a 300-500 word abstract detailing your proposed chapter, along with a brief bio (100 words) and contact information. Deadline for Abstracts: December 31, 2026. Notification of Acceptance: January 15, 2026. Full Papers: Accepted authors will submit chapters of 6,000- 8,000 words (including references) by February 31, 2027. Format: MLA 9th Edition style; Times New Roman, 12 Font Size, All submissions must be original and not under review elsewhere. Submission Email: Please send materials to brechtinindia@gmail.com with the subject line "CFP: Brecht in India Submission." I particularly welcome contributions from scholars, practitioners, and emerging researchers across India, with an emphasis on diverse regional expertise. Publication Details All accepted papers will undergo a rigorous peer-review process. The volume will be published by a reputable academic publisher to ensure scholarly rigor and global reach. The Publication of the Edited volume is anticipated in mid-2027. For any questions, please contact me at brechtinindia@gmail.com. I look forward to your insights as we collectively map Brecht's national footprint in India. Sincerely, Dr. Raghavendra H K Assistant Professor, Department of English, Jnanabharathi Campus Bangalore University

items.fullDescription: Call for Proposals The editorial and scientific board of the journal Co-herencia invites researchers, professors, and scholars affiliated with national or international institutions to submit proposals for thematic issues/dossiers, and to apply to serve as Guest Scientific Editors for Volume 25, Issue 48 (covering the period January-June 2028). Presentation and Scientific Scope of the Journal Co-herencia Co-herencia is an indexed scientific journal, published biannually, under Diamond Open Access with a CC BY 4.0 license, and edited by the School of Arts and Humanities at EAFIT University. Indexed in major international databases such as Scopus (Arts & Humanities, Q2 SJR), Co-herencia ensures methodological rigor, double-blind peer review, and high ethical publishing standards. The journal is published in Spanish, English, and Portuguese. Published without interruption since 2004, the journal aims to serve as a forum for interdisciplinary discussion on the contributions of the humanities and the arts to the shaping of a thoughtful, critical, and deliberative community. Its scope and thematic axes are concentrated mainly on: Literary Studies: Literary theory; Literary genres; Classical tradition; Hermeneutics; Canon, criticism, and history of literature in the Americas; Writing and orality; Translation; Reception; Literary creation; Semiotics; Editing studies; Journalism and literature; Applied literature. Philosophical Studies: Critical theory and social philosophy; Ethics; Political philosophy; Aesthetics; Epistemology; Philosophy of science and technology; Philosophy of mind; Cosmology; Philosophy of language; Argumentation theory; Rhetoric; Phenomenology; Philosophical hermeneutics; Ontology; Conceptual analysis; History of philosophy. Historical Studies: Historiography; Theory and philosophy of history; Methodology of history; Intellectual history; Conceptual history; Cultural history; Social and political history; History of knowledge; National and Latin American history; Global history; Colonial history; Memory and history; Historical geography and cartography; Imagination, speculation, and historical narratives. Arts: Mediality, transmediality, and intermediality; Creative industries; Musicology; History of music; Material and visual culture; Curatorship and museography; Sociology of the arts; Interartistic relations; Avant-gardes and artistic movements; Canon, criticism, and history of the arts in the Americas. Humanistic Studies in Dialogue with the Social Sciences: Critical discourse analysis; Plain language; Digital humanities; Cultural studies; Research-Creation; Philosophical and historical anthropology; Human geography; Environmental humanities; Medical humanities; Digital humanities; Public humanities; Qualitative analysis of quantitative methods; Clinical sociology; Studies on violence, peace, and reconciliation; Communication studies with a humanistic approach; Gender studies. Requirements for Submitting Proposals In keeping with international editorial best practices in the field of Arts and Humanities (diverse impact, editorial exogamy, international outreach, and analytical rigor), proposals submitted by candidates for guest editors must be presented in a single document (PDF or Word), written in Spanish, English, or Portuguese, and must include, in detail, the following five sections: Title of the thematic issue: it should be concise, clear, conceptually strong, and reflect the central problem to be addressed. Thematic presentation and theoretical grounding (500 to 1,000 words): propose a conceptual delimitation and a definition of the object of study, the core question, or the problematizing axis of the dossier. The proposal should also detail the disciplinary or interdisciplinary frameworks, indicating how the theme and approach engage with the journal's scientific scope. Justification and academic relevance (500 to 1,000 words): include a synthesis of the state of the art and a clear account of the novelty and relevance of the proposal within the contemporary debate in the arts and humanities. This section should ideally state the potential impact and interest the issue will generate within the international research community. Scientific biography of the prospective guest editors: a team of two to three guest editors with diverse institutional affiliations is recommended. For each team member, please indicate: full name, current institutional affiliation, highest academic degree, ORCID iD, and a summary (max. 300 words) of their research lines, ongoing projects, and recent publications in the thematic area of the proposal. List of prospective authors and articles: as evidence of the commitment to attracting original manuscripts, this section of the proposal must list between 3 and 6 potential or pre-invited authors of recognized standing or relevant emerging trajectory for the thematic issue. For each anticipated contribution, please provide: the author's full name, institutional affiliation, tentative article title, and a brief abstract (100-200 words). All manuscripts resulting from the call for the selected proposal must undergo double-blind peer review. Guest editors commit to actively participating in the preselection of manuscripts, suggesting qualified reviewers, and drafting a presentation/introduction for the dossier. Timeline for the Open Call and the Editorial Process Opening of the call for thematic issue proposals: September 1, 2026. Deadline for submission of thematic issue proposals: January 10, 2027. Evaluation of proposals by the scientific board and notification of results: January 25, 2027. Public launch of the call for the selected proposal: January 31, 2027. Deadline for submission of articles for the thematic dossier: May 31, 2027. Peer review and revision process: June-November 2027. Early publication of revised articles: October 2027-January 2028. Copyediting, XML-JATS markup, and digital layout: November 2027-February 2028. Official publication (Vol. 25, No. 48, January-June 2028): February-March 2028. How to Submit Proposals Complete proposals must be submitted electronically to the journal's official email (co-herencia@eafit.edu.co) or processed through the Co-herencia journal's OJS (Open Journal System) platform, attaching the document (PDF or Word) with the required information, using the subject line "Application for Thematic Dossier Vol. 25-48 - [Short title of the proposal]." Contacts for Further Information Editorial team of the journal Co-herencia: coherencia@eafit.edu.co Editorial assistant: Liam Agudelo Calle lagudeloc@eafit.edu.co Editor-in-chief: Andrés Vélez-Posada avelezp6@eafit.edu.co

items.fullDescription: The advancement of artificial intelligence has transformed humanities research and education, deepening computation’s influence on scholarly practice and everyday life. From the early era of “humanities computing” in the 1970s to the rise of “computational humanities” over the past decade, this trajectory highlights the enduring—and expanding—role of computation in shaping inquiry across the humanities. These intersections are especially visible in interdisciplinary work. As T. S. Eliot observes, “Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal; bad poets deface what they take, and good poets make it into something better, or at least something different.” The same spirit can illuminate how methods and tools migrate across fields.

items.location: Howard University · The Gregory J. Hampton Graduate English Student Association at Howard University
items.excerpt: In his seminal and final film Black Is…Black Ain't , the documentarian Marlon Riggs utilizes a pot of gumbo to articulate his thesis that Blackness necessitates an identity built on multiplicity, complication, and depth, a production requiring expansiveness in its sustained attention (Riggs 1995). Such a vision contests and destabilizes narratives...
items.fullDescription: In his seminal and final film Black Is…Black Ain't , the documentarian Marlon Riggs utilizes a pot of gumbo to articulate his thesis that Blackness necessitates an identity built on multiplicity, complication, and depth, a production requiring expansiveness in its sustained attention (Riggs 1995). Such a vision contests and destabilizes narratives depicted within the film that sought to limit Black identities and identifications, and it cuts against the second half of his title, which suggests Blackness in terms of negation, evasion, and minimization. The title to this conference continues a conversation with Riggs and also with Ralph Ellison, Ama Ata Aidoo, Toni Morrison, Stuart Hall, and centuries of international Black thought. By doubling down on the "is" and considering contradictory, harmonious, and contrapuntal accounts of the many ways Blackness is and can be, the Gregory J. Hampton Graduate English Student Association hopes to encourage a maximalist exchange with its conference, being held March 25-26, 2027, as a contemplation of storytelling and its connections to productions and identities of Blackness. We also seek to do commemorative work as we honor the career of Dr. Jimisha Relerford, a graduate of our program and member of the Howard community who passed recently. Her dissertation broke critical ground in its study of Black women's satire. We thus encourage the submission of papers about Black satire, especially Black women's work in the genre. Writers such as Leone Ross, Danzy Senna, Fran Ross, and Zadie Smith, all of whom were discussed in Dr. Relerford's dissertation, utilize satire to comment on and transform notions of Blackness. We hope to continue Dr. Relerford's work by contemplating how storytellers work within this genre to talk about identity. We additionally encourage work on Afrofuturism and speculative Black texts in reference to our organization's namesake, a pillar in Afrofuturist study. In addition to recognizing the intellectual impacts of Drs. Relerford and Hampton, this conference serves as a milestone, marking the tenth conference our organization has hosted in honor of Black literary study. Given Black academia and HBCUs's influence on identity and storytelling around it, we also welcome papers grounded in studies of scholarly impacts on identity as seen in multimodal narratives, productions, protests, and criticism. We additionally invite papers in the following areas that intersect with identity and identification study in story: African Studies African-American Studies Caribbean Studies Disability Studies Ecocriticism and Ecopoetics Diaspora, Ethnicity, and Migration Studies Food Studies Hip Hop Humor Literary History Protest and Rhetoric Queer Studies Television and Film To submit a paper or panel to our conference, please email an abstract of 250-300 words to gesasecretary@gmail.com no later than January 15, 2027. Include in your email, your name, affiliation, contact information, and a brief biographical blurb.

items.location: Faculty of Al-Alsun (Languages), Ain Shams University
items.excerpt: Every act of communication, interpretation, and representation is an act of framing. In literary analysis, a “frame” might define genre, direct narrative perspective, or position a text within a historical moment. In linguistics, frames organize semantic understanding, govern pragmatic interaction, and underpin metaphor. In translation and interpreting, f...
items.fullDescription: Every act of communication, interpretation, and representation is an act of framing. In literary analysis, a “frame” might define genre, direct narrative perspective, or position a text within a historical moment. In linguistics, frames organize semantic understanding, govern pragmatic interaction, and underpin metaphor. In translation and interpreting, frames are negotiated, shifted, and sometimes shattered in the movement between languages and cultures. They are the selective filters that highlight certain elements while relegating others to the background, the conceptual structures that allow us to categorize, interpret, and communicate complex realities.

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS The Politics of Care in Higher Education: Pedagogies, Communities, and Institutional Tensions Eds. Gretta Sayers, Dominique Hétu, and Mousumi Majumder This edited collection offers a timely contribution to the growing body of scholarship on care in higher education (Child & Marvel, 2023; Johnston, 2024; Evans, 2025; Boden et al., 2026). Moving beyond celebratory narratives that romanticize care, treat it as inherently benevolent, or present it as a natural and uncomplicated good, this volume approaches care as a complex and contested practice shaped by institutional structures, power relations, material conditions, and unequal distributions of labour. It examines how care operates simultaneously as a pedagogical ethic, relational practice, and institutional discourse, while foregrounding the tensions and contradictions that emerge in its enactment in higher education. We seek contributions that examine both the transformative possibilities and the political contradictions of care in academic life, engaging urgent concerns surrounding precarity, burnout, institutional rhetoric, and collective responsibility while offering grounded and theoretically rigorous pathways for reimagining academic communities. Guided by an editorial team working across science, arts, and music, the volume approaches care as a question that exceeds disciplinary boundaries and conventional academic forms. We welcome interdisciplinary contributions exploring pedagogies of care in academia as relational, political, ethical, and institutional practices, and particularly encourage critical perspectives attentive to the tensions between care as transformative praxis and care as institutional discourse. In keeping with this interdisciplinary and expansive orientation, we welcome not only scholarly analysis but also contributions that engage pedagogical and institutional questions through research-creation, creative and arts-based methodologies, embodied and relational inquiry, and other forms of knowledge-making attentive to care, reciprocity, and collective responsibility. Possible topics may include, but are not limited to: Communities of Practice, Solidarity, and Collective Care Focus on the relationships, networks, and collective structures through which care is enacted, sustained, and negotiated within and beyond academic institutions. Contributions may critically examine communities of practice, mentorship, solidarity, belonging, and collective responses to precarity, exclusion, and institutional change. Communities of practice as spaces of relational learning and mutual support Collective care and solidarity within academic communities Faculty, staff, student, and intergenerational communities of care Mentorship, sponsorship, and peer-support networks Community-based and grassroots care practices Communities of resistance and alternative academic cultures Care infrastructures within and beyond institutions Transnational, intercultural, and multilingual communities of practice Critical and Decolonial Theorizations of Care Feminist, decolonial, anti-racist, Indigenous, disability, queer, and intersectional approaches to care Care as relational, political, ethical, and collective practice Relational accountability, reciprocity, and responsibility Distinctions and tensions between care, compassion, empathy, wellness, and support Decolonizing care and questioning dominant or universalized understandings of care Care, power, and the politics of recognition and belonging Care, Institutions, and Structural Conditions Who is responsible for care? Institutional accountability and the challenges of "walking the talk" The instrumentalization, depoliticization, or weaponization of care "Care-washing," compassionate governance, and institutional contradictions Structural inequities and institutional barriers to caring practices Equity, accessibility, and accountability in institutional approaches to care Care as institutional discourse, managerial language, or policy framework Labour, Power, and Unequal Expectations of Care Gendered, racialized, colonial, and ableist distributions of care labour Emotional, affective, and relational labour in academia Invisible, undervalued, and uncompensated care work Faculty, staff, and student wellbeing beyond individualized frameworks Burnout, exhaustion, and care fatigue Boundaries, refusal, and care without self-erasure Institutional responsibility and the redistribution of care work Care, academic precarity, workload, and cultures of overextension Precarious labour and the politics of academic support Educational Leadership, Governance, and Institutional Contradictions Focus on educational leadership, governance, and institutional decision-making as sites where commitments to care encounter institutional hierarchies, competing responsibilities, material constraints, and unequal relations of power. The tensions between relational leadership and hierarchical authority Who is expected, authorized, or positioned to make decisions about what counts as care and for whom. Institutional commitments to care alongside austerity, restructuring, precarity, workload intensification, and performance management The contradictions of leaders being asked to enact care while administering policies or decisions that may produce harm Care as institutional responsibility versus the individualization or downward delegation of caring labour Governance, consultation, and participation: whose voices are heard, recognized, or excluded in institutional decisions about care Care, accountability, and evaluation: the challenges of recognizing caring practices without rendering care measurable, performative, or managerial Leadership, refusal, and complicity: the limits of care within institutions whose structures may themselves reproduce inequity Research, Knowledge Production, and Ethical Scholarship Focus on care as an epistemological, methodological, and ethical framework for research and knowledge production. Contributions may explore how care shapes scholarly inquiry, research relationships, academic publishing, and the production, circulation, and validation of knowledge. Collaborative, participatory, and community-engaged research methodologies Communities of practice as sites of collective knowledge production Decolonial, Indigenous, and community-accountable research practices Knowledge production, epistemic justice, and the ethics of listening Care as a research methodology and analytical framework The production, negotiation, and contestation of safe spaces in research and educational contexts Slow scholarship and alternative temporalities of knowledge production Critical and Creative Interventions Arts-based and creative approaches to care Case studies of care-based initiatives and institutional tensions Failures, ambivalences, and unintended consequences of care Pedagogies of refusal, repair, and institutional critique Reimagining academic cultures through justice-oriented and decolonial care Futures of care in higher education We particularly welcome contributions that critically and creatively engage the possibilities and limits of care, foreground questions of equity and justice, and explore the conditions under which pedagogies and communities of practice may foster, constrain, or complicate more accountable, inclusive, and transformative academic cultures. Please submit your detailed abstract (max 500 words, in a .docx or PDF file) to carecommunity@brandonu.ca by Jan. 15, 2027 , along with a bio (250 words). Detailed Abstract Requirements Submissions should include a detailed abstract of up to 500 words outlining the proposed contribution. The abstract should present: its central argument, question, or inquiry; its conceptual or theoretical grounding; its methodological and/or creative approach; the texts, creative works, practices, or other materials on which the contribution will draws. Proposals may also take the form of research-creation projects or involve alternative, multimodal, or community-engaged approaches to knowledge production and dissemination. In such cases, the abstract should clearly describe the proposed form and its relevance to the contribution. Contributions should normally range between 4,000 and 8,000 words. Creative and hybrid contributions that take forms for which word count is not the most appropriate measure are invited to discuss format and length with the editors. Tentative Timeline: Call for chapter proposals: Sept. 1, 2026 Chapter proposals due: Jan. 15, 2027 Initial proposal decisions: Early Feb. 2027 Full chapters due: Sept. 2027 Editorial feedback: Nov. 2027 Revised chapters due: May 2028 Manuscript submitted to the publisher: June 2028 Works Cited Boden, C., et al. items.fullDescription: Punk has never stayed where it was put. Emerging from the economic, political and cultural upheavals of the 1970s, punk became music, style, attitude, subculture, political language and cultural mythology. From London, New York, Sydney, Belfast, Berlin, Tokyo and Jakarta, punk travelled rapidly while taking radically different local forms. It transformed music and fashion, challenged conventions of gender and sexuality, generated distinctive visual and material cultures, and provided a language through which alienation, anger, resistance and belonging could be expressed. Yet punk has also become something it once appeared determined to resist: heritage, commodity and nostalgia. Torn clothing and safety pins entered high fashion. Punk records became collectors' items. Posters and fanzines entered museums and archives. Bands once associated with underground scenes became canonical figures in popular music history. Punk aesthetics circulate through advertising, television, film and social media, while successive generations continue to rediscover, appropriate and reinvent punk. The Popular Culture Research Network (PopCRN) invites proposals for an interdisciplinary conference exploring punk as a major formation in popular culture, from its historical emergence to its contemporary afterlives. The conference asks what happens when punk moves beyond the scene and becomes popular culture. How has punk been represented, remembered, commercialised, institutionalised and reinvented? Who has been included in dominant histories of punk, and who has been marginalised? How do histories of punk change when examined through race, class, gender, sexuality, disability, age, place and nationality? Can punk retain oppositional force once its sounds, images and objects circulate through mainstream culture? Papers might examine punk through music, film, television, fashion, photography, art, literature, comics, performance, celebrity, journalism, advertising, material culture, museums, archives, digital culture, fandom or everyday life. Possible topics include: Origins, scenes and histories: CBGB and New York punk; London and the Sex Pistols; The Clash and political punk; Ramones and the aesthetics of speed and simplicity; Patti Smith and punk poetics; Australian punk and bands such as The Saints and Radio Birdman; local scenes and regional histories; punk behind the Iron Curtain; punk outside Britain and the United States; post punk, hardcore, anarcho punk and other transformations of the form. Race, class and politics: punk and working class identity; unemployment and economic decline; anti establishment politics; Rock Against Racism; punk and anti fascism; race and the whiteness of punk histories; Black punk; Indigenous punk; migration and diaspora; colonialism and postcolonial punk; nationalism and punk; policing, surveillance and censorship; punk as protest. Gender, sexuality and the body: women in punk; Siouxsie Sioux, Poly Styrene, Debbie Harry, Patti Smith and other punk icons; queercore; punk masculinities; Riot Grrrl; sexuality and transgression; beauty, ugliness and bodily refusal; hair, tattoos, piercing and bodily modification; punk ageing and the changing punk body. Fashion, style and material culture: Vivienne Westwood and Malcolm McLaren; bondage trousers, leather jackets, ripped clothing and safety pins; DIY fashion; hairstyles and cosmetics; punk typography and graphic design; album covers; badges and patches; record collecting; fanzines, flyers and posters; punk bedrooms, clubs and record shops; the movement of punk style from the street to the runway. Sound, Performance and the Punk Aesthetic: noise, distortion, speed and brevity; amateurism and anti virtuosity; screaming and vocal performance; three chord aesthetics; live performance; pogoing and moshing; stage violence and confrontation; audience participation; punk humour, obscenity and provocation; the aesthetics of ugliness and deliberate failure. Global Punk: punk in Aotearoa New Zealand, Japan, Indonesia, China, Eastern Europe, Latin America, Africa and the Middle East; punk under authoritarian regimes; Indigenous punk; postcolonial punk; migration and diaspora; translation and localisation; how punk changes as it moves between cultures. Punk on screen: Jubilee (1978); The Great Rock 'n' Roll Swindle (1980); Sid and Nancy (1986); Dogs in Space (1986); The Decline of Western Civilization (1981); This Is England (2006); punk documentaries and biopics; fictional punks; punk television; punk soundtracks; punk as shorthand for danger, rebellion and social disorder. Media, technology and DIY culture: independent labels; pirate and community radio; cassette culture; photocopying and the fanzine; punk photography; alternative publishing; bootlegs; punk journalism; online archives; social media; streaming and the digital rediscovery of punk; DIY culture before and after the internet. Punk, commerce and contradiction: punk and the music industry; selling rebellion; punk in advertising; luxury fashion and punk aesthetics; celebrity punks; authenticity and accusations of selling out; punk merchandise; nostalgia markets; reunion tours; anniversaries and reissues; punk as brand. Punk celebrity: Sid Vicious as punk celebrity; Debbie Harry and celebrity femininity; Johnny Rotten and the transformation of punk notoriety into media celebrity; punk autobiography; celebrity ageing; the punk icon as commodity. Memory, heritage and afterlives: museums and exhibitions; archives and personal collections; punk heritage tourism; oral histories; documentaries and retrospectives; anniversaries; canon formation; forgotten punk histories; ageing punks; intergenerational fandom; the preservation of ephemeral culture; whose punk becomes history? After punk: post punk, goth, hardcore, grunge, emo and alternative music; Riot Grrrl; punk's influence on fashion and visual culture; punk aesthetics in contemporary protest; new global punk scenes; TikTok and punk revivalism; Gen Z encounters with punk; the continuing circulation of DIY and anti establishment cultures. Please submit abstracts (200 words) and author details via our online portal by 31 July 2027. Notification of abstract acceptance is 31 August 2027. Registration is free. The conference is welcoming of early career researchers, postgraduates, Indigenous scholars, people with diverse identities, and industry experts or food practitioners.
